cards.title: Conversational Agents in Augmented Reality: A Systematic Review
cards.meta: 2026 · ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems · doi 10.1145/3815590 · Route C

rows.value: S2CW-C1A1ECB859E747F62BC14515
other
review or meta analysis, framework or design space, failure or counterevidence

A PRISMA systematic review of 44 studies (2007-2025) in which a conversational agent is placed inside an augmented-reality scene and evaluated with human users, from six databases with no date limit. Speech is the input in 42 of 44 and head-mounted displays carry 25; agent-based dialogue management appears in 14 studies, 12 of them published after 2023, and 10 of those 14 run on OpenAI models. Three things are worth carrying. The measurement stops at the encounter: 35 of 44 studies measured attitudes and 32 usability, 26 social presence, 24 any task or performance metric, 15 acceptance and 7 privacy, with 25 of 44 using bespoke questionnaires against 8 uses of the System Usability Scale — and nothing at all measured about the person after the session. The authors say the rest themselves: novelty may inflate engagement, short laboratory studies threaten external validity, most studies compare only against no agent, and the literature's positive tone partly reflects publication bias. And capability is not monotonic: an agent whose context-awareness is inaccurate is trusted less than one that never claimed awareness, and in a language-learning study participants abandoned the agents and read the captions instead.

medium · A competently reported PRISMA 2020 review with a verbatim search string, six databases, no date restriction, three screeners, piloted criteria, consensus decisions, kappa of 0.783 at title and abstract and 0.819 at full text, and a five-item Joanna Briggs quality appraisal applied independently by two researchers with 34 of 44 studies scoring four or more. Four limits. The funnel is oddly reported — 571 citations, 284 excluded at screening, then 38 full texts plus 65 from an update, 59 excluded, 44 included — so the arithmetic of the first stage cannot be reconstructed from the text. The synthesis is narrative, explicitly not a meta-analysis, so every pattern is the authors' reading of 44 heterogeneous studies. The outcome evidence is overwhelmingly self-reported, which the authors themselves flag as the key limitation of the base. And the corpus is small prototypes: cohorts typically 10 to 30, mostly university students, field settings in only six of 44. Carry the counts of what was measured, the named failures and the authors' own account of the evidence base; do not carry any claim that these agents work.

sections.title: 6 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: Order the six things this literature measures by their distance from the moment of use and the counts fall monotonically: attitudes 35, usability 32, social presence 26, any objective task or performance metric 24, intention to adopt 15, privacy 7. There is no seventh category, because nothing here is measured about the person once the session is over. Mapped onto the three measurement families — the encounter, the output, the person afterwards — this corpus is 80% the first, 55% the second and 0% the third, and the instrument counts repeat the pattern: 25 of 44 studies used questionnaires they wrote themselves against 8 uses of the System Usability Scale, 5 of NASA-TLX and 4 each of the Temple Presence Inventory and technology-acceptance scales. That is the same ad-hoc dominance the creativity-support review found across 101 usability assessments. What makes this instance useful is that it comes from a field with no learning vocabulary at all: nobody here claims the agent teaches anything, so the missing family cannot be dismissed as an oversight in an educational literature. It is what happens by default when a support is evaluated.

(PDF p. 23) What the 44 studies measured, in counts — What the 44 studies measured: attitudes or affective appraisals in 35, usability in 32, social presence in 26, concrete task-usage or performance metrics in only 24, technology-acceptance intentions in 15 and privacy perceptions in 7 — which the authors read as roughly half the papers prioritising subjective impressions over objective behavioural evidence, and as evaluation practices that privilege immediate experiential qualities.
quotes: As detailed in Table 11, the distribution of research indicators shows that the evaluative emphasis in the field is skewed toward high-level perceptions of the system, rather than deeper organisational or ethical concerns. Most of the studies (35 of 44) measured participants’ attitudes or other affective appraisals, and 32 studies assessed usability or ease-of-use. This confirms that first-order user satisfaction and system operability continue to dominate the AR-CA research agenda. Measures of social presence were also common, reported in 26 studies, signalling the growing recognition of this construct as a critical determinant of an agent's success, particularly for embodied designs. In contrast, only 24 studies captured concrete task-usage or performance metrics, indicating that roughly half of the papers still prioritise subjective impressions over objective behavioural evidence. Even more strikingly, explicit assessments of technology acceptance intentions appeared in just 15 studies, and privacy perceptions were addressed in a mere seven. Taken together, these frequencies suggest that current evaluation practices privilege immediate experiential qualities, while prospective adoption factors and privacy implications remain comparatively under-examined areas that warrant systematic attention as AR-CA mature toward real-world deployment

rows.value: (PDF p. 23) Instruments: bespoke questionnaires against standardised scales — The instruments: bespoke five- or seven-point questionnaires in 25 papers, semi-structured interviews in eighteen, the System Usability Scale eight times, NASA-TLX five, Temple Presence Inventory variants four, technology-acceptance measures four, and specialised constructs such as trust or working alliance once or twice each, with six studies adding physiological or behavioural sensing — a picture the authors describe as heavy reliance on custom self-report instruments.
quotes: Methodologically, the majority of projects relied on ad-hoc, task-specific questionnaires, often five- or seven-point Likert formats—to capture usability, presence, or acceptance constructs; such bespoke instruments appeared in 25 papers. Semi-structured interviews served as the principal qualitative complement and were reported in eighteen studies. Among standardised instruments, the System Usability Scale (SUS) was most prevalent, appearing eight times, followed by the NASA-TLX workload inventory (five uses) and variants of the Temple Presence Inventory (four uses). Technology-acceptance measures derived from TAM or UTAUT were employed four times, whereas more specialised constructs—trust, working alliance, empathy, simulator sickness, or social connectedness—surfaced only once or twice each. Six studies integrated physiological or behavioural sensing (e.g., eye tracking, electro-dermal activity, heart-rate variability, interpersonal distance) to triangulate subjective data with objective response. The overall picture indicates heavy reliance on custom self-report instruments, moderate uptake of classic usability/workload scales, and relatively sparse adoption of advanced presence, trust, or biosensing measures—suggesting scope for more standardised, multi-modal evaluation protocols in future AR-CA research

rows.value: (PDF p. 22) What UX outcomes are taken to be, and the six indicators — What the review means by an outcome, stated plainly: UX outcomes refer primarily to self-reported perceptions captured under study conditions, coded across six indicators — attitude, usability, social presence, task usage, technology acceptance and privacy — of which social presence and task usage were newly introduced for this review.
quotes: We use “UX outcomes” to refer primarily to self-reported perceptions captured under study conditions. Detailed information is provided in A.2: Participant information, data collection tools and findings. In our systematic review of 44 articles, 23 employed quantitative methods, 21 used qualitative methods, and 28 adopted a mixed-methods approach combining both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. To further investigate the dimensions used to measure user experience in these papers, we expanded the existing indicators and added new ones based on the study by Harrington et al. [41]. We coded the studies based on the following research indicators: attitude, usability, social presence, task usage, technology acceptance, and privacy. Attitude examined self-reported beliefs such as perception, willingness to use, and enjoyment. Usability focused on metrics related to the system's performance (e.g., efficiency, satisfaction, ease of use, effectiveness, or learnability). Social presence primarily assessed the effectiveness of CAs in terms of their human-like characteristics [101], such as anthropomorphism, conversational capability, and embodied representation. Task usage looked at user data related to task execution, such as usage frequency, duration, task completion speed, accuracy, and task load. Technology acceptance explored users' acceptance of the technology, their willingness to continue using it, and their likelihood of recommending it. Privacy examined concerns related to privacy, trust, or credibility

rows.value: (PDF p. 23) Participants across the 44 studies — The participants: cohorts typically 10 to 30 with a median near twenty, a few pilots as small as two and field surveys up to eighty, recruitment dominated by university students aged 18 to 35, gender imbalances common, and field settings limited to six healthcare or safety-training deployments with the remainder in laboratory or classroom conditions.
quotes: Across the 44 empirical studies reviewed, participant cohorts were generally modest in size, typically ranging from 10 to 30 individuals with a median near twenty; only a handful of investigations employed very small laboratory pilots (e.g., n = 2) or larger field surveys (up to n = 80). Recruitment was dominated by university student populations in the 18‑to‑35‑year age bracket, although notable exceptions included pre‑school children (4–8 years) in language‑learning experiments, middle‑aged or senior adults in professional health‑care scenarios, and special‑needs groups such as children on the autism spectrum or patients undergoing physiotherapy. Gender distribution tended to be mixed, but imbalances were common: several studies reported strongly male‑skewed technical samples, whereas at least three health‑oriented trials were overwhelmingly female. Field settings were comparatively rare, limited to six health‑care or safety‑training deployments; the remainder were conducted under laboratory or classroom conditions

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The authors have assembled, in pieces and without ever putting them together, a complete argument against reading their own headline finding at face value. The abstract says user experience reports are broadly positive. The paper then says: novelty may inflate engagement and nobody knows whether it lasts; the studies are short and in laboratories, which threatens external validity and the persistence of the effects; most comparisons are against having no agent at all rather than against an alternative; the outcomes are post-hoc questionnaires capturing perception rather than behaviour and are exposed to recall bias and demand characteristics; samples are small and mostly students; and the peer-reviewed base is biased toward publishable successes. Against the two-part test all 44 studies fail both halves — the measurement is taken during the session and inside the arrangement that delivers it — and this review is unusual in stating as much itself, instructing the reader to treat the positive patterns as perceptions under study conditions. The gap is not in the caveats. It is that no study exists that would settle the question, and the review's own recommendation for future work asks for longitudinal in-the-wild deployment rather than for a measurement after the agent is switched off.

(PDF p. 25) Novelty, and whether the engagement would last — The novelty caveat, in the authors' words: some observed engagement may partly reflect a novelty effect associated with new technology, it remains unclear whether such responses would be sustained over longer-term use, and engagement is inherently subjective since what one user finds supportive another finds distracting — pointing to a need for personalisation in timing, frequency and style that most current systems do not address.
quotes: In some studies, these more favourable affective responses were also accompanied by greater behavioural engagement, such as users speaking more frequently or for longer with a more expressive agent. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Some of the observed engagement may partly reflect a novelty effect associated with new technology, and it remains unclear whether such responses would be sustained over longer-term use. In addition, engagement is inherently subjective: what one user finds supportive or entertaining may be distracting to another. This suggests a need for greater personalisation in the timing, frequency, and style of agent interaction, which most current systems do not yet address

rows.value: (PDF p. 34) Methodological gaps across the 44 studies — The methodological gaps, stated by the authors: small samples constraining statistical power, imbalanced demographics, and above all reliance on short-term laboratory experiments as a major threat to external validity — raising questions about the long-term persistence of the observed effects, with novelty often cited as a confound that may inflate engagement, and with many studies comparing their system only to a no-agent baseline rather than to another strategy or over realistic durations.
quotes: Finally, the scientific evaluation of these systems suffers from several recurring methodological limitations. Many studies are conducted with small sample sizes, which constrains statistical power and limits the certainty of the findings [1,8,70,82,116]. Many also suffer from imbalanced demographics, particularly regarding gender [1]. The reliance on short-term, laboratory-based experiments is a major threat to the external validity of the research. This approach raises questions about the long-term persistence of the observed effects and their generalisability to the complexities of real-world contexts [58]. The novelty of the technology itself is often cited as a potential confounding factor that may inflate user engagement in the short term [75]. To advance the field, there is a clear need for more robust, longitudinal, and comparative evaluations. Many studies compare their novel system only to a “no agent” baseline. More work is needed that directly compares different advanced strategies against one another and evaluates systems over realistic durations of use

Additionally, some of the included studies had small sample sizes [54,62,70,82], which constrains statistical power and limits the generalisability of study-level conclusions. Moreover, the heterogeneity of devices, tasks, contexts, and outcome measures limited our ability to quantitatively aggregate effects; accordingly, we adopted a narrative synthesis approach rather than meta-analysis. Where findings diverged across studies, we interpreted them as conditional on contextual factors (e.g., device form factor, coupling with AR context, and study setting) and report them as patterns and trade-offs rather than universal effects

rows.value: (PDF p. 1) Abstract — The review in one paragraph: 44 peer-reviewed studies from 2007 to 2025, speech the predominant input at 95%, head-mounted displays most frequent at 66%, 41% coupling speech with contextual information, agent-based architectures powered by large language models with 12 of the 14 published after 2023, and user experience reports broadly positive but limited by long-term engagement, privacy risk and hardware.
quotes: We conducted a systematic review of 44 peer-reviewed studies (2007–2025) using predefined search and screening procedures. Across the included systems, speech is the predominant input modality (95%), and head- mounted displays (HMDs) are most frequently used (66%). Many prototypes couple speech with contextual information such as location or object recognition (41%) to adapt conversational behaviour. We also observed a strong trend in dialogue management toward agent-based architectures powered by Large Language Models, with 12 of the 14 agent-based systems being published after 2023. Our analysis resulted in the development of a framework for AR- CA interaction, which positions systems along two dimensions: Presence Form and Context Awareness. The framework reveals an emerging trend toward dynamic, context-aware interaction. User experience reports are broadly positive, but limitations include challenges with long-term engagement, privacy risks, and hardware constraints

This approach raises questions about the long-term persistence of the observed effects and their generalisability to the complexities of real-world contexts [58]. To advance the field, there is a clear need for more robust, longitudinal, and comparative evaluations. Many studies compare their novel system only to a “no agent” baseline. items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: Three statements in this review say, from three directions, that more capable support is not monotonically better support. The first is abandonment: in a language-learning study the agent and the live captions competed for attention and participants ended up reading the captions and ignoring the agents — a support that was present, functioning, and simply not used, which is a category the corpus has little else in. The second is an inversion of trust: an agent that claims to understand the situation and gets it wrong ends up trusted less than an agent that never claimed to, and the authors generalise it to the class — when sensors are inaccurate or responses lag, trust collapses more severely than with simpler systems. The third is the usability curve: for a simple task the plain system is easiest, context-awareness pays as the task gets harder, and a badly implemented advanced feature leaves the system worse than the baseline it was meant to improve. The practical consequence is that the choice to add capability carries a downside branch whose size depends on reliability, and reliability is exactly what the hardware section of this review says the field does not have.

rows.value: A key challenge reported was information overload. In a language-learning study [8], the virtual agents and the live captions competed for the user's attention. Many participants ended up just reading the captions and ignoring the agents... One study [1] compared an aware agent with a unaware agent and found that while the aware agent was trusted, the unaware one was the distrust by users. This suggests that providing inaccurate or unreliable contextual feedback can be more damaging to user trust than providing no contextual feedback at all... Yet, their effectiveness is fragile; when sensors are inaccurate or responses lag, user trust collapses more severely than with simpler systems... But, if these advanced features are poorly implemented—for example, with inaccurate speech recognition—the system can become harder to use than the simple baseline.

rows.value: (PDF p. 21) Inaccurate awareness is worse than no awareness — A capability that inverts: aware agents generally outperform unaware ones but are vulnerable to tracking errors that undermine confidence, and in the one head-to-head comparison the aware agent was trusted while the unaware one was distrusted, which the authors read as inaccurate or unreliable contextual feedback being more damaging to trust than no contextual feedback at all.
quotes: confidence, such as tracking errors that cause a mismatch between the real and virtual worlds. This highlights an important condition: the agent's awareness must be accurate and reliable. One study [1] compared an aware agent with a unaware agent and found that while the aware agent was trusted, the unaware one was the distrust by users. This suggests that providing inaccurate or unreliable contextual feedback can be more damaging to user trust than providing no contextual feedback at all

rows.value: (PDF p. 29) Fragility of the more capable agents — The fragility finding: context-aware agents achieve demonstrably higher social presence, trust and task efficiency, yet their effectiveness is fragile — when sensors are inaccurate or responses lag, user trust collapses more severely than with simpler systems, leaving designers with the problem of deciding if and when to act so that assistance is timely and helpful without being intrusive.
quotes: efficiency. Yet, their effectiveness is fragile; when sensors are inaccurate or responses lag, user trust collapses more severely than with simpler systems. This creates a unique situation for designers: deciding if and when to act so that assistance is timely and helpful without being intrusive

rows.value: (PDF p. 25) The usability curve — The usability curve: basic technical problems — speech-to-text errors, gesture difficulty, controller and camera failures, long response times, instability, ambient noise — hold these systems back, and for simple tasks a basic system is easiest while context-awareness becomes valuable as the task gets more complex.
quotes: However, the usability of these systems is often held back by basic technical problems. Frustration from speech-to-text errors or difficulties with the hand gestures required by AR headsets are common complaints. Additional usability and robustness issues were also reported across several studies. These included problems with controllers [82], camera recognition [70], long voice response times [103], overly complex system behaviour [18,102], system instability [115], and limited types of feedback [65]. Ambient noise was also found to interfere with system use [38], further reducing interaction quality and overall usability. This suggests a “Usability Curve” for AR agents: for simple tasks, a basic system is often the easiest to use. As the task gets more complex, advanced features like context-awareness become more valuable

rows.value: (PDF p. 33) The integration gap between language and avatar — What large language models cost: two to three seconds of latency making one system unsuitable for rapid tasks, up to five seconds on weak networks, output sometimes vague and effectiveness dependent on the user's ability to formulate precise questions — a new user burden of prompt engineering — and an integration gap in which nuanced language is delivered by avatars with minimal expressivity, breaking social realism.
quotes: The integration of LLMs, while powerful, introduces a new set of technical and experiential challenges. Latency is a critical issue. The 2-3 second interaction latency reported for the system [69], largely attributable to the LLM processing time, renders it unsuitable for tasks requiring rapid performance. Similar performance issues and latency were noted in this study [51], and the reliance on cloud-based models creates a strong dependency on high-quality wireless networks, where weak signals can cause response delays of up to 5 seconds [48]. The quality of LLM-generated content can also be uneven. The chatbot in this 2025 study [75] was sometimes perceived as vague, and its overall effectiveness was highly dependent on the user's ability to formulate precise and effective questions. This points to a new form of user burden: the need for “prompt engineering” to elicit the desired information. Furthermore, an “Integration Gap” is emerging between the linguistic sophistication of LLMs and the expressive capabilities of the avatars that deliver their output. quotes: The benefits of rich embodiment, however, are not absolute and appear to be contingent on the user's primary task. While embodied, expressive agents consistently score higher on metrics like social presence and engagement [58,86,97], a counter-narrative emerges around task-specific utility. For instrumental tasks where the user's attention need be focused on the real world, such as a complex assembly procedure or reading text, a visually rich agent can become a source of cognitive or visual interference. This is supported by findings that a disembodied voice may be superior for tasks with high visual load [37]. In sum, embodiment in AR-CA follows an evolutionary arc—from disembodied to fixed avatars to fully situated actors—and each step upward in corporeality affords richer social presence at the cost of greater technical and attentional overhead. Disembodied agents excel when visual bandwidth remain uncompromised; fixed embodiments add relational cues that boost engagement in tutoring and coaching; situated agents unlock compelling perceptions of awareness and trust but demand sophisticated hardware and risk overloading users whose primary task is not social. This embodiment-utility trade-off underscores a central HCI design imperative: the agent’s physical form should be matched not to technological aspiration alone but to the attentional profile of the task, the sensory context of the device, and the cognitive bandwidth of the user

quotes: Where non-context-aware agents prove the importance of an embodiment and simple interaction, context-aware agents demonstrate that relevance and adaptive behaviour are what drive deeper engagement and performance. Despite these benefits, physical hardware remains a major problem, with frequent complaints about bulky headsets, limited field of view, and poor battery life [48]. Instead of building a highly complex agent, it appears that it can be more effective to identify and configure a single critical contextual cue for a given task, such as location for a tourism app or gaze for a hands-on task. items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: Contingency is the load-bearing word in this review, and it means something with a horizon of one turn. A system qualifies as conversational because it produces outputs contingent on the user's input; a system is excluded for non-contingent output. That is contingency on the last utterance, not on what the person can do. The second sense has no vocabulary here at all: across 56 pages scaffold, fading, withdraw, Vygotsky, transfer and self-regulation are each zero, and the sole occurrence of the substring fade is the folding artefact inside of a device. Nor is there a model of the person: the only user model in the corpus is Satori's Belief-Desire-Intention model, which infers what the user is trying to do, not what they are able to do, and the review's own tally of what agents perceive lists object location, appearance, body movement, gaze, physiology and other people's faces — the scene, never the competence. Initiative stays with the person in 19 of 25 context-aware cases and with the agent in 6, of which only two are genuinely proactive. So this is a literature that has borrowed the scaffolding tradition's central word for the property of taking turns, while modelling everything about the user's situation and nothing about the user's ability.

For the purposes of this review, we apply an operational definition of CAs in AR as systems that support two-way conversational exchange with users in an AR environment. This definition includes rule-based chatbots, LLM-driven agents, embodied avatars, and multimodal assistants, provided that the system engages in turn-taking and produces outputs contingent on the user’s input. In other words, a system was considered conversational not because of any specific input modality, embodiment, or underlying architecture, but because it responded to what the user said or did in an interactionally meaningful way

rows.value: (PDF p. 6) Contingent response as the inclusion criterion — The screening rule that follows from the definition: 571 citations, three researchers, two stages, and an exclusion of one-way systems that deliver information without generating responses contingent on user input — with the criterion resting on the presence of contingent responses rather than on the input modality, so constrained-input systems that still take turns were kept.
quotes: Our initial database search yielded 571 citations. After removing duplicates, three researchers conducted a two-stage manual screening process based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria shown in Table 2. We defined “conversational” interaction as a two-way exchange where the system responds to what the user says or does (i.e., turn-taking). We therefore excluded one-way systems that deliver information without generating responses contingent on user input (e.g., scripted monologues or broadcast-style guidance), regardless of whether the interface used speech, touch, or other inputs. Some included systems used constrained inputs (e.g., buttons or predefined options) but still supported turn-taking; our exclusion criterion was based on the presence of contingent responses, not on the input modality

rows.value: (PDF p. 21) Proactive assistance, the two systems that attempt it — The two proactive systems, both from 2025: Satori used a user model to guess the user's goals and provide guidance rated as timely and effective as a human expert's, and SocialMind acted as a real-time social coach with 95% of participants willing to use it and many reporting reduced mental workload when they felt stuck — with the authors noting that proactivity requires a delicate balance and that some participants were uncomfortable talking with someone they knew was being helped by an AI.
quotes: Proactive agents are the most advanced systems in this review, as they actively offer help without waiting for a user's command. This shows how CAs are evolving from simple tools into true assistants. The key studies, “Satori” [69] and “SocialMind” [117] were both published in 2025 and focus on everyday life, representing the current state of the art. The “Satori” system used a user model to guess the user's goals and provide proactive guidance. Its help was found to be as timely and effective as that from a human expert. Similarly, “SocialMind” acted as a real-time social coach during live conversations. The results were notable, with 95% of participants willing to use the system and many reporting that it reduced their mental workload, helping them when they felt stuck

rows.value: (PDF p. 22) How the two proactive systems decide when to help — How the two proactive systems decide when to intervene: Satori runs a Belief-Desire-Intention user model over a multimodal GPT-4V back-end, detecting task-step completion and showing an upfront confirmation screen so users can veto wrongly inferred goals; SocialMind intervenes mid-utterance from a cache of social-factor templates or a two-second speech stream, refreshing at most every three seconds — and both papers acknowledge their prediction models remain imperfect.
quotes: Both “Satori” and “SocialMind” address the critical “when to help” dilemma by using LLM-powered forecasting to time their interventions, though they operate at different granularities. “Satori” intervenes at the task-action boundary. It employs a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) user model with a multimodal GPT- 4V back-end, using an early detection system to provide guidance the moment a task step is completed. To prevent premature interruptions, it also presents an upfront confirmation screen, allowing users to veto incorrectly inferred goals before the agent proceeds. In contrast, “SocialMind” is tuned for the faster pace of live conversation and intervenes mid-utterance. It first attempts a rapid response by checking a social- factor-aware cache of pre-generated templates. If no match is found, it streams 2-second speech snippets to an LLM to infer the speaker's intent in real-time, refreshing its suggestions no more than once every three seconds to avoid overwhelming the user. Both studies candidly acknowledge that their prediction models remain imperfect and are still constrained by hardware capacity and real-time processing limitations

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: Two boundary conditions here are not visible anywhere else in this corpus. The first is that part of the cost of the support is paid by people who are not using it. Ninety-five per cent of participants would use the real-time social coach themselves; only about eighty per cent would talk to someone who was using one. Users felt self-conscious speaking to an agent in public. Privacy concern extends explicitly to bystanders, whose surroundings an always-on head-worn camera captures and who never consented. Every other support in this review is judged by the person holding it; this one has an acceptability that third parties partly determine, which generalises to any support that is worn, spoken to, or visible in shared space. The second is a boundary the authors name and cannot locate: these systems are meant to augment rather than replace human capability, and the evidence they cite for the boundary existing is that an agent could not fully substitute for a teacher and that some patients preferred a real person. That is a limit discovered by users declining the substitution, not a limit designed in. Nothing in the 44 systems specifies what the agent should decline to do.

cards.title: Empowering patient autonomy: The role of large language models (LLMs) in scaffolding informed consent in medical practice

rows.value: other
concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle, measurement or method

A philosophical article in Bioethics arguing that large language models could operationalise Wilkinson and Levy's scaffolded model of autonomy in medical informed consent. It matters to this review for one reason above all others: it is a full-strength statement of a second scaffolding tradition that owes nothing to Vygotsky. Its scaffolds come from distributed cognition and the extended mind, and its central claim is that epistemic scaffolds are not helpful additions to an otherwise independent process but are constitutive of autonomy itself. Across eleven pages the word scaffold appears 46 times and Vygotsky, zone of proximal development, fading, fade, withdraw and contingent appear zero times. The authors then meet the dependence objection head on, name it autonomy atrophy, cite GPS and Plato on writing, and reject the criterion this review is built around: the key question, they say, is not whether unsupported capabilities diminish but whether the integrated system of human plus technological support produces better outcomes, so some loss of unaided ability may be an acceptable trade-off. They also state a measurement problem worth carrying everywhere: if a support works, decisions change, and if it manipulates, decisions change, so outcome differences cannot tell the two apart. They propose five process metrics instead and build none of them. No system was built, no patient was studied, and the data availability statement records that no data were generated or analysed.

medium · As philosophy this is careful, well-sourced work by authors who wrote the model they are extending, published in a peer-reviewed bioethics journal, and it anticipates its own objections better than most. As evidence about supports it carries nothing: no system was built, no patient or clinician was studied, and the data availability statement says no data sets were generated or analysed. Every design proposal, every failure mode and every safeguard is asserted, and the paper is honest that the capability questions it raises remain empirical ones requiring investigation. The claims to carry at strength are the conceptual and methodological ones, which are about arguments rather than outcomes: what this tradition means by scaffolding, why its authors think unaided performance is the wrong criterion, and why a change in decisions cannot discriminate between a support working and a support steering. Treat the four-phase consent framework, the cultural adaptation proposals and the five evaluation metrics as designs awaiting a first test. Note also that the paper's own model is the subject of its argument, which gives it a stake in the conclusion.

sections.title: 6 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A second scaffolding tradition, stated at full strength by philosophers who built the model, and it owes nothing to developmental psychology. Its sources are distributed cognition and the extended mind, its examples are maps and calculators rather than a tutor's prompts, and its central move is that dependence on external epistemic structure is not a deficit to be worked off but part of what makes a decision the person's own. The consequence for this review is precise. In the developmental sense a scaffold is temporary, pitched at what the person cannot yet do alone, and withdrawn as competence grows; on that account removing it is the test of whether it worked. In this sense a scaffold is permanent and partly constitutive, so removing it does not reveal an ability underneath, it removes an ability. The counts make the split visible rather than rhetorical: across eleven pages scaffold appears 46 times while Vygotsky, zone of proximal development, fading, fade, withdraw and contingent appear zero times. That is not an oversight in a paper of this care. It is what the theory entails, and any synthesis that treats every use of the word as one construct will merge two positions that disagree about the thing the review most wants to know.

rows.value: Wilkinson and Levy claim that these scaffolds are not merely helpful additions to an otherwise independent process, but rather actively shape our cognitive processes and are therefore constitutive of genuine autonomy itself. ... Just as physical scaffolding provides necessary support for construction, epistemic and social scaffolding promotes autonomous decision-making by supporting understanding, deliberation, and value application.

quotes: The model of “scaffolded autonomy” proposed by Wilkinson and Levy goes beyond relational accounts by recognizing our “epistemic dependence” on others in decision‐making to help us understand and apply our values to complex choices [1]. Just as physical scaf- folding provides necessary support for construction, epistemic and social scaffolding promotes autonomous decision‐making by supporting understanding, deliberation, and value application

rows.value: (PDF p. 1) Abstract, the scaffolded model — The abstract's statement of the model: traditional autonomy emphasises independence and epistemic individualism, recent philosophical work says autonomous decisions are inherently dependent on epistemic and social supports, and Wilkinson and Levy's scaffolded model shows everyday decisions relying on distributed cognition and on epistemic scaffolding from consulting others to using maps or calculators.
quotes: The principle of (respect for) patient autonomy has traditionally emphasized independence in medical decision‐making, reflecting a broader commitment to epistemic individualism. However, recent philosophical work has challenged this view, suggesting that autonomous decisions are inherently dependent on epistemic and social supports. Wilkinson and Levy's “scaffolded model” of autonomy demonstrates how our everyday decisions rely on distributed cognition and various forms of epistemic scaffolding—from consulting others to using technological aids like maps or calculators

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Introduction, individualism as the target — The position being argued against: a Western individualistic conception of autonomy emphasising independence, under which a language model looks like an unwelcome layer between the patient's authentic self and their decision.
quotes: Medical ethics has been shaped by a distinctly Western, indi- vidualistic conception of autonomy that emphasizes indepen- dence in decision‐making [3, 4]. The informed consent process emerged as the primary mechanism for operationalizing respect for autonomy. Those who hold individualistic accounts em- phasize an agent's capacity to reflect on and identify with their motivations, acting on desires that one reflectively endorses [5–7]. Yet, when it comes to medical decisions, the formal consent process typically centers on patients making indepen- dent choices based primarily on a single conversation with their doctor

The developmental sense of scaffolding names a temporary support, calibrated to what the learner cannot yet do alone, that is withdrawn as competence grows. The sense used here comes from distributed cognition and the extended mind, and it names a permanent external structure that partly constitutes the capacity it supports; on that account removing it does not reveal an underlying ability, it destroys the ability. items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the case against the review's own central question, argued rather than assumed, and it deserves to be quoted rather than paraphrased. The authors name the worry precisely, autonomy atrophy, illustrate it with GPS and way-finding, trace it to Socrates on writing in the Phaedrus, and conclude that the unit of evaluation should be the person plus the tool, not the person alone. Two things bound it. The example does the work and the example is unusually favourable: writing is durable, universally available, inspectable, does not change its answer and cannot be withdrawn by a supplier, none of which holds for a consent system that may be offline, updated, discontinued or simply wrong. So the argument shows that capability loss is acceptable when the external resource is reliably present, which is a condition, and the paper does not test that condition for its own case. And the authors then concede the point they have just argued against, saying physicians will probably have to keep some basic competence unaided, without naming which, at what level, or how it would be maintained once routine explanation has been delegated. The requirement is stated and left unbuilt in the same section that says it does not matter.

rows.value: The key question is not whether these specific capabilities might diminish, but whether the integrated system of human plus technological support enables better outcomes. ... If LLMs can help create more thorough understanding, better value-aligned choices, and more authentic consent processes, then some reduction in our ability to perform these tasks without technological assistance may be an acceptable trade-off for improved supported decision-making. ... That said, it seems likely that physicians will be required to maintain some basic competencies without technological support.

(PDF p. 8) Section 3.2, autonomy atrophy named — Autonomy atrophy named: reliance on the support might gradually diminish physicians' confidence in evaluating consent without it and patients' ability to process medical information independently, as GPS is said to weaken natural way-finding.
quotes: A related concern might be raised about what we might call “autonomy atrophy”—the possibility that reliance on LLM sup- port could gradually diminish both physicians' and patients' native capabilities in the consent process. Just as GPS navigation might weaken natural way‐finding abilities, extensive reliance on LLMs for medical consent might reduce physicians' confidence in eval- uating consent without technological support or patients' abilities to process medical information independently

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) Section 3.2, Plato on writing — The historical answer offered: Socrates in the Phaedrus argued writing would produce forgetfulness because learners would not practise memory, and history shows the benefits of writing as external memory far outweighed any loss, expanding collective cognitive capability.
quotes: This concern mirrors a much older debate about technolog- ical augmentation of human capabilities. In Plato's Phaedrus, Socrates argues against the technology of writing itself, claiming that it would lead to the atrophy of memory and genuine understanding. He warns that writing would create “forgetfulness in the minds of those who learn to use it, because they will not practice their memory. Their trust in writing, produced by external characters which are no part of themselves, will discourage the use of their own memory within them” [51]. Yet, history has thoroughly demonstrated that the benefits of writing as an external memory system far outweigh any reduction in individual memorial capabilities. The technology of writing has not weakened human thinking—rather, it has dramatically expanded our collective cognitive capabilities by allowing us to build on and engage with recorded knowledge in ways that would be impossible through memory alone

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) Section 3.2, the trade-off accepted — The trade-off accepted explicitly: some reduction in the ability to explain procedures, work through risks or structure information without technological support may be more than compensated for, and the key question is not whether those capabilities diminish but whether the integrated human-plus-technology system produces better outcomes.
quotes: Similarly, while LLM assistance might indeed lead to some reduction in physicians' and patients' abilities to communicate complex medical information without technological support— such as explaining technical procedures in accessible language, systematically working through risks and benefits, or structur- ing information in easily digestible ways—this may be more than compensated for by the enhanced ability to support better overall decision‐making when the technology is available. The key question is not whether these specific capabilities might diminish, but whether the integrated system of human plus technological support enables better outcomes. Research already shows that healthcare professionals generally lack proper consent training and supervision [52, 53]. If LLMs can help create more thorough understanding, better value‐aligned choices, and more authentic consent processes, then some reduction in our ability to perform these tasks without tech- nological assistance may be an acceptable trade‐off for im- proved supported decision‐making

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) Section 3.2, the retained floor of unaided competence — The floor conceded: physicians will likely be required to maintain some basic competencies without technological support, much as basic arithmetic is still taught despite calculators and basic navigation despite GPS.
quotes: That said, it seems likely that physicians will be required to maintain some basic competencies without technological sup- port. The goal should be to develop implementation frame- works that leverage LLM capabilities while maintaining core human skills—much as we continue to teach basic arithmetic despite the ubiquity of calculators or basic navigation despite GPS availability

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) Section 3.2, the empirical questions left open — The open empirical questions the authors set and do not answer: how integration affects physicians' development of consent-related skills, whether it enhances or diminishes their ability to recognise coercion or undue influence, and how it affects confidence and competence in ethically complex cases.
quotes: Moreover, concerns about potential impacts on physician capabilities remain empirical questions requiring investigation. Rather than assuming skill degradation, we need research ex- amining how technological support affects physicians' capabil- ities over time. It is possible that LLM assistance could actually enhance physicians' abilities by providing consistent models of good consent practices, or by freeing up cognitive resources to focus on more nuanced aspects of patient interaction. The key research questions include the following: How does LLM inte- gration affect physicians' development of consent‐related skills? Does technological support enhance or diminish physicians' ability to recognize subtle forms of coercion or undue influ- ence? How might LLM assistance impact physicians' confidence and competence in handling ethically complex consent sce- narios? Future studies should examine these outcomes as LLMs are implemented in clinical settings

Having argued that unaided ability is the wrong criterion, the authors concede that physicians will probably need to keep some basic competence without the system, and then say nothing about which competences, at what level, how they would be maintained once routine information delivery has been delegated, or how anyone would know they had eroded. items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A measurement problem that reaches well past consent. Whenever a support is meant to improve a judgement rather than to speed a task, the observable signature of the support working and the observable signature of it steering are identical: the person's decisions change. An outcome comparison against an unsupported group therefore cannot discriminate between the two, which means a large part of the evaluation literature on decision supports is measuring something that does not answer the question it was asked. The authors' response is to move evaluation to the process, and their Box 3 list is more useful than most: alignment between the choice and previously expressed values, stability of the choice on reconsideration, retention of the key decision factors immediately and after a delay, the patient's sense of ownership, and their ability to explain the choice in their own terms. Two of those, retention after a delay and articulating the rationale unaided, are support-removed measures, which is worth noting in a paper that has argued unaided performance is the wrong criterion. None of the five is defined operationally, validated, or tried. It is an agenda, and it is the right agenda.

rows.value: Any observed differences in decision patterns between scaffolded and unscaffolded choices cannot straightforwardly be interpreted as evidence of problematic steering. Indeed, if the scaffolding is working as intended (i.e., helping patients better understand their options and more effectively align choices with their values), we would expect to see systematic differences in decision patterns... The critical question, therefore, is not whether LLM scaffolding influences decisions, but whether it does so in ways that support rather than undermine authentic choice.

One possible approach would be to compare decision patterns between LLM‐scaffolded and traditional unscaffolded consent processes. If systematic differ- ences emerge in treatment choices between these two groups, this might seem to indicate problematic steering by the LLM system. However, this comparative approach presents a complex methodological challenge. Any observed differences in deci- sion patterns between scaffolded and unscaffolded choices cannot straightforwardly be interpreted as evidence of prob- lematic steering. Indeed, if the scaffolding is working as intended (i.e., helping patients better understand their options and more effectively align choices with their values), we would expect to see systematic differences in decision patterns (Box 2). Information retention: Evaluating patients’ under- standing of key decision factors both immediately and after a delay. 4. If systematic differ- ences emerge in treatment choices between these two groups, this might seem to indicate problematic steering by the LLM system. However, this comparative approach presents a complex methodological challenge. Any observed differences in deci- sion patterns between scaffolded and unscaffolded choices cannot straightforwardly be interpreted as evidence of prob- lematic steering. Indeed, if the scaffolding is working as intended (i.e., helping patients better understand their options and more effectively align choices with their values), we would expect to see systematic differences in decision patterns (Box 2). These differences could reflect enhanced rather than compro- mised decision‐making

rows.value: medium · The impossibility argument is sound as stated and the proposed replacement is untested, undefined operationally, and partly circular against the failure mode the paper itself identifies.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The most distinctive failure mode in the paper and the one least represented elsewhere in this corpus. A support built to help you apply your values can prevent you from forming them, because the questions it asks and the order it asks them in already propose an answer to the thing being settled. The concrete mechanism given is good: a value-clarification exercise that sequences its prompts a particular way implicitly suggests a trade-off rate between length of life and quality of it, which is precisely the judgement the patient was there to make. This is a hazard specific to supports for value-laden choices rather than for accuracy, and it is invisible to the usual instruments, because a patient whose preferences were formed by the interface will report that the decision matched their values and that they owned it. The paper's other named failure modes belong on the same list and are more familiar: click-through habituation, where a consent dialogue becomes a procedural hurdle like terms and conditions; automation bias, deference to the system as more objective than one's own judgement; and blindness to distress in a text-only channel, which removes the cue a clinician uses to decide that a person needs more help. All are asserted. None is measured.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The single most transferable sentence in the paper, and a design-space axis this review should carry. A new support never enters an empty space. The person already has family, colleagues, notes, written materials, previous conversations and other professionals, and the question a design has to answer is whether it adds to that set or quietly replaces it. The paper's own proposals show what supporting rather than screening off means concretely: translating a technical explanation so the patient can take it to their family, generating discussion guides for those conversations, helping the patient reconcile what different advisers said. The opposite design absorbs those conversations into the interface, and the patient ends up better informed and more alone. The reason this matters for evaluation is that displacement is invisible to a comparison against nothing: the tool and the supports it displaced produce the same measured outcome, so a study finding that supported patients understand more cannot tell whether the network around them shrank. The claim is a design recommendation with no implementation and no test, and it names a failure mode that the field's standard evaluation cannot see.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: Two moves worth keeping. The first is the comparator: the baseline for a support is current practice, not an idealised unsupported person, and current practice here is a clinician whose framing is unrecorded, whose prescribing shifts with small gifts from industry, and whose incentives vary with the payment model. A review that judges supports against an imagined unbiased human will systematically overstate their harm. The second is auditability: a system's ordering, framing and follow-up questions can be logged and analysed, while a clinician's cannot. That is a real asymmetry and it is a property of a governance regime rather than of a technology. The paper says as much without drawing the conclusion, listing what auditability would require, mandatory disclosure of commercial relationships, independent auditing for biased recommendations and separation of developer and provider finances, none of which exists. Absent that, a deployed system is less inspectable than a clinician and worse in one respect the paper does not note: a clinician's idiosyncratic framing varies between patients, while a system's is uniform, so a systematic bias reaches every patient identically instead of being averaged away.

rows.value: As Thaler and Sunstein argue regarding choice architecture generally, such influence is unavoidable - information must always be presented in some order and framed in some way, whether by human physicians or by AI systems. The relevant question is not whether influence exists, but how it compares to existing practices and how transparently it can be examined and optimized. LLMs offer a potential advantage here: their decision-making processes can be systematically audited, documented, and regulated in ways that individual clinician decision-making cannot be.

cards.title: From Answer Givers to Design Mentors: Guiding LLMs with the Cognitive Apprenticeship Model

rows.value: other
primary empirical, framework or design space, measurement or method

A CHI paper that turns Collins, Brown and Newman's cognitive apprenticeship into a system prompt and tests it against plain ChatGPT with 24 visualization practitioners. It is one of the very few systems in this corpus that instructs its support to recede: the appendix tells the model to provide support and gradually withdraw it, to help the user perform the task on their own, and not to provide a full solution. The behavioural result is the strongest thing here and it is measured on the right side of the conversation. Against the baseline, the model generated solutions 32 times instead of 243, users wrote 178 words per turn instead of 67 while the model wrote fewer, sessions ran twice as many turns, and the share of user utterances that answered a question from the system rose twelvefold. So the work moved from the machine to the person, which is what the design intended. What is not shown is anything about the person afterwards. Both sessions lasted ten minutes, every outcome is a process trace or a perception rating, and whether the model actually faded within a session is never checked.

medium · The process measurements are good and unusually well suited to this review: 24 practitioners, within-subject, counterbalanced order, transcripts coded against two named schemes with Cohen's kappa of 0.79 on 50% double-coded logs, and the counts reported separately for mentor-driven and mentee-driven behaviours so the reader can see who did the work. The limits are equally clear. Each condition ran ten minutes on the participant's own artifact, so the comparison is between two brief conversations rather than between two ways of learning. Every outcome is either a conversational trace or a Likert perception, several of the reported differences are not significant and are described as comparably better anyway, and the qualitative claims rest on a handful of participants. Most importantly for this card, the system's central instruction — provide support and gradually withdraw it — is never verified: no analysis tests whether support declined across the turns of a session, and no measurement is taken after the session at all. Carry the interaction counts and the prompt design with confidence; carry nothing here as evidence about what any practitioner retained.

sections.title: 4 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is what withdrawal looks like when the support is a language model, and it deserves recording precisely because it is so unlike everything else in the corpus. The mechanism is a sentence in a system prompt: provide your support and gradually withdraw it, help them perform tasks on their own, do not provide a full solution. There is no schedule, no diagnostic, no representation of what this user can now do, and no threshold at which anything changes. The fading is delegated wholesale to the model's reading of the conversation in front of it. Set against the argumentation review's finding that the only fading anyone builds is a fixed timetable, and that the timetable does worse than never fading, this is a genuinely different move: support that could in principle recede when this particular person stops needing it, because the thing deciding is reading what they just said. Whether it does is not established. No analysis tests whether support declined across the turns of a session; the evidence offered is that annotators labelled 26 turns as scaffolding against none in the baseline, which counts occurrences and not a trajectory. So the card carries this as the clearest instance in the corpus of contingent withdrawal being attempted, and as an instance of it going unverified.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The strongest result here, and the measurement worth stealing, is that the counts are split into what the system did and what the person did, and both are reported. On the system side the change is stark: solutions generated 32 times against 243, with scaffolding appearing 26 times and never once in the baseline. On the person side, bounding the problem 16 times against 1, articulating 18 against 2, exploring and reflecting appearing at all rather than never. The verbal inversion states it most simply — talking to plain ChatGPT the machine wrote 287 words a turn and the user 67, talking to the mentor the user wrote 178 and the machine 156. And the discourse-act split says what changed in kind rather than volume: requests for information fell by more than half while utterances answering a question from the system rose twelvefold, so the user moved from extracting content to being asked things. That is a measurable property of an arrangement, not a perception of one, and it is close to what this review wants — evidence about who is doing the cognitive work. What it is not is evidence about capability. Every one of these numbers describes the conversation, and the conversation lasted ten minutes.

Nothing is measured after the treatment ends in time: the perception survey follows immediately and the interview follows both sessions. Ten minutes per condition on the participant's own artifact makes that inevitable rather than careless — there is no post-support task to give in a ten-minute session — but it means the paper's claim that the design fosters reflective practice is a claim about ten minutes of talk. The two systems were anonymized as Version A and Version B, and the order of exposure was counterbalanced across participants to mitigate ordering effects. items.lead: The perception results are weaker than the behavioural ones and should be read that way. One difference is large and clean: self-awareness of design decisions, 4.16 against 2.92 with d = 0.853, which is a substantial effect on a self-rating that matches what the transcripts independently show. items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The most transferable finding in the paper, and one this corpus has not had stated this way. Preference for the reflective system depends on where in the project the person is standing: essentially everyone in exploration and nearly everyone in development preferred it, and those closer to evaluation did not. That is contingency at the level of the work rather than of the learner. The expertise-reversal literature gives the version indexed to the person — support that fits a novice becomes redundant for the same person later — and this adds an orthogonal axis, because a single practitioner passes through exploration, development and evaluation on one project in a week. A support that recedes as competence grows would still be wrong for an expert in an exploratory phase and wrong for a novice about to ship. The interview material gives the mechanism in the participants' own terms: a split between wanting an answer giver and wanting a thought partner, with differing tolerance for the engagement burden. Read next to the finding elsewhere in this corpus that the dominant failure of a support is that nobody uses it, this is the reason why — the cost is paid now and the benefit, if any, arrives later. The base is 24 participants split across three phases, so the percentages rest on very small cells.

cards.title: Towards a Framework for Understanding and Assessing Critical Thinking in Generative AI-Enhanced Learning Environments: A Scoping Review

rows.value: S2W-9BE1B88EB6B31543ECD2E9B6
other
review or meta analysis, framework or design space, concept or theory

A 2026 scoping review of 29 empirical studies on critical thinking in generative AI learning environments, and the most useful thing in it is what it shows about the word scaffolding. The review makes a scaffolding pathway one of its two organising constructs and defines it as the tool reducing lower-order cognitive demands so learners can spend more effort on higher-order reasoning: 72.4 per cent of the corpus is placed on that pathway, 24.1 per cent mixed, one study negative. Fold the whole text and scaffold appears 14 times while fading, fade, withdraw and withdrawal appear zero times each, the sole contingen is contingent upon self-regulatory discipline, the sole transfer sits inside a reference title, and Wood, Bruner and Ross are absent; the construct reaches this literature through Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and the more knowledgeable other, and arrives with both the adjustment and the removal stripped out. Two other things are worth carrying. The review names an offloading pathway where the very ease of use that makes the tool usable produces superficial engagement, and it proposes deliberate pedagogical friction, try-first rules, staged access and accountability prompts, as the remedy, which puts the decision to withdraw help inside the learner rather than the system. And its own headline about measurement does not survive its own numbers: the abstract says the majority assessed critical thinking through context-embedded performance tasks, while the findings report 37.9 per cent standardised inventories, 41.4 per cent adapted scales and only 20.7 per cent researcher-developed rubrics, from a search string that required scale, instrument, survey or questionnaire vocabulary to be present at all.

medium · As evidence about whether generative AI helps thinking this bears very little weight, and the authors mostly say so: a scoping review by two people of 29 studies from three databases over 27 months, no quality appraisal and no risk-of-bias assessment by explicit choice, grey literature searched only through the first 100 Google Scholar hits under a stated stopping rule, instruments not required to be validated, and the impact finding delivered as a vote count of 21 positive against 7 mixed and 1 negative across studies the review itself calls too heterogeneous to compare. Extraction was by one reviewer cross-validated by a second with no agreement statistic and no inter-rater reliability anywhere, and the declarations page calls the work a conceptual paper for which no data were generated. What the card does rest on is different in kind: what a 2026 review means by scaffolding, what vocabulary it has and lacks, and whether its abstract matches its own tables. Those are claims about the text, checkable against the text, and the counts behind them are reproducible from the page bytes bound to this card.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is what scaffolding means in a 2026 review of 29 studies: the machine takes the low-level work so the person can spend their effort higher up. That is a claim about division of labour and it says nothing about adjusting the help to what the person can already do, and nothing about ever reducing it. The absence is checkable rather than impressionistic. Folding the whole extracted text to letters and digits, scaffold appears 14 times, including as one of the review's two organising pathways and in its own extraction table; fading, fade, withdraw and withdrawal appear zero times each; the single occurrence of contingen is contingent upon the self-regulatory discipline, which is a different idea; the single occurrence of transfer sits inside the title of a Halpern reference; delayed appears zero times. Wood, Bruner and Ross are absent from the article and from its reference list. The construct arrives instead through Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and the more knowledgeable other, which the review says nearly a third of the corpus uses, and that route carries help pitched above independent capability but not help calibrated turn by turn and then removed. For a review of supports this is a lineage datum with a date on it: as of 2026, in the largest current application area, scaffolding has become a synonym for offloading the easy parts, and the two properties that made it a mechanism rather than a metaphor have been dropped.

rows.value: In most studies (72.4%), GenAI functioned as a scaffold by reducing lower-order cognitive demands (e.g. information retrieval or drafting), thereby enabling greater investment in higher-order reasoning and synthesis... items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A short list of concrete design moves, each of which is a way of making the support arrive later or cost something: attempt the task before the help unlocks, release the tool in stages, require an account of what was accepted or discarded, and monitor how much the person is leaning on it. These are the closest thing in this literature to contingency, since try-first at least makes the help follow an attempt, and they are reusable outside education wherever a generative tool sits next to work someone is supposed to be learning to do. Two things bound them. They are fixed policies, not responses to performance: everyone attempts first, everyone gets the same staging, and nothing changes as the person improves, so friction is a constant tax rather than a schedule. And they are recommendations, not results. The review runs no test of its own; the strongest primary support in its table is a single randomised trial of guidance-based use against unguided use, and the general prescription is assembled from a corpus with no quality appraisal. The interesting move is where the review puts responsibility: self-regulation is named the control layer that decides when and how much to use the tool, which assigns the job of reducing help to the person being helped rather than to the system or the teacher.

cards.title: Creating a lean mind-set: Change of practice towards early treatment

rows.value: S2W-5F8526F4AFF670B42A77EEF2
other
primary empirical, framework or design space, failure or counterevidence

A qualitative study of how a Norwegian hospital's human resource development unit introduced lean thinking to clinicians, read explicitly through a scaffolding lens with three phases: cognitive scaffolding to make lean seem worth learning, peer-to-peer scaffolding through a shared paper-aeroplane exercise, and then fading, in which the unit deliberately pulled back and handed responsibility to the clinical departments. It is the rare paper in this corpus where withdrawal is designed, executed, and then evaluated. The evaluation is unflattering and that is what makes it valuable. The clinicians say the support left too early; the HR director says staying would have built a house of cards; the authors conclude the fading was not adapted to the individual learner and was not mastered. The clinical work succeeded and saved lives, the method never spread beyond the units that took part, and each side now believes the other owns the knowledge.

medium · As a qualitative case this is well constructed and unusually candid. The scaffolding frame is declared in advance rather than fitted afterwards, the three phases are tied to dated project stages across several years, the tables lay out activity, rationale and result per phase so a reader can see what was claimed from what, and the authors report interview quotations that contradict their own framing rather than smoothing them. The withdrawal is genuinely observed rather than proposed. What limits it is that nothing is measured about any person. There is no assessment of what any clinician could do before or after, no comparison unit, no count of anything; the evidence is interviews and observation at one hospital, and the fading verdict rests on differing recollections from parties with a stake in the answer. The one hard outcome, reduced waiting time for thrombolysis, is a clinical process result and not a measure of learning. Carry the fading account, the disagreement and the spread failure; carry no effect on capability.

sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is the most usable operational statement of withdrawal in the corpus, and its hardest clause is the one everyone else omits: the scaffolder must allow for failure without assisting. That single requirement explains why fading is rare. A support that must watch someone fail and hold back is accepting a worse immediate outcome for a better later one, and no measurement taken during the arrangement will ever reward that trade — every in-session metric this review has met would score the restraint as a decline. The distinction between what members wish for and what they need is the second hard clause, and it puts learner-requested help and learner-assessed readiness firmly outside the definition. The three-way outcome taxonomy is worth reusing as it stands: a smooth handover, a crash landing where what previously seemed clear now seems complicated, and a passive process defined by the absence of interaction. That third case is the one to watch for, because a study distinguishing only success from failure cannot tell it from the first — silence after withdrawal looks identical whether the learner is coping or has quietly stopped.

This fading activity is called 'adaptive fading'... a 'crash landing' for those clinicians who are unable to put new ideas into practice since what previously seemed clear now seems more complicated, or a passive process in which the non-presence of interaction and dialogue describes the process further.

quotes: Noroozi et al. (2018) state that fading is a dynamic activity in which the scaffolder adjusts the degree of fading based on the needs of an organisation’s members. This means that fading is about distinguishing between the wishes of an organisation’s members and their need for support – and the scaffolder must allow for failure without assisting. This fading activity is called ‘adaptive fad- ing’. In the context of this study, it can be about not discussing lean so much and not providing existing examples or tools, only encouraging clinicians to find their own solutions with lean – handing over responsibility to them. This can be a smooth process in which the clinicians take responsibility and practice lean in a way that supports their needs, a ‘crash landing’ for those clini- cians who are unable to put new ideas into practice since what previously seemed clear now seems more complicated, or a passive process in which the non-presence of interaction and dialogue describes the process further (Molloy et al., 2014

rows.value: (PDF p. 6) Soft and hard scaffolding in an organisation — The soft and hard distinction in an organisational setting: soft scaffolding is dynamic situation-specific aid given on the fly, requiring the unit to continuously diagnose learners' understanding and provide timely support based on their responses, with a normative element about respecting participants' autonomy and discretion; hard scaffolding is static support anticipated and planned in advance from the typical difficulties of a task, which organisationally means more structured activities narrowing discussion to certain tasks and issues.
quotes: On the one hand, soft scaffolding comprises the facilitation of interactive discussions and guidance from, in this case, HRD, and such soft scaffolding comprises dynamic, situation-specific aid given to help with the adult learning process (Knowles et al., 2014). Scaffolding requires HRD to continu- ously diagnose the understanding of learners and provide timely support based on the learners’ responses (Weber and Feintzeig, 2014). This type of assistance is generally provided “on the fly”, and comprises support or guidance that is given when needed. Soft scaffolding also has some normative statements, such as promoting a form of collaboration that respects the participants’ rights to autonomy and discretion, while ensuring the effective exercise of those rights as a part of an interactive and supportive process. Hard scaffolding, on the other hand, is static support that can be anticipated and planned in advance based on the typical difficulties of a task (Brush and Saye, 2002). In an organisational context this could be learning activities that are more structured by narrowing the discussions to include certain tasks and issues in relation to the organisational goals that promote more disciplined arguments and interactions among the learners (Hawkins et al., 2017

quotes: A key idea in Vygotsky’s (1978) social learning theory is ‘the zone of proximal development’, which describes the distance between what a learner is capable of doing without support and what they are capable of doing with support. This support is used synonymously with the term scaffold- ing (Bruner, 1990), which entails helping learners complete only those elements that are within their range of expertise. Scaffolding works best when learning participants share and experience intersubjectivity, working together towards the same goal, helping each other to develop new knowledge. The learning takes place both individually and through social interaction and dialogue, which results in new understandings and further learning
