items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the corpus's only recorded argument between a support and the people it supported about whether it should have stopped, and both sides reason correctly from different premises. The department head and the doctor experienced the withdrawal as abandonment at the moment the real work began, and their complaint is not that they could not cope — they say they did well — but that the knowledge then failed to travel. The HR director's reply is the textbook rationale almost verbatim: carrying the load would do the departments a disservice and build a house of cards rather than a foundation. Neither is wrong, and this is not resolvable by better diagnosis of learner readiness, because the two parties want different things from the support. One wants a competence transferred; the other wants a change propagated. That distinction is worth carrying out of this paper: withdrawal timed for the learner's independence and withdrawal timed for an innovation's diffusion are different problems with different optima, and here they pulled in opposite directions inside one project. The scaffolding literature only has vocabulary for the first, which may be why the second went unplanned.

rows.value: (PDF p. 18) No seamless transition, and each side thinks the other knows — What the disagreement produced: the departments held a different view of how the unit should assist, and the tension is clearest where the unit fails to create a seamless transition from driving the process to cheering from the sidelines; the authors suggest it may have failed to clarify expectations, that it could perhaps have been faded out more gradually so the methodology gained a foothold in more of the hospital, and that the perception of who knows lean has now changed, with the departments thinking lean is something the unit knows while the unit thinks it is something the participating departments know.
quotes: The above quotes show that the hospital units had a different view of how HRD should assist in the learning process. This tension becomes even clearer when HRD fails to create a seamless transition from being the actor responsible for the driving process to becoming an actor who ‘cheers’ from the sidelines. HRD may have failed to clarify its expectations with the units, but it succeeded in its role as scaffolder by supporting, motivating and guiding the process of implementing lean method- ology in some hospital departments. In a hospital that is located in many different areas, HRD, with its centralised position, could contribute to sharing lean knowledge further in the organisation. Perhaps HRD could have been faded out more gradually, so that the lean methodology gained a foothold in several parts of the hospital. Nevertheless, all in all, the project has been a success that saved many lives, and HRD has been an important temporary support during the process. This hospital won the lean award in 2016 for the same-day surgery project that involved several hundred employees. However, as the findings suggest, it is difficult to involve other units in the hospital with lean. Also, the perception of who is familiar with lean in the organisation has changed. Currently, the hospital units think that lean is something HRD knows, whereas HRD thinks lean is something the hospital units that participated in the lean project know

rows.value: (PDF p. 17) What phase 3 actually did — What the fading phase consisted of: across 2019 to 2020 the unit challenged the hospital departments to own the process while it stayed in the background and answered questions; the same groups from the earlier exercise each performed a value stream analysis of stroke treatment and compared results, finding that taking patients directly to the MRI room would cut waiting by 15 to 20 minutes, identifying several time thieves, and together reducing the waiting time for thrombolysis treatment, which the authors say saved the lives of several patients.
quotes: In phase 3 (2019–2020) of the project, HRD challenged the hospital units to own the process itself, where HRD was in the background and answered the questions from the hospital units. In the first activity of this phase we observed the value stream analysis of the treatment of stroke patients. The participants were the same groups that partici- pated in the aeroplane activity. Each group had to perform the same value stream analysis before everyone gathered to compare the results. By mapping all the stages the patient had to go through before receiving treatment, they found that if ambulance personnel transported the patient directly to the MRI examination room, this would reduce the waiting time by 15–20 minutes. They also found several time ‘thieves’ when all the results were compared, and together they managed to reduce the waiting time for thrombolysis treatment, which saved the lives of several patients

rows.value: (PDF p. 18) The two incompatible accounts, side by side — This is the corpus's only recorded argument between a support and the people it supported about whether it should have stopped, and both sides are reasoning correctly from different premises. The department head and the doctor experienced the withdrawal as abandonment at the moment the real work began, and their complaint is not that they could not cope but that the knowledge then failed to travel. The HR director's reply is the textbook rationale, almost verbatim: carrying the load would do the departments a disservice and produce a house of cards rather than a foundation. Neither is wrong, and the disagreement is not resolvable by better diagnosis of learner readiness, because the two parties want different things from the support — one wants competence transferred, the other wants a change propagated. That is a distinction this review should carry: withdrawal timed for the learner's independence and withdrawal timed for the innovation's diffusion are different problems, and this case shows them pulling in opposite directions inside a single project.
quotes: This different perception of the role of HRD emerges in these two quotes: The job began and HR was gone. There are probably other actors besides HR that should be credited for the success of this project. HR knew what they were doing; we did not. So why they left us so early in the process, I’ll never know. We did well, although much of the lean thinking stopped with us. HR could have helped us to spread the ‘good news’ – so to speak. (Doctor) Why HRD withdrew early is explained here: HR is not supposed to own the process. HR is a support and guide in the process, and if we start to pull all the load then we have done the hospital units a disservice. items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The costed result of the withdrawal sits in one table cell and deserves lifting out: it created dedication within the participating departments and made it hard to transfer the method to any other department. Read with the discussion, the pattern is that handing over responsibility produced deep local ownership and stopped the diffusion, because the only actor with a whole-organisation view had stepped back to management level and stopped seeing the units at all. So the property that made the supporter useful in the first place — sitting outside any single department while understanding the whole hospital, which is exactly how the paper justifies its involvement early on — is the property destroyed by fading. That is a mechanism worth naming: where a support's value comes from a vantage point rather than from expertise, withdrawing it removes the vantage point, and nothing the learners acquire can substitute, because the vantage point was never theirs to acquire. The second half of the explanation is equally useful and more general. The clinicians returned to their uni-professional learning activities once the cross-disciplinary arrangement ended, which is reversion of the setting rather than forgetting by the person — the capability may well have survived while the conditions for exercising it did not.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Two things here are worth carrying and neither appears elsewhere in the corpus. The first is a cost of successful fading: if the support did its job, the people who received it own the achievement and the supporter is invisible in the record. The authors report exactly that, with informants declining to credit the unit because the clinicians did the hard work. That is the intended effect and simultaneously a standing disincentive for any supporter whose budget depends on being seen to contribute. Every other paper in this corpus treats the failure to fade as an oversight or an instrumentation gap; this one exhibits a structural reason to keep a support in place that has nothing to do with the learner, and it predicts where fading will be rarest — wherever the supporter is separately accountable for demonstrating impact, which describes most funded educational technology. The second is the end state, and it is the sharpest single fact in the paper. The departments think lean is something the support unit knows; the unit thinks lean is something the departments know. Both believe the handover went to the other party. That is what an unmeasured transfer of responsibility looks like from the inside: with no assessment either side would accept, there is no fact of the matter about whether anything was handed over, and each side's belief drifts toward what is convenient. Note that this is a best case for detection — few identifiable people, a named capability, three years of contact — and it still came out ambiguous. A tool study inferring internalisation from usage logs is attempting something much harder with far less.

The study operationalizes prior guidance on visual markers for continuous AI support and methodological work treating machine learning as a design material. It also interprets imperfect CADe through the prior “second observer” framing. cards.title: Mesh: Scaffolding Comparison Tables for Online Decision Making
cards.meta: 2020 · Proceedings of the 33rd Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology · doi 10.1145/3379337.3415865 · Route C

rows.value: S2CW-DDBBEAD3556CCCD46E58E33D
other
primary empirical, framework or design space, design principle

A browser tool that builds a product comparison table as you research: pull in options from your tabs, add criteria, and every cell fills itself from the reviews. Its design contribution is unusual and worth taking seriously — it targets the cost curve rather than the task. In an ordinary spreadsheet each new criterion costs you a pass over every option you already have, so the work grows as the table does; Mesh auto-fills, so the marginal cost stays flat and, in the authors' phrase, changes the cost structure from increasing cost to increasing payoffs. The second thing it does is refuse to decide for you: the automatic rating is shown, and the user can overwrite it with their own, in a different colour, which then drives the weighted total. Three studies found it faster (2.3x), more accurate against gold answers, and lower in workload, with summaries rated more insightful by third parties. Nothing was measured about the user afterwards; the tool was present throughout every study.

medium · A well-constructed systems paper with three studies of different kinds — a within-subject counterbalanced lab study with gold-standard answers, a between-subject lab study whose output was rated blind by five independent crowdworkers, and a week-long field deployment on participants' own real purchases with logged interaction counts. That combination is stronger than the usual single-session demonstration. Four limits. Both lab studies used Mechanical Turk workers paid three dollars for twenty to twenty-five minutes, which bounds the effort anyone brought to a task that is not theirs. The field deployment has five participants. Study 1 reports a mean and a median that point in opposite directions for the same accuracy comparison, which looks like a transposition and is left uncorrected. And the outcomes are efficiency, workload, and third-party ratings of what the participant produced with the tool in front of them; nothing measures the person once the tool is gone, and nothing checks whether the decisions were good. Carry the design contribution and the interaction costs; carry no claim about what users learned.

sections.title: 4 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A design axis this review has not recorded and should. Nearly every support in the corpus is described by what it supplies — a prompt, a hint, a worked example, a template, a script — and evaluated by whether supplying it helped. This paper describes its contribution by how the marginal cost of the user's own work scales. In a spreadsheet each new criterion costs a pass over every option already in the table and each new option costs a pass over every criterion, so the more thoroughly you work the more expensive thoroughness becomes; the analysis ends when the person tires, not when they are satisfied. Auto-filling flattens that curve, and the authors are precise about the consequence: greater investment now yields increasing payoff rather than increasing cost. Stated generally, a support can be characterised by whether it lowers the cost of one act or lowers the growth rate of the cost of doing more of them, and the second is the more interesting kind because it changes what a person will attempt rather than how well they do what they had already decided to attempt. Two cautions. The claim is architectural rather than demonstrated — no study varies table size and measures the curve — and all three studies fix the task, which is exactly the design that cannot see the effect the claim is about.

quotes: Instead of fully automated or manual approaches, we introduce Mesh, a hybrid approach aimed at scaffolding decision making by helping users progressively build up a comparison table that reﬂects their personal criteria and evaluation of evidence. Mesh lowers the cost of pulling in information, organizing it by users’ criteria, and helping users keep track of their judgments as they evaluate evidence. Importantly, by auto-ﬁlling the cells when new criteria or options are added throughout the process, Mesh makes adding to the table stay at a constant cost as the table grows, changing the cost structure to provide an increasing payoff with greater user investment. Finally, Mesh helps keep users on track by prioritizing where to look, which criteria are most important, and reﬂecting their current beliefs for each option through an overall weighted average

rows.value: (PDF p. 12) The conclusion and the contribution claim — The contribution as the conclusion states it: a new process that scaffolds the iterative building up of context and changes the cost structure from increasing cost to increasing payoffs as the number of criteria and options grows, with the three studies showing lower interaction costs and better accuracy on objective criteria, more insightful and confident summaries on subjective ones, and better prioritisation of discriminative criteria in the field.
quotes: This design is novel because it introduces a new process that scaffolds the iterative building up of context, and changes the cost structure from increasing cost to increasing payoffs as the number of criteria and options grow. Through three rounds of lab and ﬁeld deployment studies, we uncovered deep insights into how Mesh can beneﬁt online sensemaking in the context of product comparison research. In Study 1, we found evidence that Mesh not only lowered in­ teraction costs (i.e., shorter time spent and lowered perceived effort), but also led to participants ﬁnding more accurate in­ formation when working with objective criteria (e.g., water tank capacities for espresso machines). In Study 2, when dealing with subjective criteria (e.g., ease of use for espresso machines) we found evidence that participants who used Mesh were more insightful and conﬁdent about their choices com­ pared to participants who used a Google Spreadsheet baseline. Finally, in Study 3 we tested Mesh in the wild with participants conducting their own tasks over a longer period of time and found that Mesh allowed participants to better prioritize their effort on criteria that were more discriminative, and was able to capture their interpretations of data to keep track of their progress

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The clearest concrete mechanism in this corpus for keeping a human judgement authoritative over a computed one. The system shows its own aggregate from the reviews in yellow; the user can replace it with their own in purple; the replacement, not the original, then drives the weighted total that ranks the options. Three properties make it worth copying. The machine value is a default rather than a verdict, so the user is never put in the position of arguing with the system. The override is visually distinct, so the provenance of every cell stays legible at a glance — which is the transparency pole that the embedded-scaffolding tradition deliberately abandons when it hides support so that users are less likely to notice it. And the override propagates, so disagreeing with the tool changes what the tool recommends rather than being filed as a note beside an unchanged recommendation. Set this against the software-engineering taxonomy in which the developer reviews the AI across all eleven interaction types and the AI never assesses the developer: this is what the reviewing half looks like when it is actually designed, and P3's quote is a person exercising it. The honest caveat is that the paper reports the override being used but never asks whether the users who overrode did better than those who did not.

rows.value: Instead of automating away the role of the user, our approach focuses on helping users scaffold their decision-making throughout the process, maximizing their ability to apply their personal context and interpretation to evidence while reducing the costs for doing so... users can overwrite the default Amazon ratings with their own (in purple) based on their own interpretation of data... Three properties make it worth copying. The machine value is a default rather than a verdict, so the user is not asked to argue with it. The override is visually distinct, so the provenance of every cell stays legible. And it propagates, so disagreeing with the tool changes the tool's recommendation rather than being recorded as a note beside it. Set that against the software-engineering finding that in eleven interaction types the developer reviews the AI and never the reverse: this is what the reviewing half looks like when it is designed rather than assumed, and it is a good deal rarer in practice than the taxonomy implies.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: Sorted into the three measurement families, every outcome in this paper is family one or family two. Time, accuracy against gold answers, NASA-TLX workload, perceived performance, satisfaction and confidence all describe the encounter with the tool. The third-party-rated summaries describe the output of the encounter. Nothing describes the person afterwards. For a UIST systems paper that is an ordinary and defensible choice, and it is worth recording precisely because the paper argues something about the user: its stated aim is that people build up a better understanding of their criteria and their options, and understanding is the one thing none of the instruments touch. Study 2 comes closest, because the participant writes the summary rather than the system — but with the tool on screen, and what the summary demonstrates is that the table was read, not that anything was retained. A single extra condition would have closed the gap: ask the Study 2 participants to advise on a sixth vacuum with the tool closed, which is the two-part test applied to a twenty-minute study. Two smaller notes. Study 1's accuracy comparison reports a mean of 8.50 against 5.83 and medians of 7 against 9, which point opposite ways and look like a transposition left uncorrected. And both lab studies ran on Mechanical Turk at three dollars for twenty to twenty-five minutes, which bounds how much effort anyone brought to somebody else's purchase.

rows.value: (PDF p. 10) Field deployment usage — The word scaffold appears sixteen times in fifteen pages and means, throughout, structured support that lowers cost. Fading, withdrawal, contingency, temporary and Vygotsky are absent. The only progression in the paper is the user moving through phases of their own task, from gathering evidence to deciding, with the system unchanged behind them. This is the standard HCI usage and there is nothing wrong with it, but it is worth noting what the design would have to add to satisfy the criterion Kollar and Fischer take from Pea — that without fading the external tool is distributed intelligence rather than a scaffold. Mesh is unambiguously the former, and the interesting thing is that it is designed to be: its contribution is a cost curve that rewards continued use, which is the opposite of a support designed to become unnecessary. Both are legitimate goals. The corpus needs them distinguished, because the same word is doing duty for both.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Confidence is a headline outcome in two of the three studies and nothing checks it against anything. Study 2's fourth rating asks whether a summary makes a reader feel confident; the field study reports that four of five participants bought things and felt confident in the decisions. Neither asks whether the confident decisions were any better. That matters more here than it usually would, because the paper's own premise is that online review evidence is messy, biased, conflicting and increasingly fake — the introduction notes fake reviews may now be the majority in some categories. A support that makes people feel more certain about evidence the paper itself describes as unreliable has an obvious failure mode, and the design does one thing that could aggravate it: the weighted average produces a single number ranking the options, computed from ratings the system extracted, presented as the tool's summary judgement. It also does one thing that mitigates it, which is the override. Neither is evaluated against decision quality. The corpus has one sharp result on exactly this point — in the game-scaffolding experiment perceived learning ran opposite to measured learning, so the support doing the most real work felt worst — and it is enough to make confidence unusable as a proxy. Confidence is a legitimate thing to want from a decision aid. It is not evidence that the aid worked.

cards.title: Beyond Accuracy: The Role of Mental Models in Human-AI Team Performance

rows.value: S2BW-B4812DC95481ECDE6FF7B624
other
concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle, primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

The paper is conceptually grounded in mental-model and appropriate-trust traditions and operationalizes AI-competence knowledge as a user's learned approximation of the AI's error boundary. In controlled repeated advice-use studies, it treats reward feedback and the learnability of failure structure—its parsimony, stochasticity, and human-visible dimensionality—as conditions shaping reliance and human-AI team performance.

medium · The paper provides direct controlled evidence and complete page-grounded reporting for its central effects. Confidence in broader transfer is limited by the game-like binary interaction, behavioral proxy for mental models, Mechanical Turk population, 25 workers per condition, bottom-quartile observation removal, synthetic error boundaries, and absence of post-support or field-deployment measurement.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · S2-CLAIM-001
items.lead: Repeated outcome feedback can support calibration of a user's mental model of where an AI succeeds and fails. The evidence concerns within-session behavioral adaptation in a simplified accept-or-override task, not independently elicited, durable, or cross-domain learning.

rows.value: Reward feedback across repeated AI-advised decisions lets people learn when to trust the AI; in the controlled task, average simple regret decreased with interaction as workers approached the optimal reliance policy.

cards.title: Cognitive Aids in Acute Care: Investigating How Cognitive Aids Affect and Support In-hospital Emergency Teams

rows.value: S2W-1BF5BAEA31693D38B8B53CBB
other
primary empirical, concept or theory, failure or counterevidence

Two versions of a tablet application for the leader of a hospital resuscitation team were compared in 33 full-scale simulated cardiac arrests with real emergency teams: one that only records what was done, and one that adds timers, warnings and a prompt to consider the cause of arrest. Adding the decision support changed nothing measurable. Technical performance was 40.8 against 33.7 per cent, p = .140; the team performance score was 73.3 against 68.9 per cent, p = .515; and subjective workload was 6.18 against 5.81 on a 20-point scale, p = .368, even though the richer version carried more reminders and was used more often. The authors use their own null to attack the standard explanation of why such aids help, that they cut workload and free mental bandwidth, and propose instead that an artefact does not lighten a task but swaps it for another one: without the aid remembering the steps is a memory task, with it the same steps become a reading task, and the two-minute rhythm check stops being something to remember and becomes something to notice. Their strongest observation is physical rather than cognitive. Frequent use went with less time doing manual work, and less manual work went with more diagnostic talk and higher team scores; holding the tablet may help by occupying the hands that would otherwise join in. The words fade, fading, withdraw, scaffold, transfer and retention appear nowhere in the paper.

medium · The evaluation is unusually realistic for this literature: real emergency teams rather than one clinician and actors, full-scale simulation on an instrumented manikin, objective measures logged by the manikin and the application, and a blinded external rater. That makes the nulls worth something. But it is 33 team leaders in one German hospital, and the authors state three limits themselves: the condition was assigned by session rather than randomised, no a priori power analysis was done for the main outcome, and one rater produced every team score on an instrument with known reliability problems. The correlations that carry the mechanism are Spearman coefficients over 33 observations and none of them fixes a direction of causation. The framework in the second half is argument, not result: it explains findings that already existed, some of them other people's, and none of its three perspectives is tested here. The card leans on the nulls, which are clean, and on the task-substitution analysis, which does not depend on the sample.

sections.title: 7 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is a direct attack on the standard story about why an external support helps, and it is unusual because the authors run it against their own data. The story says the artefact carries some of the mental load, leaving capacity for the harder thinking. Four things are set against it here: their own workload measure did not move between a leaner and a richer version of the same tool, a separate study found no workload difference between a checklist and none, the literature on remembering intentions says the cost being relieved is close to zero when good cues exist anyway, and these artefacts demonstrably change physical behaviour and speech, which a purely cognitive account does not predict. For a review of supports this matters beyond medicine, because reduced cognitive load is the most commonly asserted and least commonly measured mechanism in the whole literature. What the argument does not establish is that load never falls; it establishes that in one well-instrumented comparison it did not, and that the theory predicted no reason it should.

rows.value: In the medical literature, cognitive aids have been described in a classic information-processing view. Cognitive aids assist memory and reduce workload or free up mental bandwidth and therefore allow staff to focus more attention on team coordination and complex decision-making... Such an explanation seems unsatisfying for several empirical and theoretical reasons. First... the workload measure in the present study showed no differences between the DocuApp and the CaApp even though the latter included more reminders and was used more frequently... Second, prospective memory research... suggests that, if good environmental cues are provided... the cognitive costs of remembering to remember are very small or there are no costs at all.

Cognitive aids assist memory and reduce workload [44] or free up mental bandwidth [21] and therefore allow staff to focus more attention on team coordination and complex decision-making. Sarcevic et al. [54] considered checklists as memory externalization tools. By referring to distributed cognition [28,29], Sarcevic et al. expand the unit of analysis beyond the team leader’s individual cognition and considered the team leader and the list as the unit of analysis. However, at the core, the checklist is still considered as tool that prompts or aids memory of the artefact user

quotes: However, the medical epidemiological approach provides limited insights into how cognitive aids work [33]. Indeed, the explanations of how these artefacts work can be summarized as classic cognitive psychological explanations. rows.value: (PDF p. 9) Section 4.1, the first objection, the workload null — The first objection, from their own data: participants said informally that the applications were good memory aids, yet workload did not differ between the two versions although the cognitive aid carried more reminders and was used more, and another study found no workload difference between a checklist and no checklist.
quotes: First, despite informal feedback by the participants, that the applications were good memory aids, the workload measure in the present study showed no differences between the DocuApp and the CaApp even though the latter included more reminders and was used more frequently. Similarly, Parsons et al. [50] reported no differences in subjective workload between a trauma resuscitation checklist group and the no checklist group

rows.value: (PDF p. 9) Section 4.1, the second objection, prospective memory costs — The second objection, from the literature: research on remembering intentions finds that when good environmental cues are present the cognitive cost of remembering to remember is very small or absent, so a workload reduction was not to be expected.
quotes: Second, prospective memory research – the research on how humans remember intentions at the right time in the future – suggests that, if good environmental cues are provided, such as in the form of checklists, the cognitive costs of remembering to remember are very small [58] or there are no costs at all [57]. Considering the prospective memory literature, the aforementioned workload findings do not seem surprising

rows.value: (PDF p. 9) Section 4.1, the third objection, behaviour and communication change — The third objection: these artefacts change physical behaviour and communication, as in this study's association between frequent use, more diagnostic statements and less hands-on time, and in the finding that different instructions for the same checklist changed the leader's interaction style.

In the present study, frequent application use was associated with more diagnosis-related statements and less hands-on time. Similarly, Zhang et al. [65] reported that instruction on how to use a checklist changed the interaction style of the team leader. In particular the comparison of two applications (e.g., the present study) and one checklist with different user instructions [65] challenges a classic information-processing view on artefact use in acute care

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the most reusable sentence in the paper and it belongs in any account of what a support does. An external aid does not remove work; it substitutes one kind of work for another, and the substitution can be named in advance. Remembering the steps becomes reading them. Remembering to do something in two minutes becomes noticing a colour change. Both substitutions trade retrieval for perception, and both mean the person is now doing a task they were not doing before, with its own failure modes: you can fail to look, fail to notice, or misread. It also explains why two designs with identical content can produce identical outcomes and completely different processes, which the authors illustrate with a study where a context-sensitive and an alphabetic aid gave the same medical performance while the first demanded significantly longer interaction. For a review this reframes the whole question of what to measure: comparing outcomes with and without a support tells you nothing about which task the person is now performing. The claim is conceptual. It is illustrated with two worked examples and it is not tested, and no measurement in this study distinguishes reading from remembering.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The paper's own hypothesis failed. Adding timers, escalating colour warnings, a prompt to consider the cause of arrest and a reminder about a drug produced no detectable improvement over an application that only recorded what was done, on guideline conformance, on team performance or on workload. The one thing that did differ is that people used the richer version more. That combination, more use and no more benefit, is the useful shape here: the added content was consumed and did not show up anywhere in what the team did. The authors' explanation is a ceiling, and they support it with a real number, 29 of 33 teams keeping the no-flow fraction under 15 per cent against roughly 24 per cent in published real resuscitations, which makes it plausible for that one variable. It does not cover the rest of the table, where both groups were mostly outside the recommended bands on compression depth, adrenaline timing and rhythm-check timing, so there was room to improve and no improvement appeared. Read as evidence this is a failure to detect: 17 against 16 leaders, no randomisation, and by the authors' own admission no power analysis. Read as a warning it is worth carrying: a support can be measurably more used and measurably no more useful.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The correlations tell a coherent story that the group comparison does not. Leaders who used the tablet more had better team performance, spent less time doing manual work themselves, and said more about what might be causing the arrest; and more diagnostic talk went with better team performance. But none of it reached the clinical measures: technical performance correlated with neither team performance nor application use, and diagnostic talk did not correlate with it either. So the support is associated with a different way of leading and not with a different medical result, at least at this sample size. That gap is worth carrying by itself, because process improvements are what most support evaluations report and this study shows one that stops before the outcome. The causal direction is open in the way correlations always are, and here it is genuinely ambiguous: a leader who prefers to stand back and coordinate would use the tablet more, keep their hands free and talk more, without the tablet having caused anything. Four coefficients over 33 observations cannot separate those.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: This is the paper's most interesting and least tested idea: the aid may work as an object rather than as information. Holding a tablet occupies the hands, and hands that are occupied cannot join in the chest compressions, so the leader is pushed into delegating and coordinating, which is what the team performance instrument rewards. The authors' own correlations are consistent with it, since more use went with less manual work and less manual work with more diagnostic talk. If it is right, several things follow that a review should care about. The content of the aid is doing less work than everyone assumes, which would explain why two versions with very different content produced identical performance. Any physical object of similar size would do part of the job. And a class of support becomes available that works by constraining the supported person rather than by informing them, which is a genuinely different mechanism from the ones this literature usually names. It is also a speculation, flagged as such by the word may. No condition here gave anyone an object without content, nobody was asked to keep their hands free without a tablet, and the correlation it explains is one of four in a sample of 33.

rows.value: In acute care crisis, staff frequently want to get hands-on, contribute, and 'do something to help'. Such involvement can make it hard to stay on top of the global situation - so-called situation awareness - and can result in fixations errors. By holding a physical artefact, the team leader is forced to not engage in manual hands-on tasks. In such a situation, tasks are delegated and communication and coordination becomes more important. ... The positive association of cognitive aids use and non-technical performance in the present study and previous studies may well be due to holding the artefact in the hand and disengaging from the manual operations and focusing on higher level activities.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: A support that encodes an order of operations is competing with the situation in front of the person, and in time-critical work the situation usually wins. items.lead: Two design rules, both about what to leave out, and both transferable. cards.title: Using Learners' Self-Explanations of Subgoals to Guide Initial Problem Solving in App Inventor

rows.value: other
primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, design principle

A 120-person laboratory experiment in which every participant wrote their own names for the functional pieces of a programming procedure, and the manipulation was whose names got printed above the practice problems that followed. Three versions: nothing, the participant's own labels, or labels written by a computer scientist and an instructional designer. On an assessment taken minutes later with all materials taken away, the participants working from their own labels scored 21.6 out of 25, against 18.8 unscaffolded and 17.1 with the expert labels. The expert labels did not beat no labels at all. The paper's own reading is that imposing an expert's organisation on someone who has already built their own does not help them in any way, and it reaches for the memory literature on subjective organisation to explain it. Two things make the result awkward for the usual subgoal story. Labels a rater judged good were no better than labels a rater judged poor, so what worked was the authorship rather than the quality. And nothing else moved: cognitive load, self-rated understanding, confidence about solving new problems and time on task were all flat, so the only signal of the better scaffold was the score. Read the design before borrowing the headline. The decomposition stayed the experts' throughout: the worked example arrived already cut into subgoals, repeated instances were marked as belonging to the same subgoal, and half the participants were told what each subgoal was about. The learner supplied a name for a slot someone else had cut.

medium · Read the main effect as solid and everything hung on it as suggestive. The comparison of learner-written against expert-written labels is a clean randomised contrast at p < .001; the claims that expert labels never help, that quality does not matter, that load and confidence are unchanged, and that elicitation method is irrelevant are all absences of a detected difference in cells of twenty, and one of them is reported through a statistic that does not test what it names. The value to this review is the shape of the finding rather than its precision: a support was removed before the outcome was measured, authorship of the support mattered more than its judged quality, and none of the usual process instruments registered any of it.

sections.title: 7 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: Worth the card on its own, because the corpus is short of supports that are removed before the outcome is measured, and this one is. Everyone solved the practice problems; the difference only appears on the unaided test, which is the direction a review of designed supports should want and rarely gets. The size is real but should be quoted honestly: 2.8 points on a 25-point scale against a standard deviation of about 3.9, so roughly two thirds of a standard deviation, from a support that consisted of two words printed above a blank, met four times in ten minutes. The word relatively large in the text is not supported by the rubric printed beside it. The claim's boundary is that all six groups wrote labels, so this is not evidence that self-explaining beats not self-explaining; it is evidence about whose words are printed on the next page. And immediate means immediate: the test follows the practice problems by minutes, in the same room, on the same app.

rows.value: Scaffolding learners' first attempts at problem solving with subgoal labels that they constructed while studying worked examples can improve later problem solving performance compared to unguided or expert-guided initial problem solving attempts. Practice problem scaffolding affected performance, F(2, 114) = 9.81, p < .001: participants scaffolded with their own constructed labels (M = 21.6) performed statistically better than those scaffolded with expert-constructed labels (M = 17.1, Mean Difference = 4.55, p < .001) or with no scaffolding (M = 18.8, Mean Difference = 2.80, p = .024).

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the scarce half of the paper and the reason to keep it. A correct, expert-authored, semantically loaded annotation, sitting exactly where the learner needed it, did nothing, and its group scored lowest. The condition attached to that failure is unusual and portable: the recipient had already built their own account of the same procedure. Two cautions on how far it travels. It is a null in forty people, and the paper turns it into a claim about advanced learners who were never in the room. And the authors choose the weaker of two readings. They say the expert labels did not help; the numbers equally support the reading that meeting an expert's version of what you have just explained to yourself costs you something, which is precisely the mechanism these same authors proposed in the study this one builds on and then leave lying there.

rows.value: Receiving expert-constructed labels as scaffolds did not improve performance: participants who received scaffolding with expert-constructed labels did not perform statistically differently from those with no scaffolding, Mean Difference = 1.75, p = .28, and the group that had already seen the expert labels as feedback did not perform differently from the no-feedback group. The conclusion the authors would like to draw is that expert labels, at least static ones, do not provide helpful support to learners during practice problems, and that imposing expert-constructed labels on participants who had developed their own effective organization of the procedure did not seem to help the participants in any way.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: This is the correction the review needs to attach to the paper before citing it, and the authors state the facts plainly enough that it is not a hostile reading. Subgoal labels are one of the most cited mechanisms in this corpus and this study is filed under learner-generated structure. It is not. The structure was the experts': the example arrived pre-cut, the repeated instances were marked as belonging together, and for half the sample a hint said what each group of steps was for. The learner wrote a name into a slot. That is still an interesting act, and the results say it matters who writes the name, but the useful design lesson is a division of labour rather than a handover. The expensive, structural half stays with the designer, which is also the half the paper says self-explanation was never meant to save. Any system claiming to let people build their own scaffolds should be asked which half it is actually giving away.

By asking students to self-explain subgoals, the process of identifying subgoals becomes shorter because the instructional designer needs to only parse one subgoal from the next, not come up with a context-independent description of the subgoal that would explain its function to a novice.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The most useful idea in the paper for this review, resting on the weakest analysis in it. The idea is that the property making a support work can be invisible to the person who would normally be asked to judge it: an expert rater ranked these labels and the ranking predicted nothing, while authorship predicted a lot. That directly threatens the standard practice of validating a designed support by expert review, and it is exactly the sort of claim this review should be collecting. The analysis behind it does not carry that weight. The test printed for label quality is character for character the main effect of elicitation method from the previous page, including a degrees of freedom pair that a two-level factor cannot produce, so quality was proxied by condition and never regressed on score. Then the conclusion argues backwards from the outcome to the labels being high quality after all, which contradicts the null it just reported. Table 3 adds a further doubt: the label called worse, naming the actual clap being touched, is at least unambiguous, and the study found no cost to it.

rows.value: Participants who constructed better labels did not perform better than those who constructed worse labels. Seventy-five per cent of participants who constructed labels with hints made context-independent labels compared with thirty-five per cent of those without hints, and both groups made between four and seven per cent incorrect labels, yet despite the differences in quality there was not a concomitant difference in performance. The quality of the subgoal labels constructed by learners was not a significant predictor of problem solving success, so it might be the case that learners can create labels that are beneficial to them but that an instructional designer would not recognize as a good label.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: Kept because the pattern of nulls is more useful to this review than the positive result. A support moved an outcome by most of a standard deviation while leaving no signature in load, in time, in self-rated understanding or in confidence. Two consequences follow. First, the mechanism the authors propose, that the learner's own labels reconnect the practice problem to knowledge they built, predicts a process difference that this study looked for and did not find, so the mechanism remains a story. Second, and more portable, the learner could not tell. If a review wants a case where subjective measures fail to track the effectiveness of a designed support, this is a clean one, and the confidence rating even trends the wrong way. The obvious caution is that these are nulls on thin instruments, mostly single items, and that nothing was recorded about what people did while the labels were in front of them.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: Recorded because it names the motive that usually goes unstated and because the inherited finding is sharper than anything this study measures. The motive is arithmetic: two experts and one to two hours for half an hour of instruction, which is why the field keeps trying to get somebody cheaper to write the labels. The inherited finding is that support for writing your own explanation is non-monotonic, and the reason offered is a devaluation mechanism worth carrying into the review of model-generated support: show someone a better-looking version of what they just worked out and they abandon their own and try to memorise yours, losing the benefit of having worked it out. That mechanism predicts this paper's central null, where expert labels on the practice problems bought nothing, and the authors never join the two up. The caution is that none of it is tested here, and the two conditions that produced the non-monotonicity were dropped rather than replicated.

Prior work demonstrated that guiding learners to create their own explanations of subgoals can improve their problem solving performance, but that learners performed best with just enough support and that too much or too little support hurt performance, because learners who received hints and then also saw the expert's labels discounted the value of the labels that they had constructed.

cards.title: Concordancers and Dictionaries as Problem-Solving Tools for ESL Academic Writing

rows.value: other
primary empirical, measurement or method, failure or counterevidence

Six Korean ESL graduate students in Toronto were given a browser bundling five concordancers and three dictionaries, trained on it for three hours each, and screen-recorded while writing a real term paper or research proposal; 515 of their 3,170 queries were coded into 245 problem spaces and each outcome judged correct or incorrect against the text they produced. Three numbers make it worth keeping. The tool worked best where it was needed least: on problems where the writer already had a candidate in mind it produced correct text 76.8% of the time and was abandoned in 10.5% of cases, while on problems where the writer had no candidate the figures were 59.2% and 28.2%. Writers could not tell when it had failed them: of the 51 consultations that ended in incorrect text, 20 were perceived as successfully solved, and 13 of the 170 correct outcomes felt unsatisfactory. And the two resources added specifically for academic writing were the two least used, under 5% of queries each and gradually dropped, while the bilingual dictionary the participants had used for years was the most used at 25.6% despite training aimed at the concordancers. Every outcome was measured with the tool on screen; the gains in awareness, confidence and independence are final-interview self-reports.

medium · Six participants, one first language, one university, no control group, no randomisation, so nothing here is an effect estimate; the author states the small n and the group-level reporting as limits himself. Three further things. The same person recruited the participants, delivered the three hours of training, gave the feedback, ran the recalls, built the coding scheme and coded the data; two other coders checked 20% and agreement on the outcome dimension was 84%, with disagreements deliberately left unresolved, so the headline 69.4% rests on one rater's judgement of correct text. Only 515 of 3,170 queries, about 16%, were analysed. And the design measures conduct and product during tool use, never after it. Against that, the counting is careful for a study this size: problem spaces rather than queries are the unit, the confirmatory and compensatory split is defined before outcomes are coded, and objective outcome and participant satisfaction are recorded separately, which is what makes the mismatch finding possible. Treat the internal contrasts as informative and the absolute rates as descriptive of these six people.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A query-based support pays out in proportion to what the user already knows. When these writers had a candidate expression in mind and only needed it checked, the suite produced correct text in 76.8% of cases and was given up on in 10.5%. When they had no candidate — the case the tool exists for — it produced correct text in 59.2% and was given up on in 28.2%, so almost three in ten of those attempts ended with nothing. The mechanism is structural rather than particular to concordancers: a search interface can only be asked what its user can already formulate, and a well-formed question is itself most of the answer. So the yield of this whole class of support scales with the competence it is supposed to compensate for. This is the same routing failure that appears elsewhere in this corpus as weak learners being weak help seekers because they do not realise they need help, arriving from a different direction: not who asks, but what can be asked. It also sets a boundary on the paper's own framing — the suite is described as extending cognitive powers, and the extension is largest where the power was already there.

rows.value: In terms of problem type, the rate of positive effects from RS consultation was considerably higher with confirmatory problems. Out of a total of 142 confirmatory problems, 109 (76.8%) led to a correct text compared to 61 (59.2%) of compensatory problems. Meanwhile, the rate of abandoned consultations was much higher with compensatory problems (28.2%) than with confirmatory (10.5%). This result demonstrates that the participants had greater difficulties solving compensatory problems than confirmatory problems by consulting the suite.

At the query level, the participants carried out more verification queries seeking answers to whether questions than elicitation queries for what or how questions at a ratio of 3:2 (see Table 3). These results suggest that the participants consulted RS to confirm their existing linguistic knowledge more often than to seek linguistic items that were beyond their current linguistic repertoires

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) The distinction that carries the paper: confirmatory and compensatory problems — The two problem types: confirmatory, where the writer already has a linguistic item in mind or on the page and is checking whether it matches the intended meaning or context, and compensatory, where the writer cannot convert the intended meaning into text and is trying to extract a candidate from the resources.
quotes: First, problems were classified into two types: confirmatory and compensatory. Confirmatory problems refer to instances where writers tried to confirm the accuracy or appropriateness of a certain linguistic item they already had in mind or in writing in terms of its match with the intended meaning or context. Compensatory problems refer to instances when writers tried to extract a linguistic item from the reference resources that could express the intended meaning accurately and appropriately

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) The headline outcome: correct, incorrect, abandoned — The headline result over 245 problem spaces: 170 or 69.4% produced correct text, 31 or 12.7% produced incorrect text, and in the remaining 44 or 18% the participant gave up on the consultation because nothing relevant could be found in the results.
quotes: RS consultations proved to be overall helpful to the participants in problem solving during their writing assignments. In 170 problem spaces (69.4%), RS consultation had a positive effect and resulted in a correct text formulation or revision. However, RS use led to an incorrect text, having a negative effect in 31 problem spaces (12.7%). In the remaining 44 problem spaces (18%), the participants abandoned RS consultation due to difficulties finding relevant items from the query results

rows.value: (PDF p. 15) What the partnership actually supplied — What the partnership delivered: a division of labour in which the suite supplied items the writers could not access instantly because they had been neither acquired nor fully internalised, and let them test and readjust their form-meaning mappings, so that writer and tool jointly solved problems the writer alone could not have solved as effectively.
quotes: By and large, RS was shown to serve as an intellectual partner to the participants through a cognitive division of labor and to enhance their intellectual performance for solving lexico-grammatical problems that arose while writing. To give only the simplest description of the typical division of labor that happened in problem solving, RS provided the participants with lexical and grammatical options that they would not have been able to access instantly, as these items had been neither acquired nor fully internalized (i.e., compensatory problem solving). RS also made it possible to test and readjust their form-meaning mappings (i.e., confirmatory problem solving). As such, the participants and the suite jointly solved linguistic problems in ways that the participants alone would not have been able to do—at least not as effectively

Where the writer already had a candidate and only needed it checked, the suite produced correct text 76.8% of the time and was abandoned in 10.5% of cases. Where the writer had no candidate — precisely the gap the tool exists to fill — the figures were 59.2% and 28.2%, so nearly three in ten of those consultations ended with the writer giving up. A query interface can only be asked what its user can already formulate, and the better formed the question the better the answer, which means the yield of this class of support scales with the competence it is meant to compensate for. That is the same shape as the finding elsewhere in this corpus that weak learners are weak help seekers because they do not realise they need help: there the routing failure is in who asks, here it is in what can be asked.
quotes: In terms of problem type, the rate of positive effects from RS consultation was considerably higher with confirmatory problems. rows.value: medium · The contrast is large, internally consistent across two different measures, and drawn within the same participants and the same coding pass, which insulates it from the missing control group. It rests on one rater's correctness judgements with 84% agreement on a fifth of the data, on six people, and on 16% of the queries they performed.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The study coded the text and the writer's satisfaction separately, which lets it report how often the writer was wrong about the tool. Twenty consultations ended in incorrect text that the writer believed had gone well; thirteen consultations produced correct text that felt like failures. The asymmetry matters: undetected failure is the commoner error, and one named cause is the tool itself, since a web search returned enough hits on an ungrammatical string to confirm it. This is a third independent demonstration in this corpus that asking a user whether a support helped measures something other than whether it helped — alongside the design study where objective comprehension separated the conditions while self-rated ease was identical in both, and the game study where the best-performing children rated their own learning lowest. The consequence for withdrawal is direct. Any regime in which the learner elects to stop using the support depends on the learner detecting when it is no longer needed or no longer working, and here they could not, in the direction that flatters the tool. Note the size: 20 and 13 out of 245, established by one coder's judgement of correctness.

rows.value: The problem-solving performance rates presented above, however, did not necessarily match the participants' perceptions of the consultation results. The participants were dissatisfied with 13 out of the total 170 problem spaces where RS consultation had a positive effect whereas 20 problem spaces ended up with an incorrect text even though the participants perceived them as successfully solved. These mismatches were caused by different factors such as a wrong solution retrieved from the query results or misapplication of the chosen solution to writing.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A support can damage the work it supports without ever giving a wrong answer. What the tool changed was not only how long a decision took but which decisions felt worth making: its availability raised the salience of the problem class it handles, so writers attended to wording at the stage when their own goal was content, and one reported losing the thread of what he was trying to say. The condition is stated precisely and is a design-space dimension worth naming: the misalignment is between the writer's current goal and the tool's affordance, so the same support is an amplifier at the editing stage and an interference at the drafting stage. That gives a reason to remove a support that has nothing to do with dependence, learning or fading — the support should be absent when the goal it serves is not the goal in hand — and it generalises directly to any always-available assistant embedded in a composition environment. Two cautions. The evidence is interview and stimulated recall from six people, with no measure of writing quality, no time-on-content data and no comparison against writing without the suite. And the same participants reported the opposite effect too, saying the tool let them venture beyond their current repertoire, so the sign depends on the stage rather than on the tool.

rows.value: However, the presence and use of RS heightened their awareness of language problems and provided a means to address them on the fly. Sometimes these affordances offered by RS led the participants to focus on linguistic features of writing more than they normally would. It is on these occasions that the main goals of the participants and the affordances of the tool were misaligned and thus RS consultation felt like an extra cognitive burden. This misalignment often took place at the drafting stage of writing, when their attentional resources were mainly focused on content.

(PDF p. 15) The mechanism of the distraction, named — The mechanism of the misalignment: these writers had no language-learning goal, but the tool's presence raised the salience of language problems and offered a way to act on them, so they attended to form more than they otherwise would; the burden appeared most at the drafting stage when attention was on content, matching earlier reports that corpus tools made writers focus unnecessarily on linguistic structure at the expense of content.
quotes: However, the presence and use of RS heightened their awareness of language problems and provided a means to address them on the fly. Sometimes these affordances offered by RS led the participants to focus on linguistic features of writing more than they normally would. It is on these occasions that the main goals of the participants and the affordances of the tool were misaligned and thus RS consultation felt like an extra cognitive burden. This misalignment often took place at the drafting stage of writing, when their attentional resources were mainly focused on content rather than on rhetorical concerns. This resonates with the evaluative comments by some participants in Hafner and Candlin (2007) that using corpus tools made them focus unnecessarily on linguistic structure at the expense of content

rows.value: (PDF p. 13) The support competing with the task it supports — The cost side: the consultation cycle was cognitively taxing because it required decisions at every step while attention was already committed to the writing, and participants became engrossed enough to lose the thread of their content, one saying it can easily distract you and that he was tempted to use every resource to confirm accuracy.
quotes: also cognitively taxing, as it required them to make decisions at every step, when much of their attentional resources were already consumed by other various aspects of the writing task at hand. Closely related, some participants also reported that they sometimes became so engrossed in their RS consultations that they had their flow of thoughts interrupted in terms of global content of their writing, especially at the drafting stage. This point was poignantly expressed by Ian: (…) what bothered me a little was that it can easily distract you from your writing. You cannot afford to be interrupted while writing down what is shaping up in your head in terms of content. But when I use this tool, I am tempted to use each resource here to confirm the accuracy

rows.value: (PDF p. 15) Amplification and burden, traced to a goal mismatch — The reversal: a suite meant to amplify cognition was sometimes experienced as cognitively taxing, and the author traces the conflicting perceptions to misalignment between the participants' goals and the tool's affordances.
quotes: While the reference suite was supposed to amplify their cognition in problem solving as described above, the participants sometimes found the use of the tool to be cognitively taxing. Most of these conflicting perceptions among participants of the current study can be traced back to misalignments between the goals of the participants and the affordances offered by the tool

rows.value: (PDF p. 15) What the partnership actually supplied — What the partnership delivered: a division of labour in which the suite supplied items the writers could not access instantly because they had been neither acquired nor fully internalised, and let them test and readjust their form-meaning mappings, so that writer and tool jointly solved problems the writer alone could not have solved as effectively.
quotes: By and large, RS was shown to serve as an intellectual partner to the participants through a cognitive division of labor and to enhance their intellectual performance for solving lexico-grammatical problems that arose while writing. To give only the simplest description of the typical division of labor that happened in problem solving, RS provided the participants with lexical and grammatical options that they would not have been able to access instantly, as these items had been neither acquired nor fully internalized (i.e., compensatory problem solving). RS also made it possible to test and readjust their form-meaning mappings (i.e., confirmatory problem solving). As such, the participants and the suite jointly solved linguistic problems in ways that the participants alone would not have been able to do—at least not as effectively

rows.value: (PDF p. 1) Abstract — The study's own summary: the suite served as an effective cognitive tool extending the participants' powers on lexical and grammatical problems, the individual resources each had unique functions suggesting concordancing is best used in combination, and some participants had difficulties stemming largely from the nature of their writing tasks, their writing stage and the goals arising from them.
quotes: Results showed that while the reference suite served as an effective cognitive tool extending the cognitive powers of the participants in solving lexical and grammatical problems, the individual resources in the suite were each shown to have unique functions for which they were best suited, suggesting that concordancing may optimally be consulted in combination with other resources. However, some participants also experienced difficulties in using the tool stemming largely from the nature of their writing tasks and writing stages, and different goals and needs arising from them. This paper concludes by discussing theoretical and pedagogical implications of the findings

rows.value: (PDF p. 15) The mechanism of the distraction, named — The distraction finding is a mechanism, not a complaint about usability. The tool did not merely take time; it changed what the writer attended to, raising the salience of the class of problem it solves at a stage when the writer's own goal was content. So a support can degrade the work it supports without ever giving a wrong answer, simply by making its own sub-problem feel urgent. That generalises immediately to any always-available assistant embedded in a composition tool, and it gives a reason to withdraw a support that has nothing to do with dependence or with learning: the support should be absent when the writer's goal is not the one it serves. Note that the paper reaches this from interviews and stimulated recall, with no measure of writing quality or of time on content, so the mechanism is described rather than demonstrated.

rows.value: medium · The mechanism is described consistently by several participants and matches an independent earlier report, but it rests entirely on self-report from six people with no behavioural or product measure and no unsupported comparison condition.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Fit to the stated need predicted use backwards. The two components added specifically because these were academic writers — a scholarly search engine and per-discipline custom search — took under 5% of queries each and were gradually dropped, while the general bilingual dictionary the participants had used for years took a quarter of all queries in spite of three hours of training and personal feedback aimed at the concordancers. Every reason given is about the conditions of the work rather than the quality of the resource: deadline pressure left no room to explore, the narrow corpora returned too few hits to decide on, and the doctoral students said their own reading already supplied field vocabulary. The transferable point is that a support's chance of being used is set largely outside the support, by what the person already knows how to drive and how much time the surrounding work leaves. It also gives this corpus a clean instance of an entrenched worse-fitting tool beating a better-fitting new one, which is a competing explanation for many adoption failures that get read as design failures. And it is the only place in the paper where anything is withdrawn: the withdrawal is learner-elected, applies to a component the learners judged useless rather than one they had outgrown, and is reported without any measure attached.

rows.value: Meanwhile, GS and CSE were consulted the least, accounting for less than 5% of all queries... Last, the participants consulted Naver more than any other resource (25.6%), even though the training and feedback during the study were focused on the various, often novel, ways of solving linguistic problems using the concordancers.

(PDF p. 14) The purpose-built resources were the least used — The purpose-built components failed in use: the two resources added to serve academic writing accounted for under 5% of queries each, because under deadline the participants could not afford to explore genre patterns, because the engines returned no or few hits, and because doctoral students said their own reading already gave them discipline vocabulary — so the author reclassifies them as research tools for writers with time rather than reference tools for writers without it.
quotes: Meanwhile, GS and CSE were consulted the least, accounting for less than 5% of all queries, and were mainly used to check register. This was a somewhat surprising result, as these two search engines had been included in the suite specifically to meet the needs of academic writing and to compensate for the weaknesses of Google. In actual use, however, the participants could hardly afford to explore discipline- or genre-specific textual patterns using these resources as they were working on their papers under pressure with tight deadlines. Even when the participants did use these resources to check whether a certain string was in the right register, GS and CSE often returned no or few hits of the queried item, making the participants dismiss them as too small to be useful. Also worth noting is that some participants, especially PhD students, pointed out that they did not feel much need for a discipline- specific corpus because they had their own content knowledge and readings to turn to for usages of discipline-specific vocabulary. These findings, in sum, imply that GS and CSE would be more usefully consulted as research tools that help writers discover discipline-specific textual patterns and genre characteristics when given sufficient time and motivation as in Lee and Swales’ (2006) experimental course. These resources may still be lacking as reference tools that can assist time-constrained writers in finding immediate solutions to problems

rows.value: (PDF p. 14) Training aimed at the concordancers, use went to the familiar dictionary — Where the queries actually went: the bilingual dictionary took 25.6% of all queries, more than any other resource, even though the training and feedback targeted the concordancers, because the participants were doing a great deal of first-to-second-language translation, had used that resource for years and knew exactly what to query, and it was versatile — under deadline they turned to the familiar.
quotes: Last, the participants consulted Naver more than any other resource (25.6%), even though the training and feedback during the study were focused on the various, often novel, ways of solving linguistic problems using the concordancers. This frequent use of the bilingual dictionary by the participants can be linked to a few factors. First, the participants performed a higher number of translation queries than expected for students of their academic level. This shows that that they performed a great deal of conceptual and textual L1 to L2 translation. Second, the participants had already been using this resource for years prior to the study, so they knew very well what to query and where to click. Third, Naver was the most versatile resource in RS proving extra linguistic information such as synonyms and collocations. While working on the real-life writing assignments that came with tight deadlines, the participants often turned to this familiar resource that served multiple purposes

rows.value: (PDF p. 13) The one thing that was withdrawn, and who withdrew it — The only support that stopped being used: the two academic search engines were intended for checking register, and the participants gradually stopped using them as they found the resources too small to supply enough data to decide on.
quotes: The final resources that drew a common response were GS and CSE. The participants all mentioned that these two Google resources were intended for checking the register of given linguistic items but they gradually stopped using them over time as they realized these resources were too small in size to provide sufficient data on which to base their decisions

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Each resource used for its own purposes — Each resource acquired a distinct role in use — the bilingual dictionary for second-language equivalents, Google for simple confirmation, the two tagged corpora for collocation — and in about a quarter of problem spaces several resources were combined to corroborate or extend a first result.
quotes: A general trend emerged, suggesting that each resource had a unique set of predominant purposes for which it was consulted. For example, the participants preferred to consult Naver for L2 equivalent, Google for simple confirmation, and COCA and JTW for collocation (see Table 4). Another closely related finding was that in about a quarter of the total problem spaces, the participants consulted different resources in combination within a given problem space to corroborate or expand on initial query results. This overall trend demonstrates that the participants were aware of what information each resource provided and strategically used each resource for a distinct purpose

quotes: Next, they received three hours of individual tutoring from me, which covered basic corpus linguistics concepts, the purposes for which each resource in RS can be consulted, and strategies for their effective use. After using RS for a few weeks independently whenever they needed to consult reference resources, the participants recorded their uses of the suite for an hour using a free screen-recording software (BB Flashback) installed on their computer. While watching the screen-recorded videos together, I provided each participant with feedback on how to improve his or her RS consultation
