But the cohort is six people, two resources were technically deficient during the study, and no comparison exists against a setting without deadline pressure.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The support never changes and is never removed; what is supposed to change is the person's stance toward it. Two moves make that explicit. Contingency is retained as a value but relocated from the tool to the human wrapper around it — training should be progressive and contingent on individual abilities, while the suite itself is identical for everyone throughout. And dependence is answered by instruction rather than withdrawal: students are told to stop expecting the resource to work for them and to accept that greater autonomy brings greater responsibility. The participants themselves name what is missing, and it is contingency's other half: unlike a tutor, the suite leaves the user to ask the right question and judge the answer, with no guarantee. Nothing in the system models what this writer can already do — monitoring runs one way, the writer evaluating every result and the suite evaluating nothing about the writer, the same asymmetry this corpus records in software-engineering tools. The stance is a defensible position and joins the small group of papers here arguing that some supports are permanent by design. But the evidence offered for it is of the wrong kind: awareness, confidence and a sense of independence, all self-reported at a final interview with the suite still installed, in a study whose own data show these writers misjudging their success 20 times. Nothing measures what any participant can write without the tool, and the comparison that would have started to answer it is listed as future work.

rows.value: Jae and Goeun pointed out that unlike getting support from a human tutor or expert, it is still almost solely the user's responsibility to find a solution by feeding the right query terms into the resources and making the correct judgments about the results, and even then there is no guarantee that the solution found is the right one... Firstly, learner training should be progressive and contingent on the abilities and traits of individual learners... students should be taught to abandon the expectation that reference resources work for them... the greater autonomy afforded by reference resources comes with a greater responsibility for their own writing and learning.

rows.value: (PDF p. 12) What the participants said they gained — What participants reported gaining: greater attention to accuracy and appropriateness, increased lexico-grammatical awareness, and increased if not dramatic confidence amounting to a sense of independence, with one participant saying he had felt helpless before and now believed he could produce refined text given time and motivation, and that the suite helps users edit their writing on their own.

cards.meta: 2012 · Proceedings of the 25th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology · doi 10.1145/2380116.2380125 · Route C

framework or design space, design principle, primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

CrowdScape operationalizes prior HCI techniques rather than an explicit learning or scaffolding theory: Task Fingerprinting supplies behavioral traces, Shneiderman’s dynamic queries supply immediate linked feedback, and parallel coordinates represent patterned outputs. These sources are instantiated in the system’s measurement and interaction design; claims about users developing mental models remain author interpretations supported by grounded cases rather than measured learning outcomes.

medium · The system mechanisms, grounded cases, counterexample, and limits are clearly reported, but evidence comes from four author-conducted exploratory cases without controlled comparative evaluation. Claims about mental models, decision improvement, efficiency, learning, and the instrumentation trade-off therefore remain bounded or unmeasured.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CL-01-INTEGRATED-EVIDENCE
items.lead: Pairing representations of work products with process traces provides a triangulation scaffold for quality-control sensemaking: organizers can compare what was produced with how it was produced and form revisable interpretations where fixed correctness signals are weak.

rows.value: For creative or complex work, post-hoc output analysis and behavioral traces are insufficient alone but provide complementary insights in concert; unifying them helps users understand how worker behaviors correlate with end products and act on task or submission decisions.

cards.title: Distributed Cognition as a Lens to Understand the Effects of Scaffolds: The Role of Transfer of Responsibility

rows.value: S2W-7492F3CEDC874E5F80A1A5FC
other
concept or theory, lineage or history, review or meta analysis, framework or design space, design principle, failure or counterevidence

Belland reframes scaffold transfer through distributed cognition: support can carry information and process load, but the learner must retain executive control over choices, consequences, and action paths and develop schemas that later incorporate tool-supported processes. The paper draws explicitly on Wood’s scaffolding and fading, Hutchins’s distributed cognition, Perkins’s person-plus account, Salomon’s effects-with/effects-of distinction, Langer’s mindfulness, and transfer work by Bransford and Schwartz. It translates these traditions into four design guidelines, but neither the combined package nor the proposed distributed-cognition mechanism is directly tested.

medium · The paper offers a transparent analytical review and framework derivation with several bounded findings from cited studies. Its central distributed-cognition mechanism, the four-guideline package, and durable transfer claims are not directly tested, and reviewed evidence comes from heterogeneous tasks, populations, and scaffold systems.

items.heading: Claim 1 · C-001
items.lead: The field should not treat improved supported performance as evidence of durable learning. Transfer is a separate target concerning later capability and who carries responsibility for task execution.

rows.value: Scaffolding has two distinct effects: higher performance while support is present and greater skill resulting from having used support. Achieving the latter requires transferring responsibility from the student–scaffold system to the student.

When considering scaffolding, there are two effects of interest: effects with scaffolding, or
the extent to which scaffolding helps learners perform at a higher level while using it, and effects
of scaffolding, or the extent to which having used the scaffolding leads to greater skill (Salomon

also perform the task unaided in the future. To promote the effect of scaffolding, one needs to
promote the transfer of responsibility from the student and scaffolds to just the student.

Can a similar strategy to that of Kayluga and Sweller (2005) be used with scaffolds that

problems have multiple possible solutions and multiple solution paths (Jonassen 2000).

(PDF p. 8) First full paragraph under “Implications of a distributed cognition model for scaffold design.” — The proposed mechanism is that learners form schemas incorporating processes formerly supported by tools, enabling revised approaches to later tasks.
quotes:
Central to distributed cognition is the idea that, after the distributed cognition system has
operated for some time, one tool or one individual can be taken away and the remaining
individuals and tools can adjust (Hutchins 1995). This can happen when individuals create
schemas that incorporate processes supported by tools (Greeno and van de Sande 2007;
Hollan et al. 2000; Vosniadou 2007). Such schemas contain mental representations of
categories of concepts and general processes by which individuals make sense of the world
and perform actions (Johnson-Laird 1980). Thus, the effect of computer-based scaffolds
may be in students’ creation of schemas that guide subsequent approaches to problem
solving (Salomon et al. 1991). When students engage in new tasks, their revised schemas
guide their approaches.

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) Paragraph headed “Lynchpin of a distributed cognitive system: the executive function.” — Learners must retain executive control over choices, consequences, strategy, and action paths if they are to assume responsibility for the task.
quotes:
The ultimate determinant
of whether students can assume responsibility from a distributed cognition system is the
extent to which they maintain throughout the executive function of the system, defined as
“making choices, operating at decision points to explore the consequences of options and
select[ing] a path of action” (Bibok et al. 2009; Landry et al. 2009; Perkins 1996, p. 96;
Salomon 1993). If students are not able to make choices, explore consequences of
options, and otherwise make decisions regarding strategy, then they will not be able to
assume the responsibility of the scaffolded task (Bibok et al. 2009; Landry et al. 2009;
Perkins 1996; Salomon 1993). They then will not be able to complete the task unaided
(Bibok et al. 2009; Landry et al. 2009; Perkins 1996; Salomon 1993). Thus scaffolds
need to be designed to allow students to make choices, operate at decision points, and
select paths of action.

cards.title: Can the Interactive Whiteboard Support Young Children's Collaborative Communication and Thinking in Classroom Science Activities?

rows.value: S2W-AA3CE0D8AE562A6267B68AE5
other
primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, framework or design space

Twelve English primary teachers and their classes were filmed over three science lessons each, thirty hours in all, with one group of three eight-to-ten-year-olds per class working at an interactive whiteboard while the rest did the same task on paper; two of those groups are analysed here in transcript detail. The paper is negative in a useful way. Its own abstract says the whiteboard is not an entirely distinctive or pedagogically transformative learning resource. Two mechanisms are documented in enough detail to reuse. First, an affordance let children skip the hard part: whenever the group could not agree which category a card belonged in, they copied and pasted it into both, and the authors judge that this closed down discussion too quickly while noting that an extended search for resolution can itself aid cognitive growth. The children noticed too, one saying they were getting too used to copy-paste, copy-paste. Second, the turn-taking rule adopted to make sharing fair produced the opposite: the child holding the pen either dominated the decision or dropped out of the conversation, and in interview the children described sharing the board rather than sharing ideas. A second group with the same supports treated the talk rules as a thinking tool rather than as etiquette, and the authors say their design cannot establish why. No learning outcome is measured anywhere, which they state.

medium · An honest exploratory study whose evidence is strong for mechanism and absent for effect. Strengths: thirty hours of video across twelve classrooms with a fixed and a roving camera, field notes, pupil interviews, teacher commentaries and whiteboard screen records; transcripts printed at a granularity that lets a reader check the reading, with gaze, gesture and who is touching the screen recorded alongside the words; a named analytic scheme; deliberate searching for counter-examples such as disputes and disengagement; and teachers involved in the analysis. Bounds, most of them stated by the authors: two groups of three children are analysed out of twelve classes, and how those two were chosen from the corpus is described only as illustrative; there is no comparison condition and no measure of science attainment, which the authors say was never the aim; the target groups were selected by teachers as responsive and camera-tolerant, so the sample tilts positive; the interpretation of talk is qualitative judgement by design; and the authors state their design cannot establish whether the difference between the two groups is developmental, contextual or personal.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A support feature dissolved the task it was there to support, observed turn by turn and named by the authors as a holding strategy. The intellectual work in the activity was deciding which of two categories an ambiguous item belonged in; copy and paste let the group put it in both, so the decision never had to be made. They reached for it on nearly every card, and both the researchers and the children noticed - one child saying they had copied and pasted all of them so far, another that they were getting too used to copy-paste, copy-paste. The authors' judgement is that it closed down discussion too quickly, with the point that an extended search for resolution is itself where cognitive growth happens. This is the criterion the collaboration-script tradition states and this is it failing in the field: a scaffold should not make redundant the activities the learner is supposed to perform. Two things make it transferable. Nothing was wrong with the feature - copy and paste is neutral and in another task would be pure gain; it became a bypass only because it offered an exit from the single decision the task existed to force. And the children's awareness did not stop them, which is a warning about relying on metacognitive prompts to prevent this.

rows.value: From a cognitive perspective, it could appear that the children's use of copy and paste is becoming too automatic and easy for them, in effect closing down discussion too quickly (bearing in mind that an extended search for resolution can itself aid cognitive growth, (Howe and Tolmie 2003)). However, the children are not unaware of this. At 00.10:52, Patricia says 'I think we've copied and pasted all of them so far,' and then a few minutes later... 'Yeah, we're getting too used to copy / paste, copy / paste.'... the thinking of the Dark and Light group moved toward the acknowledgment of multiple lines of scientific argument, resolved by the children's use in this lesson of the copy-and-paste function as a sort of holding strategy.

rows.value: (PDF p. 12) The first disagreement, and how it ended — What happened in the first minute: the group split at once, with one child pursuing an argument about the earth having a light and a dark side while another proposed copying and pasting the card into both categories; the two scientific arguments were never brought together, the copy-and-paste proposal was eventually accepted, and the group turned to the technical challenge of executing it, at which point one child said there you go, now you've got two earths, using you rather than we.

rows.value: (PDF p. 13) Copy and paste closes down the discussion, and the children notice — This is a documented case of a support feature dissolving the task it was there to support, and it is unusually clean because the escape route is a specific, named affordance. The intellectual work in the activity is deciding which category an ambiguous item belongs in; copy and paste means the group never has to decide. They used it on almost every card - one child says they have copied and pasted all of them so far - and the authors judge that it closed down discussion too quickly, citing the point that an extended search for resolution is itself where the cognitive growth happens. items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: A support for fair participation produced the two failure modes it exists to prevent, and the authors report it as a repeated observation rather than an oddity. Whoever held the pen either drove the decision alone or fell silent, and both appear in the printed transcripts: one child argues her own line while holding the pen and places the card without the others; the same child, on a later turn, says almost nothing while the other two reason. The children's interview closes the case, because asked whether the board helped them share ideas they described taking turns with the object and wanting to get it done, which the authors gloss as sharing the board rather than sharing their ideas. Two general points follow. When a support is embodied in a single token - one pen, one object movable at a time - the etiquette of who holds the token can displace the collaboration the support was for, and the scarcity is often an artefact of the hardware rather than a pedagogical choice. And the failure is invisible to any compliance measure: this group followed the turn-taking rule perfectly, which is exactly how the exclusion was produced.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: Two groups, the same designed supports, two entirely different things taken from them. Both classes were given the talk rules, both had them read out at the start of the lesson, and both could recite them afterwards. One group explains them as conduct - they are easier, instead of arguing all the time, instead of shouting over each other - and one child quotes talking together helps you think while, as the authors note, that formal knowledge is not evident in what the group actually does. The other group explains the same rules epistemically: discussing and explaining why sometimes gets better answers, three brains are better than one. That gap is the whole distance between a support taken over as a way of thinking and a support taken over as a rule of behaviour, and it is invisible to any compliance measure, because both groups complied. For a synthesis this is the internalisation question in miniature and it names what would have to be measured to answer it - not whether the support is followed but what the person takes it to be for. The authors then decline to explain the difference, saying their design cannot establish whether it is developmental, contextual or personal, and that honesty is part of the value.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The paper's own summary of what a support is worth on its own, which is nothing, together with a clear statement that no outcome was measured. Both matter for a synthesis. The first is the conditionality: the board's contribution is entirely dependent on the teacher's support strategies, the classroom's social routines and the talk rules, and where those broke down - technical trouble, weak collaboration skills - the technology's contribution went to zero or worse. The second is the measurement position, stated without hedging: isolating effects on attainment was never the aim, and the study does not compare the board with alternatives. On the two-part test for a learning claim this attempts neither half, because every observation was recorded while the children stood at the board using it; the one outcome-shaped phrase in the paper, identifiable contributions to productive communication and thinking, rests on the authors' reading of two transcripts. One slip is worth flagging inside this otherwise careful account: the discussion credits the board with providing online contingent guidance and support in real time without the teacher's physical presence, and nothing in either lesson shows the board adapting to a child. It displays, moves and duplicates; every adaptive act is a person's.

rows.value: It has been observed by researchers and teachers that the mere introduction of the IWB does not in itself have a transformative effect on classroom teaching and learning and may indeed reinforce familiar patterns of teacher-pupil interaction... It was accepted from the start of this research that it would not be easy in a relatively small-scale study to isolate the effects of particular experiences of collaborative IWB-use on primary children's attainment in science.

In practice, for any group of children, this type of CSCL therefore depends in part on certain wider factors relating to the teacher’s scaffolding strategies, the influence of classroom social routines and structures, and the productive use of “talk rules” for conversation and collaborative reasoning (Mercer et al. 2010; Warwick et al. 2010). This is not a simple “all-or-nothing” finding about IWB use for collaborative purposes. The groups discussed in this paper are captured at a certain stage in their collaborative learning with the IWB and neither demonstrates extended exploratory talk (unlike some others we observed, Mercer et al. 2010). The teachers are similarly in the process of adapting their professional knowledge about IWB use. Our evidence about children’s uses of the IWB in their collaborative groupwork demonstrates a highly integrated system of physical activity, spoken dialogue, and nonverbal communication, taking place in an identifiable classroom space with the IWB and other classroom resources. The knowledge building of children and teachers is best judged in context and over time

rows.value: (PDF p. 22) Limitations, no attainment measure and no comparison — The stated limitation: it was accepted from the start that a small study could not isolate the effects of collaborative board use on children's science attainment, so the aim was the processes and nature of the communication instead, and the study does not attempt to compare the board directly with alternative ways of supporting children's learning.
quotes: It was accepted from the start of this research that it would not be easy in a relatively small-scale study to isolate the effects of particular experiences of collaborative IWB-use on primary children’s attainment in science. We aimed, rather, to focus on the processes and nature of the children’s communication and collaborative activity at the IWB, maintaining close links to the complex systems and structures of ordinary classroom practice. We assume that for some time to come English primary teachers will be in the position of employing already embedded IWBs for different purposes alongside other devices in the primary classroom environment. The specific IWB focus in this study accepts its interrelationship with other classroom resources and activities over time, and does not attempt to compare the IWB directly with alternative ways of supporting children

rows.value: (PDF p. 1) Abstract, the finding and the qualification — The paper's own verdict: the board can make some identifiable contributions to children's productive communication and thinking, but it is not seen to be an entirely distinctive or pedagogically transformative learning resource, and the children's knowledge building is closely related to their engagement with the board's affordances and their productive dialogue, essentially supported by the teacher's scaffolding strategies, the talk rules and the classroom participation structures.
quotes: Our observational analysis of two examples of children’s collaborative activity in different classrooms, together with subsequent group interviews, suggests that the IWB can make some identifiable contributions to children’s productive communication and thinking. However the IWB is not seen to be an entirely distinctive or pedagogically transformative learning resource in the primary classroom. In our developing conceptual framework, the children’s knowledge building is closely related to their active engagement in using IWB affordances and their productive dialogue, essentially supported by the teacher’s scaffolding strategies, the establishment and use of “talk rules” in conversation, and the opportunities and constraints applying in classroom participation structures. These conditions help the children to deal with interconnected social, cognitive, and technical problems arising over time

rows.value: (PDF p. 23) Conclusion, when collaboration breaks and how groups split — The conclusion's two-sidedness: children can engage effectively in the shared dynamic dialogic space, but this is by no means certain on every occasion, and in examples not included here productive collaboration was particularly disrupted by technical difficulties and by limited skills in working together; when technical problems became frustrating, groups either developed a collective self-efficacy that bonded them or abandoned the task and sought the teacher, which the authors read as a possible amplifying effect on social relations and inclusion.
quotes: The research suggests that the IWB can be used collaboratively in a variety of science activities closely related to familiar classroom practice and the children can engage effectively in the collective learning experience that we have called the “shared dynamic dialogic space.” However, this is by no means certain on every occasion. As we found in certain classroom examples not included in this paper, productive collaboration can be particularly disrupted by technical difficulties and by children’s sometimes limited skills in communicating and working together productively. There are undoubtedly potential disadvantages of IWBs in primary classrooms, including regular technical glitches, placement problems on crowded walls, health and safety issues relating to the light sources and screen quality, and so on. When technical issues became frustrating, groups in our study responded differently, either developing a collective self-efficacy through discussion which helped to bond the group practically, or abandoning the task quickly and seeking the teacher’s help. We may be seeing an amplifying effect on social relations and inclusion due to the combination of technological challenge, collaborative activity, and learning focus: when the technology is very visible and possibly frustrating a group of children may become either more collaborative or more differentiated in their complementary role taking

The authors are explicit that isolating effects on attainment was never the aim and that the study does not compare the board with alternatives. items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The paper's positive contribution is a small, concrete design space that maps interface functions to the collective cognitive work they carry, and it is worth having because it is stated at the right grain. The page sorter, showing icons of every screen in the activity, served as external memory, and teachers planned around that. Copy, paste, clone and drag support editing; self-paced screen transitions and easy switching between screens support refocusing and returning to earlier work. The large vertical screen makes a drawing an object of joint attention, so the artifact itself provokes evaluation and adjustment - one child says no, they don't look like that, and the drawing is redone. That last mechanism is the strongest thing in the paper, and it is not adaptive support at all: it is persistence plus shared visibility, which lets a group criticise its own external representation. Note the authors' caution, which is a good rule for any such mapping: they refuse a one-to-one relationship between a function and a type of thinking, since the same function serves different purposes and thinking can be supported on paper too. Set against the same paper's copy-and-paste finding, the design space has an honest shape - the same function that supported editing also supplied the escape from deciding.

This is not to suggest a limited one-to-one relationship between such IWB functions and certain types of thinking. quotes: The supporting conditions for children’s collaborative learning at the IWB are represented partly in Fig. 1 by the connection of teacher mediation with dialogic space. Three main types of teacher activity include: the use of IWB affordances to set up the task (although note that children also perceive their own IWB affordances, which may not match the teacher’s thinking); the use of other dialogic and interpersonal scaffolding strategies for supporting the children’s talk and group activity (including the introduction of “talk rules” mentioned above); and the teacher’s influence on classroom participation structures. The participation structures, defined by Cazden (1986, p. 437) as “…the rights and obligations of participants with respect to who can say what, when, and to whom,” appear in the establishment of the classroom ethos and the use of accepted routines as well as moment-to- moment social interactions. Specific participation structures (such as co-operative turn taking) provide opportunities and constraints for children

quotes: Our analysis of children’s IWB use for collaborative science learning in the primary classroom is informed by a Vygotskian, sociocultural understanding of the ways in which thinking and learning may be shared between those involved in any purposeful activity. cards.title: Concept-driven interaction design research

rows.value: other
concept or theory, lineage or history, framework or design space, design principle, measurement or method

Concept-driven interaction design research is explicitly grounded in Weick’s process view of theorizing and in HCI precedents joining artifacts, design activity, and theory, including artifact-as-theory-nexus, the task-artifact cycle, and research through design. These lineages support a design-centered, theory-oriented method in which concept artifacts embody theoretical relations, become objects of critique, and are positioned against existing concepts. The grounding is conceptual and methodological rather than an empirical outcome evaluation.

medium · The article offers explicit, transferable concepts, principles, lineage, and a detailed methodological framework, but supports them through theoretical argument and illustrative historical cases rather than systematic empirical evaluation. All effects and outcome implications are therefore retained as author proposals or bounded reviewer interpretations.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims

items.heading: Claim 1 · CL-001
items.lead: Within the review’s lens, a concept artifact is a semantic support form: a persistent, inspectable composition that externalizes theoretical relations for communal interpretation and extension. This is a bounded mechanism interpretation; the paper does not demonstrate that encountering such artifacts improves comprehension, learning, transfer, or performance.

rows.value: Concept designs can function as externalized carriers of knowledge that is not fully expressible in text: their whole composition embodies the combined knowledge shaping the design, makes emergent theoretical qualities perceptible, and can frame or challenge subsequent design work.

(PDF p. 11) Section 2.1, opening paragraph — The authors claim that a designed artifact can externalize knowledge not fully expressible in conventional textual research outputs and can frame later design work.
quotes: We argue that exploiting concept-driven design research allows us to develop knowledge that cannot be fully expressed in text or other typical research outcome formats. A theoretical concept manifested as a designed artifact can be seen as externalized knowledge; the concept itself carries most of the experience and results from the design process. The concept design becomes a carrier of knowledge but also establishes a conceptual framework and challenge for future design work. We argue that the concept’s capacity of carrying knowledge is highly desirable from a research perspective.

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Section 2.1, paragraph beginning “The key here” — The authors locate the artifact’s knowledge-carrying capacity in its embodiment of the combined knowledge that shaped the design.
quotes: The key here is that the concept carries and manifests all the combined knowledge that has influenced the design. It is in this way that knowledge is embodied in the artifact; it is not necessarily expressed in words or other descriptions, even though such descriptions do complement and strengthen the experience and understanding of the concept design.

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Section 2.1, paragraph defining the character of a concept design — The authors argue that a concept design’s whole composition exposes emergent qualities and supports rapid apprehension of its character.
quotes: Concept designs have one obvious and valued quality—anyone can almost instantly get an overall understanding of the character of the concept without any expertise or special training. The character of a concept design is the overall organizing principle that makes up the composition of the design as a whole (Nelson & Stolterman, 2003). This idea is based on the assumption that the whole reveals emergent qualities that cannot be made visible or measured as the sum of the part’s qualities. This is a core quality of any concept design and is the major reason for why concept designs have a value different from text statements or other traditional theoretical formats.

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) Section 1.3, paragraph contrasting measures of success — The authors explicitly distinguish theoretical improvement from improvement of a practical use situation.
quotes: Research aimed at theorizing has another measure of success, which is whether or not the research leads to improvement of theoretical concepts. Of course, the notion of “improvement” has to be made explicit, for instance, in the sense defined by Weick. Whether such theoretical advancements lead to improvements of a situation is of lesser interest, or maybe even of no interest at all.

cards.title: Scaffolding and achievement in problem-based and inquiry learning: A response to Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark (2006)

rows.value: other
concept or theory, review or meta analysis, framework or design space, failure or counterevidence

One half of a public disagreement, and it should be read next to the paper it answers. Kirschner, Sweller and Clark argued in 2006 that constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential and inquiry teaching all fail because they leave learners to find essential information for themselves. Hmelo-Silver, Duncan and Chinn reply that two of those five do not belong in the list: problem-based and inquiry learning are heavily scaffolded, so evidence against unguided discovery says nothing about them. They agree with their opponents that unguided and experientially based approaches lack evidence, and that the assumption behind pure discovery has repeatedly been shown to be flawed. Their positive case is a description of the guidance these approaches actually supply, in three families: making disciplinary thinking visible through modelling, coaching and fading; embedding expert guidance in hints, video and just-in-time mini-lectures; and structuring the task itself through whiteboards, routines and software that restricts what can be done when. From this they press a reversal, that modelling resembles worked examples and inquiry scaffolds resemble process worksheets, so what the other side recommends is often already inside the approaches it condemns. The evidence chapters are borrowed rather than produced here: an overlooked meta-analysis, a rereading of a study both sides cite, and effect sizes of 0.44 and 0.37 from a then-unpublished study of 1,803 pupils. They concede that controlled experiments are scarce, that self-selection affects most studies in this literature, that they are not arguing against direct instruction, and that how to balance the two is unclear.

medium · This paper measures nothing. It is a seven-page invited reply, and every number on this card reaches it from a cited study, several of them by its own authors and one unpublished at the time. What is solid is what the authors themselves assert and concede, which is on the page and quoted here: that they agree unguided discovery fails, that controlled experiments in this area are scarce, that self-selection affects most studies of problem-based learning, that they are not arguing against direct instruction, and that how to balance the two is still unclear. The description of the three families of scaffold is concrete and checkable against the named environments. What is uncertain is everything the two sides dispute: whether these approaches are the ones the opposing paper meant, since no threshold for guidance is given; whether modelling and worked examples are near enough to make one side's evidence irrelevant to the other, which is asserted not shown; and which measure counts as the outcome, the real content of the Patel dispute. The card records the disagreement without resolving it, and marks the opposing position as this paper's rendering of it.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The paper's central move, and it narrows the dispute rather than widening it. Both sides here accept that unguided discovery fails; the authors say so explicitly and cite the same source, Mayer 2004, for the point. What is contested is a classification: whether problem-based and inquiry learning belong in the class the other paper condemns. That is answerable by inspecting instances, which is what the next four pages do, and it is not answerable by efficacy evidence from either side until it is settled. Two things weaken the move. The paper gives no criterion for how much guidance takes an approach out of the minimally guided class, so any weakly guided implementation can be set aside as not a real instance. And the authors immediately perform a merge of their own, treating problem-based and inquiry learning as synonymous because they found no dimension that consistently separates them, which pools medical education, middle school science and MBA teaching under one heading. A reader should also note that the opposing definitions are quoted here with a page reference that does not match the published article, so the fairness of the rendering cannot be checked from this document alone.

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Are PBL and IL Instances of Minimally Guided Instruction?, definitions — The definitions offered: in problem-based learning students learn content, strategies and self-directed learning skills by collaboratively solving problems, reflecting and inquiring; in inquiry learning they learn content and discipline-specific reasoning by collaboratively investigating. Both are organised around authentic problems, both emphasise collaboration, and the teacher facilitates and may supply content knowledge just in time.
quotes: In PBL, students learn content, strategies, and self-directed learning skills through collaboratively solving problems, reﬂecting on their experiences, and engaging in self-directed inquiry. In IL, students learn content as well as discipline-speciﬁc reasoning skills and practices (often in scientiﬁc disciplines) by collaboratively engaging in investi- gations. Both PBL and IL are organized around relevant, au- thentic problems or questions. Both place heavy emphasis on collaborative learning and activity. In both, students are cog- nitively engaged in sense making, developing evidence-based explanations, and communicating their ideas. The teacher plays a key role in facilitating the learning process and may provide content knowledge on a just-in-time basis

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Are PBL and IL Instances of Minimally Guided Instruction? — A boundary the authors themselves erase: having examined the range of instantiations, they found no dimensions that consistently distinguish problem-based from inquiry learning and think there are no clear-cut distinguishing features.
quotes: As we have examined the broad variety of instantiations of PBL and IL, we have not uncovered any dimensions that con- sistently distinguish between PBL and IL. Indeed, we think there are no clear-cut distinguishing features

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Are PBL and IL Instances of Minimally Guided Instruction? — The consequence for the rest of the paper: the two are treated as synonymous, despite divergent origins, because in practice the environments are often indistinguishable.
quotes: Thus, in practice PBL and IL environments are often indis- tinguishable, despite divergent origins and so we treat them as synonymous in this article

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Opening, the first charge — The disagreement is narrower than the titles suggest, and the card should say so plainly. Both sides accept that unguided discovery fails. What is contested is whether problem-based and inquiry learning belong in the class of minimally guided instruction. That is a classification question about the amount and timing of guidance in a family of named practices, and it is answerable in principle by inspecting instances, which is what this paper spends its first half doing. It is not answerable by either side's efficacy evidence, because the efficacy evidence only bears on the question once the classification is settled.
quotes: There are two major ﬂaws with Kirschner et al’s argument. The ﬁrst is a pedagogical one. Kirschner and colleagues have indiscriminately lumped together several distinct pedagog- ical approaches—constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based—under the category of min- imally guided instruction. We argue here that at least some of these approaches, in particular, problem-based learning (PBL) and inquiry learning (IL), are not minimally guided instructional approaches but rather provide extensive scaf- folding and guidance to facilitate student learning

rows.value: (PDF p. 5) Scaffolds That Structure Complex Tasks or Reduce Cognitive Load, the irrelevance charge — The irrelevance move is the strongest and the most fragile part of the argument at once. If the scaffolded environments described here are not minimally guided, then studies of unguided instruction do not test them, which is correct as logic. But it makes the paper's own position hard to falsify from the other direction: any implementation that turns out to be weakly guided can be set aside as not a real instance. The paper supplies no criterion for how much scaffolding is enough to leave the minimally guided class, and its own admission that there are no clear-cut features distinguishing problem-based from inquiry learning shows how loose the category boundaries are on this side of the dispute too.
quotes: Kirschner et al. touted worked examples and process worksheets as ef- fective methods of guided learning. But PBL and IL methods employ modeling that seems very similar to worked examples as well as scaffolds to guide inquiry that strongly resemble process worksheets (e.g., Kirschner & Erkens, 2006; White & Frederiksen, 1998). We think a close analysis of IL and PBL methods indicates that they are indeed strongly guided form of instruction. Studies showing that unguided or min- imally guided instruction is inferior to direct instruction are simply irrelevant to most approaches implementing PBL or IL

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Opening, the position being answered — One limit on verifying the dispute from this document alone: the definition attributed to the opposing paper is given a page reference of p. 1, which does not correspond to the pagination of the published article it cites, and the second quoted definition carries no page reference at all. A reader wanting to check whether the characterisation is fair must go to the original. The card records what this paper says the other side claims, and marks it as this paper's rendering rather than as established fact.
quotes: The authors loosely deﬁne minimally guided instruction as a learning context in which “learners, rather than being pre- sented with essential information, must discover or construct essential information for themselves” (p. 1). They conversely deﬁne direct guidance instruction as “providing information that fully explains the concepts and procedures that students are required to learn.” In their argument, Kirschner et al. contrast minimally guided instructional approaches with ap- proaches that provide direct instructional guidance and assert that minimally guided instructional approaches are ineffec- tive and inefﬁcient

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Are PBL and IL Instances of Minimally Guided Instruction? — The collapse of problem-based and inquiry learning into one category is worth noticing because it mirrors the very move the paper objects to. Kirschner and colleagues are criticised for lumping five approaches together; here two are merged on the ground that no dimensions consistently distinguish them. The merge may well be right, and the reasons given are concrete, that medical problems supply rich data to analyse and inquiry environments pose problems and supply resources. But it means the paper's evidence sections pool studies from medical education, middle school science, MBA teaching and preservice teacher education under one heading, and any condition that varies across those settings is invisible in the pooled claim.
quotes: As we have examined the broad variety of instantiations of PBL and IL, we have not uncovered any dimensions that con- sistently distinguish between PBL and IL. Indeed, we think there are no clear-cut distinguishing features

rows.value: medium · That the described environments contain substantial guidance is easy to accept from the examples given. Whether the environments the other paper had in mind are the same ones cannot be settled from this text, and no criterion is offered for where the category boundary falls.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The substantive half of the reply, and the part most useful to a review of supports, because it is a description of mechanism rather than a defence of a camp. Three families are given, and they separate by what each acts on. The first acts on the learner's model of expertise by displaying how a competent person proceeds: a tutor pressing for causal explanation, expert video, models of argumentative give and take, storyboards that make the moves of behavioural analysis visible. The second acts on the information available, placing expert explanation where the learner has come to need it, as hints, rationale, embedded expert conversation or a just-in-time mini-lecture. The third acts on the task itself, narrowing what can be done and when: whiteboard columns for facts, hypotheses, learning issues and an action plan; an enforced plan-build-test order; automated calculation and representation. Only the third is load reduction in the strict sense. The first two add material the learner must process, and the paper concedes as much when it says scaffolding may also problematize work in order to force engagement with disciplinary frameworks. The account of scaffolding as distributed across materials, software, teacher and peers is the other transferable idea here: it means the guidance in an approach cannot be read off any single artifact.

[...] Scaffolding is often distributed in the learning environment, across the curriculum materials or educational software, the teachers or facilitators, and the learners themselves.

All these strategies can support sense making, process management, and articulation and re- ﬂection. The examples we present provide a stark contrast to the Kirschner and colleagues’ argument that inquiry and PBL environments provide minimal guidance and therefore increase cognitive load

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) Scaffolding That Makes Disciplinary Thinking and Strategies Explicit — The first family of scaffold: facilitators make key aspects of expertise visible through questions, by modelling, coaching and eventually fading their support, with an expert medical problem-based tutor shown pushing students to explain their thinking so as to build a causal explanation or identify the limits of their knowledge.
quotes: In PBL and IL environments facilitators and teachers make key aspects of expertise visible through questions that scaf- fold student learning by modeling, coaching, and eventually fading some of their support. Student learning occurs as students collaboratively engage in constructive processing. For example, in studying an expert PBL teacher in the con- text of medical education, Hmelo-Silver and Barrows (2006) showed that the teacher frequently pushed students to ex- plain their thinking to help them build a causal explanation or identify the limits of their knowledge. This helps support students in sense making and in articulating their ideas

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) Scaffolding That Makes Disciplinary Thinking and Strategies Explicit, Animal Landlord — The same family in an artifact rather than a person: in Animal Landlord students build a chronological storyboard of behavioural components from a video clip, identifying, labelling and annotating them, which makes salient the disciplinary strategies of decomposing complex behaviour, categorising the constituents and interpreting their significance.
quotes: For example, in the scaffolded software tool for analyzing animal behavior, Animal Landlord, students create a chronological “storyboard” of the behavioral components they identify in a short video clip of animal behavior. In creating this sto- ryboard students are expected to identify behavioral com- ponents, label them, and annotate their observations and in- terpretations about these components. This artifact makes salient the disciplinary strategies of analyzing animal behav- ior which include decomposing complex behavior into its constituents, categorizing the constituents, and interpreting their signiﬁcance (Golan et al., 2001; Smith & Reiser, 1998

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) Scaffolding That Makes Disciplinary Thinking and Strategies Explicit — The three tool forms named: prompts to use particular reasoning strategies; structures for students to follow or fill in, such as argument diagrams for distinguishing claims from reasons or templates for domain-specific explanations; and models of expert performance to emulate.
quotes: Many other environments provide students with: (a) prompts to use particular reasoning strategies (e.g., Derry, Hmelo-Silver, Nagarajan, Chernobilsky, & Beitzel, 2006; White & Frederiksen, 1998); (b) structures for students to follow or ﬁll in, such as ﬁlling in argument diagrams to learn to distinguish between claims and reasons (Bell, 2002; Toth et al., 2002) or templates for domain-speciﬁc explanations (Duncan, 2006; Sandoval & Reiser, 2004); and (c) models of expert performance for students to emulate (Chinn et al., 2000; Loh et al., 2001

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) Scaffolds That Embed Expert Guidance — The second family: expert information and guidance offered directly to the learner, as hints and explanations of the rationale in WISE, or as conversations with experts in embedded video clips in goal-based scenarios.
quotes: In many IL and PBL environments, expert information and guidance is sometimes offered directly to the learner. For example in WISE, students are provided with expert’s hints and explanations of the rationale underlying the processes students engage in (Davis, 2003). In some cases, such as goal- based scenarios (Schank & Cleary, 1995), expert information is offered directly to the learner through “conversations” with experts in the form of embedded video clips

rows.value: (PDF p. 5) Scaffolds That Structure Complex Tasks or Reduce Cognitive Load — The third family, in its low-technology form: the problem-based whiteboard gives the group columns for the facts of the case, evolving hypotheses, the learning issues they must read up on, and an action plan.
quotes: In PBL, structure is provided through whiteboards that communicate a problem-solving process as well through the human facilitator (Barrows, 2000; Hmelo-Silver, 2004). For example, the whiteboard provides columns for the group to keep track of the facts of the case, their evolving hypotheses, the learning issues, which are con- cepts that the group needs to learn more about in order to solve the problem, and an action plan, which helps remind the group of what they need to do

rows.value: (PDF p. 5) Scaffolds That Structure Complex Tasks or Reduce Cognitive Load — The general statement of the third family: scaffolding decreases cognitive load by structuring the task so the learner can focus on what is relevant to the learning goals, by automating data representations, calculations or storage, and by restricting the options available at any point.
quotes: Scaffolding can also guide instruction and decrease cog- nitive load by structuring a task in ways that allow the learner to focus on aspects of the task that are relevant to the learning goals (Hmelo-Silver, 2006; Salomon, Perkins, & Globerson, 1991). For example, scaffolding can reduce cognitive load by automating the generation of data representations, labor intensive calculations, or storing information. By structuring the tasks and the available functionality (e.g., in computer- based environments), scaffolding can restrict the options that are available to the learner at any point in time to make the task accessible and manageable (Quintana et al., 2004

rows.value: (PDF p. 5) Scaffolds That Structure Complex Tasks or Reduce Cognitive Load, Model-It — The worked instance: Model-It only lets students build after they have planned and only lets them test after they have identified important objects and relationships, and it converts verbally stated relationships into the mathematical formulas that run the model.
quotes: The software restricts the options avail- able to students such that students may only proceed to the build stage after they have planned their models, and they may not test it until they have identiﬁed some of the impor- tant objects and relationships in the system. Model-It further scaffolds students by allowing them to qualitatively express complex mathematical relationships as the software converts their verbally stated relationships into mathematical formulas used for running the model, thereby reducing cognitive load and situating the task within the learner’s zone of proximal development

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) The Use of Scaffolding in PBL and IL — Where the guidance sits: scaffolding is often distributed across curriculum materials, educational software, teachers or facilitators, and the learners themselves, with teachers guiding, pushing students to think deeply and modelling the questions students need to ask themselves.
quotes: Scaffolding is often distributed in the learning environ- ment, across the curriculum materials or educational soft- ware, the teachers or facilitators, and the learners themselves (Puntambekar & Kolodner, 2005). Teachers play a signiﬁ- cant role in scaffolding mindful and productive engagement with the task, tools, and peers. They guide students in the learning process, pushing them to think deeply, and model the kinds of questions that students need to be asking them- selves, thus forming a cognitive apprenticeship (Collins et al., 1989; Hmelo-Silver & Barrows, 2006

quotes: Scaffolded inquiry and problem-based environments present learners with opportunities to engage in complex tasks that would otherwise be beyond their current abilities. items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The reversal, and the claim with the most reach beyond this dispute. If a tutor's modelling and a worked example are both a display of expert performance, and an inquiry scaffold and a process worksheet are both a structure that constrains the order of work, then the design variable is not guidance against its absence but where the guidance sits, who supplies it, and when in the task it arrives. The authors press the point again later: they anticipate that the other side would claim a successful guided reading programme as their own and reply that this would only reinforce the central point, since what the other side counts as effective instruction is often compatible with inquiry learning. The resemblance is asserted rather than demonstrated. A cognitive load theorist could reply that a worked example lays out the whole solution path while a scaffold deliberately withholds it, which is precisely the difference in question, and the paper's own problematizing point concedes that some scaffolds are designed to make work harder. The irrelevance conclusion follows validly from the classification claim but inherits its weakness: without a criterion for the category, any inconvenient study can be excluded as not testing a real instance.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The most useful evidence in the paper, because it varies the order of instruction while holding the instruction itself constant, and so speaks to a question both sides could accept as well posed. The same lecture taught more when it followed an attempt to explain data than when it did not, and in the second study an exploratory first phase left ninth graders better prepared to learn from a subsequent lecture than a teacher-explained worked example did. That converts the dispute from whether to guide into when guidance should arrive, which is also what the paper's just-in-time principle says: a mini-lecture lands once students understand why they need it. Two cautions. Both results are cited in a sentence apiece with no effect sizes, sample sizes or designs reported here, so this card carries only their direction. And the second study is a comparison of two forms of instruction that both precede the lecture, which makes it evidence about preparation for future learning rather than about the value of exploration on its own.

rows.value: Schwartz and Bransford presented some students with a lecture on memory after they had tried to explain the pattern of results in data from real memory experiments. Other students received the lecture without having engaged in the inquiry activity. The students who received the lecture after trying to explain the data learned much more from the lecture. In the context of students trying to explain data, the lecture provided scaffolding that helped students make sense of the data, and hence was more meaningful than the same lecture presented not as scaffolding for inquiry but as direct instruction. [...] Schwartz and Martin (2004) found that ninth graders who initially learned through exploratory problem solving employing statistical principles learned more from a subsequent lecture than students who had initially learned from a worked example that the instructor explained in class.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The evidentiary charge, and the pattern it produces is more informative than the verdict either side draws from it. Across every review and study cited here the shape is the same: null or slightly negative on tests of declarative or basic science knowledge, positive on application, clinical reasoning, explanation quality and multistep problems. Vernon and Blake show it, Dochy and colleagues show it, the randomised crossover with MBA students shows it, no difference on declarative knowledge but more integrative explanatory essays, and the anchored instruction study shows it, no difference on single-step word problems but significant effects on multistep problems, planning and comprehension. Read without either side's framing this is a claim about outcome measures rather than about whether the approach works, and it is the most transferable thing in the paper: an evaluation restricted to recall of stated facts will find these approaches no better, and one that measures use of knowledge will find them better. The bibliographic charge itself is specific and checkable, that a third contemporaneous meta-analysis went uncited. It is also the kind of charge that runs both ways, since this paper's own selection is assembled by interested parties and includes several studies by its authors.

rows.value: Although Kirschner et al. (2006) report on several studies and meta-analyses of PBL, they overlooked other reviews that were more favorable to PBL. At around the same time as the Albanese and Mitchell (1993) and Berkson (1993) reviews that Kirschner et al. (2006) cited, there was a third meta-analysis conducted by Vernon and Blake (1993). This analysis found that medical students in PBL curricula performed slightly worse on tests of basic science knowledge but performed better on tests of clinical knowledge than traditional medical students. In a more recent meta-analysis of the effects of PBL, Dochy, Segers, Van den Bossche, and Gijbels (2003) found there was no effect of PBL on declarative knowledge tests, but studies that compared PBL students with those in traditional curricula on measures of knowledge application showed a moderate effect size favoring PBL students.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: The clearest place in the paper for a reader to watch the same result being read two ways, which makes it valuable to a review that must state a dispute without joining it. Both sides agree what the study found: the problem-based students used the hypothesis-driven strategy they had been taught while traditional students did not, and they made more errors. The disagreement is over which of those is the outcome. Treat accuracy as the criterion and the result is unfavourable; treat strategy transfer and explanation quality as the criteria and it is favourable, since the same students produced more elaborated explanations against sparse ones. The reply then makes two further moves that should be kept apart. One challenges the criterion, arguing that experts facing unfamiliar problems also reason from hypotheses rather than from data, so data-driven reasoning is not straightforwardly the expert standard. The other supplies different evidence, an experiment in which hypothesis-driven training produced better learning of electrocardiograms, and a later study finding problem-based students more accurate. That is a rebuttal by additional data, not a rereading. The authors also volunteer the original study's design weaknesses, different universities with different entering students compared at one time on one task, and note that self-selection affects most studies here, which tells against their own favourable comparisons too.

rows.value: Patel et al. concluded (and Kirschner et al. concurred) that PBL impedes the development of expert data-driven reasoning strategies. However, other research suggests that when faced with unfamiliar problems, experts go back to basic principles and effectively use hypothesis-driven reasoning rather than the data-driven reasoning used in familiar problems (Norman, Trott, Brooks, & Smith, 1994). In an experimental study comparing medical students trained to use either data-driven or hypothesis-driven reasoning while learning about electrocardiograms, the hypothesis-driven reasoning strategy led to superior learning (Norman, Brooks, Colle, & Hatala, 2000). The accuracy effect found in the Patel et al. study has not been a robust effect [...] A more recent longitudinal quasi-experimental study of first year medical students found that PBL students generated more accurate and coherent problem solutions than traditional medical students (Hmelo, 1998).

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: The direct empirical answer to a specific charge, and the cleanest disagreement in the paper because it is a contradiction rather than a reframing. The opposing claim is that minimally guided instruction produces a decrement for lower-performing students. The counter is twofold: in the genetics environment the largest gains came from general science and general biology classrooms rather than honors and college prep, and in the large urban study African-American boys closed a gap to statistical parity with girls. A third study of over 2,000 eighth graders reports higher gains for every diversity grouping. The numbers are the most specific in the paper and worth keeping: 381 students in 21 classrooms against 107 in 6; two cohorts of 1,803 intervention students in 18 schools against 17,562 comparison students over three years, with effect sizes of 0.44 and 0.37 and gains persisting up to a year and a half. Three cautions belong on the card. The largest study was in press when this was written, so nothing could be checked against a published report. All three are comparisons of intact classrooms or adopting schools rather than randomised assignments, which is the design weakness the authors themselves raise elsewhere. And the environments studied are scaffolded ones, so a defender of the opposing position could accept every result and still hold that unguided instruction hurts weaker students.

items.heading: Claim 8 · CLAIM-008
items.lead: The closing paragraph is the most honest in the paper and should be read as part of the finding rather than as politeness. Having spent five pages arguing the evidence, the authors say the yes-or-no question is the wrong one, that adequate answers about the conditions do not yet exist, that they are not arguing against direct and more heavily guided instruction, and that how to balance the two is still unclear. What they leave in its place is a set of open conditions: which circumstances, which outcomes, which valued practices, which forms of support for which populations and goals. They add one substantive constraint, that more directed guidance needs to build on student thinking, which is the same ordering principle the sequencing evidence supports. They also argue that outcomes should include epistemic practices, self-directed learning and collaboration, which are not measured on achievement tests, and answer the charge that inquiry displaces content by saying reforms make content and practices both central. That last point is asserted rather than shown; the cited support for rich content learning under inquiry models is three references in a parenthesis. For a review of supports, the useful residue of this paper is the question list, not the verdict.

rows.value: Even in this limited review of research on PBL and IL, it is clear that the claim that PBL and IL “does not work” is not well supported, and, in fact, there is support for the alternative. But we would argue that “Does it work?” is the wrong question. The more important questions to ask are under what circumstances do these guided inquiry approaches work, what are the kinds of outcomes for which they are effective, what kinds of valued practices do they promote, and what kinds of support and scaffolding are needed for different populations and learning goals. [...] In many ways, we do not yet have adequate answers to these questions concerning the conditions under which various types of scaffolded learning environments are most effective. While we are not arguing against various forms of direct and more heavily guided instruction, of the sort that Kirschner et al advocate, it is still unclear how to balance IL and PBL (which are more constructivist and experiential) with direct instructional guidance.

cards.title: Distributed learning and mutual adaptation

rows.value: other
concept or theory, framework or design space, primary empirical

A 2006 theory paper that states this review's central question in its own words and then tests it. Its frame is a two-by-two over whether the person can change and whether the environment can change, giving induction, symbiotic tuning, repurposing and mutual adaptation. The diagnosis worth carrying is that the ordinary case, a fixed well-designed support that the learner adapts to, tends to end in symbiosis: children get more efficient with base-ten blocks and become dependent on the blocks for that efficiency, and the understanding does not survive when the blocks are removed. The prediction is that letting the learner restructure the support instead prepares them for environments that lack it, and three of the authors' own studies bear it out with the same shape each time. Nine and ten-year-olds learning fractions with pie pieces, which carry part-whole structure already, matched children learning with plain tiles on the original material and lost to them on new materials, while the pie children's day-to-day performance kept regressing. Over a hundred high-school seniors who taught a computer agent and watched it play matched those who played themselves throughout the study and beat them a week later on paper questions that looked nothing like the game. Not one of the studies reports a statistical test.

medium · The ideas are unusually well aimed at this review's question and the evidence for them is reported at the level of a conference talk. Five studies are described: two on ratio with movable pieces, a three-day fraction teaching study, a gears study on dyads, a learning-by-teaching experiment and a Teachable Agent classroom study. Between them they carry one sample size, over a hundred high school seniors, one magnitude, 27 per cent less accurate, and one set of rates. No p-value, test name, interval, variance or effect size appears in twenty pages, and the central tile-versus-pie transfer comparison is reported entirely in words. The primary sources are cited and presumably carry the numbers. What can be taken from this paper is the framework, the diagnosis, the design contrast and the repeated shape, equal during learning and divergent at transfer, across three studies differing in age, materials and domain. What cannot be taken is any magnitude. The authors also state the framework's weakest point themselves: no metric for how stable or adaptable anything is, so quadrant assignment is intuition, including in their own designs.

sections.title: 6 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A support that stays fixed while the learner adapts to it produces efficiency that belongs to the pairing rather than to the person, and the paper says so with the removal named. This is this review's central proposition, written in 2006, with none of this review's vocabulary. The mechanism offered is the calculator analogy: you can learn which buttons produce the answer without learning the arithmetic that makes the buttons work, and you are then worse off anywhere those buttons are missing. What makes the claim more than a warning is that it is positional. Symbiosis is not an accident of bad design; it is the natural terminus of good design, of a well-structured environment that the learner adapts to and that does not adapt back. The authors extend it to people, where partners who have tuned to each other do not travel well to new partners, and to pilots, who cannot take their reliance on a cockpit anywhere else. The weakness is the evidence for the base-ten sentence itself, which cites no study at the point of assertion.

rows.value: In fact, one of the concerns of learning in Quadrant 1 (Induction) is that it can yield an unwanted symbiotic relation once student understanding stabilizes. For example, over time, children become more efficient at using base-10 blocks, and they become dependent on the blocks for that efficiency. Experimental studies indicate that learning with base-10 blocks does not transfer very well to symbolic tasks. The children's understanding is symbiotic on the base-10 blocks, and it does not survive when the blocks are removed.

quotes: For abilities that need to transfer from one situation to another, symbiotic tuning is not ideal. In fact, one of the concerns of learning in Quadrant 1 (Induction) is that it can yield an unwanted symbiotic relation once student understanding stabilizes. For example, over time, children be- come more eﬃcient at using base-10 blocks, and they become dependent on the blocks for that eﬃciency. Experimental studies indicate that learning with base-10 blocks does not transfer very well to symbolic tasks. The children’s un- derstanding is symbiotic on the base-10 blocks, and it does not survive when the blocks are removed

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) 4.1.2, the calculator analogy — The calculator analogy for why: a learner can induce which buttons to press without learning the arithmetic that makes the pressing work, and is then less able to work anywhere the original structures are missing.
quotes: To take the case of manipulatives in Quadrant 1, children induce how to rely on the given structure of the manipulative to solve problems. But, the children may never notice what structures in the environment made their manipula- tions eﬀective. As an analogy, it might be something like using a calculator — one can learn what buttons to press, but this does not mean one will learn the structure of arithmetic that makes the button pressing eﬀective. The conse- quence of this Quadrant 1 learning is that students may be less able to work in new environments that do not include all the structures built into their original environment

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) 3, Quadrant 2 Symbiotic Tuning — Symbiotic tuning defined, and its cost stated: components become increasingly interdependent so the learning is bound to the context, and pilots cannot transport their specialised reliance on the cockpit elsewhere.
quotes: In the symbiotic quadrant, learning is characterized by an increase in the eﬃciency of the system and the interdependence of its com- ponents. Because the components become increasingly interdependent, the learning is often bound to the context. Pilots cannot transport their special- ized reliance on the cockpit to another environment, nor can a highly special- ized cockpit transport to another setting; hence, the label “symbiotic tuning”. Adaptations to the individual and environment depend on one another to manifest themselves

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) 3, Quadrant 1 Induction — Induction defined: an unstable learner in a stable, well-structured environment, inducing its regularities, with abacus masters as the example.
quotes: In Quadrant 1 — Induction — people do not have stable, mature ideas, but they are operating in well-structured and stable environments. By induction, we do not mean a speciﬁc psychological process or learning algorithm. Rather, we mean it more broadly in the sense that a current in one wire can induce a current in another wire. Abacus masters, for example, have expansive digit spans and arithmetic abilities because they have induced a mental model that can simulate the structure of an abacus (Hatano and Osawa 1983). In Quadrant 1 people induce the regularities of a stable environment

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) 4.2, symbiotic social learning — The social version of symbiosis: partners refine shorthand and divisions of labour that are efficient for their particular lives, and that kind of learning does not travel to new situations with new people.
quotes: The Symbiotic quadrant refers to situations where individuals reﬁne stable patterns of interaction with one another. For example, partners may develop a particularly shorthand method of reference or emotional support, and they may learn to apportion chores in ways that are eﬃcient given the peculiar structure of their lives. Symbiotic learning like this does not travel very well to new situations involving new people, though people do often try to impose a set of stable behaviors into new situations with varying degrees of success

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) 2 Distributed learning and education — The distinction the paper turns on: learning yields lasting change and problem solving does not, so distributed problem solving and distributed learning are separated.
quotes: Though learning and problem solving strongly inﬂuence one another, learning yields lasting change, while problem solving does not. Thus, we distinguish distributed problem solv- ing from distributed learning

In particular, we will show that mutual adaptation prepares learners to transfer their adaptations to new environments

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) 3, Quadrant 2 Symbiotic Tuning — Symbiotic tuning is where the rest of the distributed cognition literature lives, by the authors' own account, and it is the quadrant in which the person is least separable from the setting. So the tradition's canonical achievements, the cockpit and the ship's bridge, are drawn from the region of the space where dependence is highest and transfer is worst, which is a fair charge and is made in passing.
quotes: In the symbiotic quadrant, learning is characterized by an increase in the eﬃciency of the system and the interdependence of its com- ponents. Because the components become increasingly interdependent, the learning is often bound to the context. Pilots cannot transport their special- ized reliance on the cockpit to another environment, nor can a highly special- ized cockpit transport to another setting; hence, the label “symbiotic tuning”. Adaptations to the individual and environment depend on one another to manifest themselves

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: Three studies, two age groups, two domains, and the same shape every time: no difference while the support is the one you learned on, a clear difference the moment it changes. Nine and ten-year-olds who learned fractions with plain tiles matched the pie-piece group on the pie-and-tile problems and beat them on beans and fraction bars. High-school seniors who taught an agent and watched it play matched the students who played themselves all the way through the game and beat them a week later on paper questions in forms the game never used. The practical consequence is the one this review most needs stated: any evaluation that ends when the training material ends would have concluded that the design choice made no difference, in both studies, and would have been wrong in both. It is worth noticing what is being measured. This is not the support being withdrawn and the person left with nothing; it is the support being exchanged for a different one, which is a weaker but more realistic test, and it is more than almost anything else in this corpus manages.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A design rule with a mechanism and a control condition, and it points the opposite way from usability. Do not build the structure the learner is supposed to acquire into the support; build a support the learner has to organise, and let the organising be the learning. The pie pieces show the part-whole relation and are therefore easier and teach less; the tiles show nothing and force the child to impose grouping, and the grouping is what travels. What raises this above a just-so story is the second ratio study, which rules out the obvious rival: if the pieces were simply relieving working memory, then handing children pieces already sorted into the penultimate answer should have been at least as good as letting them sort, and it was worse. So the benefit lies in performing the restructuring, not in possessing the restructured object. The same rule then generates a technology: virtual manipulatives with a replay history, so the child can watch their own restructuring rather than only its result.
