items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The same principle in the social case, and it produces a genuinely odd result: watching someone else answer questions beat answering them yourself, when the someone else was a scripted confederate on a videotape who introduced no information you had not supplied. The authors use it to argue that learning by teaching is not reducible to the individual act of explaining, since both groups explained and only one watched. For a review of supports the interesting form is more general. The thing that produced learning was seeing the consequences of what you had put into the world, which is the social version of the replay feature on the virtual manipulatives and of watching the tiles you grouped. Their gears result sits alongside it: individuals found the parity rule 14 per cent of the time, pooling what individuals already knew predicts 26.5 per cent for pairs, and pairs reached 58 per cent, so something is produced in the interaction that was in neither head. And Teachable Agents turn the principle into a product, which is where the reader should be most careful, since the same authors designed the principle, the study and the system.

rows.value: They showed that knocking out the opportunity for teachers to see how their student adapts reduces learning, even compared to teacher self-study... Participants who taught Student X, but then did self-study on the second set of questions, were 27% less accurate. Evidently, the opportunity to passively observe how one's student adapts to what she has been taught is quite valuable for adapting one's own understanding — even more valuable than teaching and then doing it oneself.

cards.title: Scaffolding Analysis: Extending the Scaffolding Metaphor to Learning Artifacts

rows.value: other
concept or theory, framework or design space, measurement or method, design principle

A theoretical article that takes the field's central term away from the objects it had been attached to. Its claim is that a scaffold is not a feature an artifact has: calling something a scaffold is the output of a comparison the analyst set up, and the analyst chooses three things, the situation of interest, the situation compared against, and the dimension of performance that counts as doing the same thing in both. The argument for this comes from outside education, from the position that any statement about a thing's function is relative to a chosen system and a chosen capacity, so a claim that a feature supports thinking is incomplete rather than merely vague. Reading the field's definitions this way turns up three buried assumptions, each of which becomes a problem when the support is a tool rather than a person. The unassisted case is obvious in tutoring and underdetermined everywhere else, and a tool that everyone has all the time may not be a scaffold at all. Something must be held constant for the comparison to mean anything, and the more a tool transforms the task the less there is left to hold, which is the diagnosis for generative assistance written twenty years early. And the original construct assumed the support would be withdrawn, which this framework drops on the ground that a built artifact cannot tune itself to a person the way a person can, at the acknowledged cost of having no way to describe learning at all. What remains is a set of named comparison shapes including a one-feature-at-a-time ablation, a rule that a comparison only reveals something when the two situations are close, and two worked design rationales for the authors' own software, one of which reports a feature the framework cannot analyse.

low · Read the conceptual claims as strong and the framework as untested. No learner is observed in the article and both worked analyses describe hypothetical students, which limits the design material but not the argument. The argument is what this card is for: that a scaffolding claim without a stated comparison is incomplete, that the comparison needs an invariant a task-transforming tool destroys, and that the base situation for a support everyone always has may no longer exist.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The most consequential claim in this corpus's own vocabulary, and it is deflationary. If it holds, then no paper can assert that its system scaffolds anything without also stating what it is being compared against and on what dimension, and almost none of them do. The philosophical grounding is what gives it teeth: asking what a feature's function is has no answer at all until you name the system it sits in and the capacity you are trying to explain, so a claim that a feature supports thinking is not underspecified, it is incomplete in a way that makes it unfalsifiable. Every card in this review that records a mechanism without a base situation is recording half a claim, and this paper is where that becomes visible.

rows.value: Scaffolds are not features of artifacts or situations, nor is scaffolding something that may be occurring or not in an observed situation. A scaffolding analysis is a comparative analysis performed on learning interactions, in which one specifies a scaffolded situation, a base situation and a target performance, and then accounts for how the differences between the situations function to change what a person can do. Because it is comparative, its results are always relative to those choices. This follows from the observation that scaffolding claims are function claims, and that function claims are only meaningful relative to a chosen system and a chosen capacity of it.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The ubiquity problem is the one worth carrying forward, because it has only got worse. A tool that everyone has all the time is hard to call a scaffold, and the paper poses that about calculators in 2004. The same question now attaches to autocomplete, search and generative assistants, where the unassisted case is not merely hard to choose but has stopped existing for the population being studied. This review will keep meeting mechanisms whose base situation nobody can specify any more, and this is where the difficulty is named.

rows.value: There is an implicit comparison at the heart of every definition of scaffolding, so it is essential to be able to state the unassisted case. Beyond tutorial interactions this becomes underdetermined: for a student solving a problem with a calculator and a diagram, the base situation could sensibly omit either, and the choices lead to very different conclusions about what scaffolding is occurring. If the notion is applied to tools without a stopping rule it becomes overly inclusive and ceases to be useful.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: This is the diagnosis for generative assistance written twenty years before it was needed. The construct's whole comparative machinery assumes the task survives the support, and a support that rewrites what the task is leaves nothing to hold constant. Scaffolding therefore stops being an available vocabulary exactly where the change is largest, which is where this review most wants to say something. The distinction between a support that redistributes the parts of a task and one that replaces the task is the sharpest thing on this card.

rows.value: For the comparison to make sense there must be something invariant, some sense in which the individual is trying to do the same thing across the two situations. Scaffolding was originally distinguished from shaping on exactly this ground: it holds the task constant and simplifies the learner's role. Once decomposability and a fixed sequence of steps are relaxed, it becomes unclear what is being held constant, and the more that learning artifacts transform the task, the harder it becomes to say the learner is doing the same thing at all.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: Three portable design moves and one mechanism worth naming. Printing an expert's tacit context onto the display, so a beginner spends their effort reading the data rather than working out where they are, is a pattern this corpus meets under many names. Taking capability away to make structure possible is the counterintuitive one and is stated plainly here: replacing a general-purpose macro facility with a small menu of operations is what allows the interface to guide anyone. And the argument tool's contribution is characterised not as prompting but as making a structure visible, so that an unanswered question shows up as a gap in a display rather than as something the student has to notice. That is a different mechanism from asking a question, and the difference is easy to lose.

rows.value: Three strategies for adapting an expert tool for learners: adding contextual information that embeds the tacit knowledge scientists use to interpret a display, strategically selecting which functionality to keep so the interface does not overwhelm, and adding pedagogically valuable functionality experts do not have. cards.title: A framework for analyzing the cognitive complexity of computer-assisted clinical ordering

rows.value: other
concept or theory, lineage or history, framework or design space, design principle, primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

The paper has mixed but substantial theoretical grounding. It operationalizes Norman’s theory of action through a modified cognitive walkthrough and operationalizes and extends Wright et al.’s distributed-resources model. It conceptually uses distributed cognition, Zhang’s account of external representations, Howes and Payne’s semantic-matching work, and Bhavnani and John’s strategic-knowledge account to explain how interface configuration redistributes cognitive work and shapes search, review, strategy, and error in provider order entry.

medium · The paper provides explicit theoretical grounding, a systematic walkthrough, and direct observations of errors and strategies. Transfer is nevertheless bounded by one commercial POE system, one simulated admission scenario, seven experienced convenience-sampled clinicians, small strategy subgroups, and several causal explanations or design implications that remain hypotheses rather than controlled comparisons.

cards.title: Understanding the differences between how novice and experienced designers approach design tasks
cards.meta: 2003 · Research in Engineering Design · doi 10.1007/s00163-002-0023-z · Route C

rows.value: S2CW-3B68EFBB4ADEAE8E6037B80C
other
design principle, primary empirical, measurement or method

The paper is conceptually grounded in novice–expert design cognition and strategic-knowledge literature and operationalizes thinking-aloud protocol analysis; it does not invoke a scaffolding theory or test a support system. Its contribution is an empirically derived repertoire of expert design strategies and an author-proposed implication for novice support.

medium · The paper provides direct naturalistic observations and explicit support implications, but only twelve designers from one aerospace company were observed on heterogeneous tasks. Design quality and support effectiveness were not assessed, behavior may have been affected by observation, and several transfer and individual-difference claims remain unverified.

cards.title: A selective synthesis of the experimental literature on dynamic assessment

rows.value: other
concept or theory, lineage or history, review or meta analysis, framework or design space, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

The paper positions dynamic assessment as an interactive alternative or supplement to static testing: learner difficulty triggers assistance, and responsiveness to that assistance becomes evidence about learning potential. It explicitly draws on learning-potential, testing-the-limits, mediated-assessment, transfer, cognitive-modifiability, and information-processing traditions. It then operationalizes this heterogeneous lineage through three overlapping assessment categories—scaffolding, coaching or mediated training, and general strategy training—and evaluates their performance effects and evidentiary limits meta-analytically.

medium · The paper directly reports its meta-analytic mechanisms, moderator findings, corrections, and limitations, but the evidence is heterogeneous, drawn from published studies with overlapping support categories, and focused mainly on immediate test performance rather than durable learning or transfer.

(PDF p. 2) Opening section, description of examiner assistance and the assisted-performance measure — Dynamic assessment responds to learner difficulty with escalating forms of assistance and measures change from unassisted to assisted performance.
quotes: To obtain information about a child’s responsiveness to hints or probes, DA approaches require the interaction of an examiner and the examinee. When a student is having difficulty, the examiner attempts to move the student from failure to success by modifying the format, providing more trials, providing information on successful strategies, or offering increasingly more direct cues, hints, or prompts. The intensity of the intervention ranges from several sessions to brief intensive prompts in one session. Thus, potential for learning new information (or accessing previously presented information) is measured in terms of the distance, difference between, or change from unassisted performance to a performance level with assistance.

rows.value: (PDF p. 22) Discussion, application of contingent scaffolding to intervention design — A cited application provides scaffolding only when difficulty occurs and uses required hints or explanations as a measure of ease of learning.
quotes: Further application is that DA provides information necessary to design intervention programs. For example, Day and Cordon (1993) provided third graders with either scaffolding or complete explanations to solve balance scale problems. As children worked on the problems, scaffolding was provided only if someone experienced difficulties. Thus, the procedures determined what children had already learned (pretest or static measure) as well as how easily they learned (the number of hints needed, the number of explanations required or DA measure).

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Opening section, two common features of dynamic assessment — Campione and Brown ground assisted change potential, while Embretson grounds prospective measurement independent of assistance.
quotes: Although DA is a term used to characterize a number of distinct approaches (see Carlson & Wiedl, 1979; Haywood et al., 1990; Palincsar, Brown, & Campione, 1991; Speece, Cooper, & Kibler, 1990), two common features of this approach are to determine the learner’s potential for change when given assistance (e.g., Campione & Brown, 1987) and to provide a prospective measure of performance change independent of assistance (e.g., Embretson, 1987 [Note: Unless otherwise indicated, citations in the text refer to Embretson’s 1987 work found in the references proper: “Toward development of a psychometric approach.”]).

rows.value: (PDF p. 14) Upward Bias subsection — Within-design estimates were sensitive to posttest variability and an upward-bias correction, after which the corrected mean weighted effect size was 0.16.
quotes: The previous analysis clearly showed that for within design studies the posttest dependent variable standard deviations are systematically larger than pretest standard deviations, and thus posttest standard deviations result in smaller ESs than those calculated using pretest standard deviations. Therefore, so as not to overestimate the influence of pretest-posttest only design studies on DA outcomes, the subsequent analyses used a weighted ES with the standard deviations of the posttest. In addition, a further correction was made by subtracting 0.76 from each ES for each dependent measure for within design studies. As stated earlier, 0.76 was estimated as the upward bias for pretest-posttest designs and well as the magnitude of the expected outcome for any reasonable type of intervention. cards.title: Debating Life on Mars: The Knowledge Integration Environment (KIE) in Varied School Settings.

rows.value: other
primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, design principle

One of the founding scaffolded-inquiry environments, taken into two urban schools in 1998 to run projects on whether there was life on Mars and why frogs were turning up deformed. Three things make it worth a card twenty-eight years later. A student the teachers had written off argued a case from multiple sources in the scaffolded debate and moved her teacher to tears, and then answered I don't know on the written post-test to questions about the same content — the two-part test, inside one student, decades before anyone named it. The author reports plainly that when the class returned to the textbook, many students went back to their old habits, and lists novelty, cameras and visiting scientists among the reasons the results might not mean what they appear to. And the only support anyone in the paper deliberately withdraws is the support given to the teachers: the researchers taught the first lessons themselves and gradually faded the scaffolds until the teachers ran the class. The student-facing scaffolds are never withdrawn at all.

low · A conference paper reporting two implementation case studies, and it does not pretend otherwise. The strongest evidence is qualitative and particular: transcripts, field notes, teacher interviews, videotaped debates, and at one school written pre- and post-tests graded by the team of teachers and researchers. The other school ran no post-test at all — debate results were the grade. No control group, no comparison condition, no effect size, and one figure of assignment completion rates is the only quantitative result offered. The author names the confounds herself and does not discount them: novelty, a public presentation with competition, graduate students, scientists and video cameras in the room, and students made to feel special. Two schools, five teachers, one six-day and one two-week project. Carry the individual cases and the author's own admissions, which are unusually candid; carry nothing that resembles an effect.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The two-part test performed inside a single student, in 1998. Janice's debate performance was taken with the arrangement fully present — the evidence base, the note prompts, a worksheet of questions to ask, adults modelling what a good question sounds like, a team beside her and an audience watching — and it was extraordinary enough to move her teacher to tears. Her post-test was taken days later, on paper, alone, on the same content, and returned I don't know. That is a measurement temporally and operationally removed from the treatment, twenty-seven years before anyone wrote the criterion down, and it disagrees completely with the measurement taken inside the treatment. The author's reading is that Janice rejects written exams as not worth her time, which is plausible and may be right; it does not touch what the pair of observations shows, which is how far apart the two measures can fall for one person on one topic. The divergence runs both ways in the same classroom, which is what makes it more than an anecdote about assessment format: another student looked disengaged throughout and topped the post-test, and an honours student who dismissed the work scored unusually low. In-arrangement performance and out-of-arrangement performance were not merely imperfectly correlated here; in three documented cases they were opposed.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: Three sentences that do more honest work than most discussion sections in this corpus. Long-term results are not in. Two weeks is not long enough for lasting improvement. Many students went back to their old habits as soon as the class returned to the textbook. That is the helped-only-while-present pattern, reported by the people who built the support, from inside the founding scaffolded-inquiry tradition, in 1998 — earlier than anything else in this review and stated more plainly than most of what came after. The confound list beside it is the same kind of candour and is worth reproducing whole: an engaging topic, the novelty of computers, an environment perhaps unique enough to break a cycle of non-performance, a public presentation with competition, and graduate students, scientists and video cameras making the students feel special. Read together the two passages say something precise: the environment produced something real while it was there, and nobody should yet believe it produced anything that outlasts it, and the author is not going to pretend otherwise. The corpus's later habit, documented across four literatures, is to report the first half and drop the second. What is missing here is only a measurement — the teacher's observation that students reverted is exactly the delayed measure the paper says it does not have.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The only deliberate fading in forty-six pages is applied to the teachers. The researchers taught the first lessons themselves, then gradually faded the scaffolds until the teachers were running the class — a genuine handover, with a recipient who ends up doing unaided what someone else did for them at the start, which is the whole of the original definition. Nothing of the kind happens to the students. The checklists, the software prompts, the debate worksheets and the modelled questions are present throughout both projects, and neither project runs long enough for anything else. This is worth stating as a pattern rather than a complaint about one paper, because the same asymmetry recurs across the corpus. Withdrawal is routine and unremarkable wherever the supporter is a person with other work to get back to: professional development, apprenticeship, research-practice partnerships, the tutoring literature the concept came from. It is rare wherever the support is a system, which has no reason to leave and every reason to stay. That suggests the constraint on fading may be economic before it is pedagogical — the same paper that fades its support to teachers notes in the next breath how large the investment required to sustain it was. Applying the framework twice, once to students and once to teachers, is the move that makes the asymmetry visible, and it is the author's own device.

items.lead: Two conditions on when the support does anything, both stated by the author and both recurring across this corpus. The first is non-use. cards.title: Interactivity and multimedia interfaces

rows.value: other
concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle

Kirsh takes apart the decision-cycle model of human-computer interaction — goal, plan, act, compare — and argues it misses most of what people actually do with their environments. Two of its assumptions fail: that we know our goals in advance, and that we have a test for when a goal has been reached. Working through a first encounter with photo-editing software he shows he had neither, and was instead developing a metric of goodness as he went along. He then adds three classes of action the model has no room for: preparation, arranging the environment so good possibilities are likely to be noticed; maintenance, keeping it in the state your plans assume; and complementary actions, moves that reorganise the world to suit how perception and memory actually work — rotating a Tetris piece on screen in 150 to 450 milliseconds rather than in the head in 700 to 1250. The paper is framed throughout by a question it does not answer: how to place enough scaffolding to guide learners in useful directions without predetermining where they will go.

medium · The argument is unusually careful for a theory paper: each claim against the decision cycle is made by exhibiting an activity the model cannot represent, and the complementary-action case is backed by the author's own Tetris timing study with real numbers. The three action classes are clean, mutually distinguishable and easy to look for in other work, which is what makes them reusable here. The limits are the kind a position paper has. The central evidence for the goal-discovery claim is a single first-person anecdote about learning a photo editor; the preparation and maintenance cases are observational vignettes — cooks, cabinetmakers, desks — cited rather than measured; and the paper appears in an instructional-science special issue while studying no learner and evaluating no learning environment. The author says as much in closing, noting he has not explained how a new theory of interactivity would affect learning environments. Carry the three action classes, the goal-discovery argument and the framing question; carry nothing as evidence about instruction.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This review's central design tension is stated here in 1997, in a learning-environment context, as an unsolved problem: place enough scaffolding to guide learners in useful directions without predetermining where they will go. It is worth quoting precisely because it names the trade rather than resolving it. The surrounding argument also says where the difficulty actually lives, which is more useful than the slogan. It is not that guidance is bad or that more of it is worse; it is that content which must be written before the learner arrives has to anticipate what they will need, and anticipation is what forecloses improvisation. That diagnosis lines up with what a later dissertation in this corpus concedes about itself — that software-encoded support is hard scaffolding, static and planned in advance — and gives the same conclusion a different route. Both say the constraint is structural rather than a matter of dosage. Note too the honest admission in the visibility principle: designers have largely succeeded at showing what actions are available and at giving immediate feedback, and have not succeeded at conveying consequences, because one action has multiple effects. Consequence is the part that would let someone judge for themselves.

quotes: One possible method of maintaining coherence without restrictive scripting is to place enough scaffolding in a learning environment to guide learners in useful directions without predetermining where they will go. This idea of indirectly pointing users in useful directions is an objective for all well designed multimedia interfaces, not only for learning environments. It is widely acknowledged (Norman, 1988; Hutchins, Hollan, and Norman, 1986) that good interfaces ought to satisfy the principle of visibility: (a) users should be able to ‘see’ the actions that are open to them at every choice point, (b) they should receive immediate feedback about the actions they have just taken – since few things upset computer users more than not knowing what a computer is doing when it seems to be churning unexpectedly, and (c) they should get timely and insightful information about the consequences of their actions. Designers have worked hard at ﬁnding ways of providing immediate feedback, and ways of exploiting natural mappings between the controls that can be acted on and the effects they have. Their goal is to make the function of knobs and buttons transparent. And indeed, they have been clever in discovering ways of satisfying (a) and (b). They have been less successful in satisfying (c) – primarily because in any interesting environment a single action may have multiple effects

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Why scripting fails for learning environments — Why the obvious approach fails: learning environments are supposed to let users discover phenomena, pose their own questions and change their minds adaptively, so users plan somewhat and improvise continuously; but in current multimedia the content must be scripted in advance and the links largely anticipated, which puts an undesirable limitation on improvisation, so the scripting model is inadequate.
quotes: Learning environments are supposed to create a context where users can discover interesting phenomena, pose their own questions,1 sketch out their own plans for deeper inquiry, and yet change their minds in an adap- tive and responsive manner depending on what they encounter. This means that while users probably engage in some degree of advance planning they are equally involved in continuous, online improvisation. This requirement, even in a weak form, poses a major problem for designers of effective learning environments. In current models of multimedia, content must be scripted in advance. The links that join pages must be anticipated – if not directly, then at least by being indexed to allow selection through online search methods or ‘pushed’ by selection criteria chosen in advance by the user. The information that is found in an environment, therefore, though not necessarily predetermined exhaustively, must be largely anticipated. This creates an undesirable limitation on improvisation. Evidently the scripting model is inadequate

quotes: Abstract. Multimedia technology offers instructional designers an unprecedented opportunity to create richly interactive learning environments. With greater design freedom comes com- plexity. The standard answer to the problems of too much choice, disorientation, and complex navigation is thought to lie in the way we design the interactivity in a system. Unfortunately, the theory of interactivity is at an early stage of development. After critiquing the decision cycle model of interaction – the received theory in human computer interaction – I present arguments and observational data to show that humans have several ways of interacting with their environments which resist accommodation in the decision cycle model. These additional ways of interacting include: preparing the environment, maintaining the environment, and reshaping the cognitive congeniality of the environment. Understanding how these actions simplify the computational complexity of our mental processes is the ﬁrst step in designing the right sort of resources and scaffolding necessary for tractable learner controlled learning environments

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: Kirsh supplies the mechanism behind a claim this corpus keeps meeting without explanation. Design research says the stopping rule and the evaluation function are personal, derived from immersion in a profession; Kirsh says why they cannot be anything else. The metric of goodness co-develops with knowledge of what is possible — as he learned what the software could do, he learned more about what he would accept — so the criterion is not something a competent person brings to a task and applies, but something the task produces in them. The distinction he draws in the endnotes sharpens it: an absolute test, like capturing the king, can be handed over intact, whereas a relational test is a threshold on a scale the person is still building. That yields a sharp prediction for this review. A support that supplies the adequacy test — a rubric, a quality score, a model that pronounces the work finished — does not merely save effort; it removes the occasion on which the person's own metric would have formed. And because nobody can miss a criterion they never developed, the failure is silent, invisible while the support is present, and detectable only once it is gone. That is the same shape as the reliance reversal found elsewhere in this corpus, arrived at from theory rather than from data.

In my case, I didn’t know how ﬁlters work, so I didn’t know that I could trace the edges of my image, and that I could sharpen them, and so on. Not knowing my options I, at ﬁrst, had quite a different idea of my overall goal. Certainly, I had little in the way of a plan. So the ﬁrst thing I did was to explore the range of what was possible. We know that workmen often change their manner of working when they change their tools. This is what I found too. After exploring the interface, and trying out the various ﬁlters one by one, then undoing their action, I was able to learn enough on-line – to learn enough just-in-time – to formulate an achievable goal and a plausible plan for attaining it. rows.value: (PDF p. 5) The decision cycle — The model under attack: interaction as a sophisticated feedback loop in which the user starts with a goal, formulates a small plan, executes it, and compares what happened with what was wanted.
quotes: The sense of interactivity which cognitive engineers have in mind when they say that an interface is interactive falls somewhere between the ﬁrst (the social sense) and the intermediate sense (the agent and its environment). For instance, in early accounts, interaction was thought to be a sophisticated feedback loop characterizable as a decision cycle. The user starts with a goal – an idea of what he wants to have happen – he then formulates a small plan for achieving this goal, say by twisting knobs, pressing buttons, dragging and dropping icons. He next executes the plan by carrying out the actions he had in mind; and ﬁnally he compares what happens with what he thought he wanted

quotes: This is a different orientation than the classical Cartesian view that we know things internally and just communicate fully intact thoughts in external vehicles. In this more dynamic interactionist view, the action of externally formulating thoughts is integral to internally formulating them too. We do not have a clear and distinct idea in mentalese awaiting expression in English or French. The very action of putting ‘thoughts’ in words helps to formulate them. If this is generally true about many of our actions it means that the goal of an interactive interface is not merely to allow users to do what they want to do, it must also allow them to discover what they want to do

rows.value: (PDF p. 10) Neither a goal image nor a test of adequacy — Kirsh supplies the mechanism behind a claim this corpus keeps meeting without explanation. Design research says the stopping rule is personal and acquired by immersion; Kirsh says why it cannot be otherwise. The metric of goodness co-develops with knowledge of what is possible — as he learned more about what the software could do, he learned more about what he would accept — so the criterion is not something a competent person has before starting and applies, but something the activity produces. That gives the review a sharp prediction. A support that supplies the adequacy test, whether as a rubric, a quality score or a model's judgment that the work is finished, does not simply save the person effort: it removes the occasion on which their own metric would have formed. And because the person cannot miss what they never developed, this failure is silent and shows up only when the support is gone.
quotes: Agents are assumed to have advance knowledge of their goals. They either know what the environment looks like when the goal state is achieved (as in tic tac toe), or they have an operational test for deciding whether a particular state qualiﬁes as a goal state. Both requirements are unrealistic. Consider my effort at creating a ﬁgure again. Did I have clear and distinct mental image of the ﬁnal ﬁgure I hoped to create? No. My understanding of how images can be transformed was too impoverished to be able to visualize what I wanted. Did I have an operational test of adequacy? Again I think not. I didn’t have an absolute test of adequacy3 because I didn’t really know the kind of ﬁgure I might hope for. I didn’t have a relative test of adequacy4 which indicated when a ﬁgure was good enough, because as I learned more about what was possible I learned more about what I would accept. I was developing a metric of goodness as I went along

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: This is the cleanest statement in the corpus of why externalisation is not storage. If putting a thought into words is part of forming it, then a support that produces the words is not transcribing something the person already had; it is doing a portion of the thinking, and the person finishes the episode without having done it. That separates two kinds of help which look identical from outside and which several papers here run together: a tool that gives you somewhere to externalise is doing something categorically different from a tool that produces the externalisation for you. The Tetris timings underwrite the first kind with numbers — rotating the piece on screen really is three to five times cheaper than rotating it in the head, the resulting mental state is the same, and nothing is lost by preferring it. That is worth holding onto, because it is a case where offloading is unambiguously good and the review should not be read as against offloading in general. But the argument does not carry over. What makes the Tetris move safe is that the player still does the deciding and the world merely computes a rotation faster than imagination can; the paper predates any technology that could supply the decision itself, so it offers no warrant for the second kind of help, and the distinction it draws is precisely the one needed to tell them apart.

quotes: Actions which re-order the world to make recall easier, to make perception and visualsearch easier, must be highly tuned to our internal processingstrate- gies. Let us call such actions complementary actions. Though rarely noticed they occur all the time. In scrabble, for instance, we ﬁnd players constantly shufﬂing their lettered tiles in the hope of creating letter combinations that trigger word recognition. Instead of mentally searching letter combinations they do part of the search in the world. The strategy is successful for some people because it lets them exploit the tendency to constantly look at the displayed arrangement. Complementary actions may be tightly coupled temporally with certain cognitive processes or they may be loosely coupled. Examples of tightly coupled actions emerged in our study of Tetris playing (Kirsh and Maglio, 1994). In that study we found that when trying to decide where to place a Tetris piece players preferred to rotate the ‘physical’ piece rather than rotate a mental image of the piece. Since it takes between 700 and 1250 ms6 to rotate a mental image of a Tetris piece, but only 150 ms to 450 ms to rotate the piece externally, a player can enter the same mental state (of knowing what a rotated piece looks like) faster and with less mental effort by performing an action externally rather than performing it mentally. No wonder subjects prefer to rotate pieces externally

In my case, I didn’t know how ﬁlters work, so I didn’t know that I could trace the edges of my image, and that I could sharpen them, and so on. Not knowing my options I, at ﬁrst, had quite a different idea of my overall goal. Certainly, I had little in the way of a plan. So the ﬁrst thing I did was to explore the range of what was possible. We know that workmen often change their manner of working when they change their tools. This is what I found too. After exploring the interface, and trying out the various ﬁlters one by one, then undoing their action, I was able to learn enough on-line – to learn enough just-in-time – to formulate an achievable goal and a plausible plan for attaining it. items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Here is a support-removal claim about a support nobody designed. The traces a worker leaves — papers spread out, places marked, lists made — are external structure built by the person doing the work, and removing them makes resuming hard. Everything else in this corpus studies support that someone provided; this is the inverse case, and it complicates the review's central question usefully. Dependence on self-built structure is not over-reliance, because the structure is a product of the competence rather than a substitute for it, and nobody would propose fading a researcher's desk. That gives a criterion worth carrying: ask whether the external structure was produced by the work or supplied to it. It also gives a design space. Preparation, maintenance and complementary action each name a kind of help with a different target — arranging things so good possibilities get noticed, keeping the environment in the state the person's plans assume, reorganising material to suit perception and memory — and none of the three supplies content or judgment. They raise the chance of a good outcome without narrowing what counts as one, which is what this paper's own framing question asks for, and almost nothing in the corpus does any of them. There is a warning attached, too: a tool that tidies a workspace is removing traces its user put there on purpose.

This setting up the environment to facilitate on-line choice and improvisation I call preparation... So a plan or program which depends on resources being in their expected places will be apt to fail unless someone in the agent's environment ensures that items find their way back to their 'proper' place.

We are not psychology subjects who must sit before screens watching one stimulus after another, each stimulus being independent of the subject’s own last action. Gibson made this point with respect to perception. It can also be made with respect to activity control. We are ourselves contributing architects of our own environments. What is done in the workplace at one moment has enduring effects on what may be done later. For instance, when we sit down at a desk to write an essay, we distribute our papers over the desktop, mark our place in books, take notes, make lists, and perform a host of sundry activities that might easily seem unworthy of mention were it not clear that if someone were to re-organize or remove any of these ‘traces’ left on our desk, our ﬂoor, and nearby bookshelves, we would ﬁnd it hard to pick up where we left off

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Agents shape their own environments; preparation defined — Preparation defined: agents leave reminders of prospective tasks, lay out equipment to constrain what they will later consider viable, and organise objects to make affordances prominent and more likely to be noticed; creative activity is both improvisational, because agents pursue possibilities as they emerge, and planful, because the skilled agent prepares the environment to maximise the chance of stumbling on good ideas — so although the agent may not know what he will create, arranging things a certain way puts him in a position to recognise unimagined possibilities, and this the author calls preparation.
quotes: and reminders of prospective tasks, lay out arrangements of equipment and resources to constrain what they will later consider to be viable actions, and organize objects to make their affordances more prominent, more likely to be noticed. In short, agents partially shape their environments of action as they go along. Revamping the decision cycle model The overhaul I propose to the decision cycle model begins by noting that the way we cope with badly formulated goals and plans is by relying on two facts: we tend to operate in the same workplace over time, and we are usually clever enough to ﬁgure out on-line what we must do next. If one observes most creative activity it is apparent that there are both planful and improvisa- tional elements to it. Creative activity is improvisational because agents are opportunistic – they pursue ideas and possibilities as they emerge, regardless of whether those ideas or possibilities have been anticipated. Creative activity is planful because the skilled agent tries to prepare the environment so that he or she has the greatest chance of stumbling on excellent ideas and possibili- ties. Thus, although an agent may not know, in advance, what he will create, he knows that by doing certain actions, or by arranging the environment in a certain way, or by laying out certain tools, he is doing the best he can to put himself in a position to recognize unimagined possibilities. This setting up the environment to facilitate on-line choice and improvisation I call preparation

rows.value: (PDF p. 13) Maintenance, and why the model cannot see it — Maintenance: environments drift toward disorder as a side effect of the actions we take, so a plan depending on resources being in their expected places will fail unless someone — the agent, an automatic mechanism, or others in the group — ensures items return to their proper place; the decision cycle cannot explain this because maintenance is done all the time and is not a sub-goal in most plans, and an observer watching a skilled agent sees actions such as clearing clutter that seem unconnected to the task and are not necessary to it, but help.
quotes: So a plan or program which depends on resources being in their expected places will be apt to fail unless someone in the agent’s environment ensures that items ﬁnd their way back to their ‘proper’ place. A certain state of the environment must be maintained or enforced, either by the agent itself, by some automatic mechanism, or by other members of the agent’s group (see Hammond, Converse, and Grass, 1995; Kirsh, 1996). The decision cycle account is not effective at explaining maintenance because maintenance is something we do all the time, it is not a sub-goal in most plans. As observers, if we were to watch the things which a skilled agent does in the course of performing some task, we would come across a variety of actions which at ﬁrst seem unconnected to the task. Clearing clutter is one of these. It is not necessary to ﬁnding what one wants, it just helps. It is good intellectual hygiene. The same might be said for putting objects back in their customary places, and so on. Resource management is a complex facet of activity in itself

cards.title: Modeling design exploration as co-evolution
cards.meta: 1996 · Computer-Aided Civil and Infrastructure Engineering · doi 10.1111/j.1467-8667.1996.tb00323.x · Route C

rows.value: S2CW-54437D49EEDE3934EB08F64C
other
concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle, measurement or method, failure or counterevidence

The paper models exploratory design as reciprocal co-evolution of problem definitions or evaluation criteria and candidate solutions, contrasting this with fixed-goal search. It derives two genetic-algorithm mechanisms—locally variable fitness within composite problem–solution genotypes and mutual evaluation between separate problem and solution populations—and relates criteria relaxation and precedent-based criteria emergence to expansion of what can be considered. These are proposed and illustrated computational mechanisms, not demonstrated user-level effects; changing goals also leaves convergence, termination, heterogeneous fitness comparison, and final usefulness judgments unresolved.

medium · The paper clearly develops and qualifies a conceptual computational framework, but it principally proposes and illustrates algorithms. Human-facing semantic-support transfer and all artifact, process, learning, and transfer effects remain untested.

cards.title: Usability Analysis of Visual Programming Environments: A ‘Cognitive Dimensions’ Framework

rows.value: S2BW-CDB8B4D038CF3C0F6130E1A8
other
concept or theory, lineage or history, framework or design space, design principle, primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

The paper operationalizes Green’s earlier Cognitive Dimensions framework as a broad-brush evaluation of visual programming environments. It grounds particular dimensions in programming-psychology and HCI work on notational structure, cognitive fit, progressive evaluation, and explicit description levels. Its theory position combines literature, prior empirical findings, craft knowledge, worked comparisons, and a small viscosity test; it is not presented as a finished cognitive model or prescriptive guideline.

medium · The conceptual mechanisms and page support are clear, and the paper includes concrete system comparisons, reported observations, and one measured viscosity test. Confidence is limited because evidence mixes prior literature, craft judgment, illustrative analysis, cited studies with sparse detail, and an N=1 straw test; several generalizations and novice implications remain untested.

cards.title: ON DISTINGUISHING EPISTEMIC FROM PRAGMATIC ACTION

rows.value: other
concept or theory, framework or design space, primary empirical

The paper that named epistemic action: a physical action taken not to advance the task but to make thinking about it cheaper. Kirsh and Maglio log keystrokes from Tetris players and find rotations and translations that a standard information-processing account has to call waste. A four-orientation piece should average 1.5 rotations if rotation only orients it; every piece is rotated more than half its possible rotations, rotation starts in earnest by 400 to 600 ms and occasionally before 100 ms, when the piece is not yet fully on screen. Their explanation is that pressing rotate is faster and more reliable than doing the same work in the head: a keypress turns a piece in about 100 ms, while their three-person pilot puts mental rotation at 800 to 1200 ms per quarter turn. In about 1 per cent of drops players walk a piece to the wall and back to count columns, and they do it from a mean height of 19 to 20 squares rather than the usual 13 to 16. Two things transfer. First, the definition: an epistemic action reduces the memory, the number of steps, or the error rate of mental computation, which is a general account of what a support does. Where Larkin and Simon explain how a representation can hold the same information yet be cheaper to think with, this paper makes the same move for actions: the world is not only read, it is rearranged so that it is easier to read. Second, an absence. Nothing here measures play with the external move taken away, no score or error rate is reported anywhere, and the size of the keystroke corpus is never stated.

medium · A strong conceptual contribution with thin empirical backing. The distinction, the three reductions and the process-dependence argument are clear and have been reused for thirty years, and the behavioural pattern is convergent: rotations exceed what orientation requires, they start before a decision could have been made, and use tracks informativeness in two separate behaviours. What bounds it is the reporting. The keystroke corpus has no stated sample size, no counts and no test statistics except one t test in Table 1; the word participant never appears; the only explicit n is three, in a pilot on a different task; the text and Table 1 disagree about the expert drop difference; and no outcome of any kind, no score, no error rate, no cleared lines, is reported anywhere. The authors flag two limits themselves: one action can serve both purposes, so the epistemic share is a residual, and their retrieval mechanism is an untested conjecture. Nothing measures what a player can do with the external move withdrawn, and the withdrawal vocabulary is absent from the text. Carry the definition, the contingency pattern and the process-dependence warning; not the milliseconds as effect sizes.

sections.title: 6 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The definition this review should carry, because it says what a support is for in terms that can be checked. A support is not defined by being an artefact, a tool or a piece of advice; it is defined by taking memory, steps or error off the person doing the work. That gives three questions to put to any support in the corpus, and a support that answers none of them is doing something else, such as motivating or constraining. The pairing with Larkin and Simon matters here. Larkin and Simon explain how two representations can hold the same information and still differ in what is cheap to infer; Kirsh and Maglio make the same move one step outward, to actions that change the representation in front of you. Together they say that a support can help without adding information, either by arranging what is there or by letting the person rearrange it. The second is the more demanding case, because the support is then partly built by its user during use, and a review that counts only designed artefacts will not see it.

rows.value: Epistemic actions -physical actions that make mental computation easier, faster, or more reliable- are external actions that an agent performs to change his or her own computational state, by reducing the memory involved in mental computation, the number of steps involved, or the probability of error.

quotes: Let us call actions whose primary function is to bring the agent closer to his or her physical goal pragmatic actions, to distinguish them from epistemic actions. As suggested earlier, existing literature on planning (Tate, Hendler, & Drummond, 1990), action theory (Bratman, 1987), and to a lesser extent decision theory (Chernoff & Moses, 1967) has focused almost exclusively on pragmatic actions

quotes: Typical epistemic actions found in everyday activities have a longer time course than those found in Tetris. These include familiar memory-saving actions such as reminding, for example, placing a key in a shoe, or tying a string around a finger; time-saving actions such as preparing the workplace, for example, partially sorting nuts and bolts before beginning an assembly task in order to reduce later search (a similar form of complexity reduction has been studied under the rubric “amortized complexity;” Tarjan, 1985); and information gathering activities such as exploring, for example, scouting unfamiliar terrain to help decide where to camp for the night

This is the action-side twin of Larkin and Simon's computational equivalence, which asks the same question of a representation held still. Kirsh and Maglio's addition is that the person can reach out and change the representation to make it cheaper, which means the support is partly built by its user in the moment of use.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The mechanism claim, and the one with numbers behind it. People will push work out of the head and into the world when the external route is cheaper, and the gap here is an order of magnitude. Three separate observations point the same way: the rotation count exceeds what orientation alone requires, rotation starts before a decision could have been reached, and the internal alternative is slow in a way that scales with how much of it is needed. For a review of supports the useful generalisation is that the deciding quantity is a comparison, not an absolute: a support is taken up when it beats the internal route on time, memory or reliability, which also predicts that a support slower than thinking will be ignored however well designed. What the paper does not show is that the external route produces better play. No score, error rate or line count appears anywhere.

rows.value: Zoids can be physically rotated 90 degrees in as few as 100 ms, whereas the authors estimate 800 to 1200 ms to rotate one mentally, so players rotate far more often than orientation requires and begin doing so before they could have chosen a placement.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The contingency result, and the most quietly useful thing in the paper. Support use is not a habit; it is switched on by the expected payoff of using it. The ambiguity contrast has a control built into it: pieces ambiguous in shape alone are already identifiable from the column they start in, so rotating them buys nothing, and those are precisely the pieces that attract no extra rotation. The drop-height result is the same shape of finding in a second behaviour, with the cost side moving too, since a check from high up wastes less. For a review of supports this predicts that uptake data are not a measure of a support's worth but of the local ratio between what it tells you and what it costs, and that a support which is ignored may simply be being used rationally. The limit is that payoff here is inferred from the structure of the task, never from a measured improvement.

rows.value: Players rotate a partly hidden piece more when it is ambiguous in both shape and position than when it is ambiguous in shape alone, and they perform the translate-to-wall verification routine from a mean height of about 19 to 20 squares against an ordinary drop of about 13 to 16, more often the higher the drop.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: A lineage claim with a consequence the paper does not draw. If expertise partly consists in knowing which external moves to make, then some of what the expert has is not inside the expert, and closing the external route removes part of the skill rather than merely slowing it down. items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: The methodological claim, and the one a synthesis should take most seriously because it constrains synthesis itself. Classical value-of-information lets you price a piece of knowledge without knowing anything about the reasoner. Kirsh and Maglio argue that epistemic actions break that: the worth of a rotation at 500 ms depends on which internal process is running at 500 ms. Generalised, this says a support has no context-free value, and that pooling effect sizes for a support across tasks pools quantities that are not commensurable. It also cuts the other way, as a warning about this paper's own reach: the authors close by asserting that the idea holds generally throughout all of human activity, which is an extrapolation from one game, and their own argument is the reason to distrust it.

rows.value: Simple economic models of cost and benefit fail for epistemic actions because the benefit depends in considerable detail on just what computations the agent is performing when undertaking the action, so planning cannot proceed without regard to the specific mechanisms of perception, attention and reasoning.

cards.title: Design prototypes: A knowledge representation schema for design

rows.value: S2CW-FF27B9B16CE52C1800EB17F5
other
framework or design space, concept or theory, design principle

The paper that gave design research its function-behaviour-structure framework. Gero starts from the observation that there is no direct transformation from what you want an artifact to do to what the artifact is, and proposes behaviour as the bridge: function becomes expected behaviour, expected behaviour selects structure, and the structure's actual behaviour is compared back. Around that he builds design prototypes, a schema holding function, structure, expected and actual behaviour together with the relational, qualitative, computational and context knowledge that connects them. Two things make it worth carrying here. He calls structure the syntax of a design and function its semantics, and says a CAD database holds only the syntax, so a translation to the semantics is needed — the earliest clean statement in this corpus of what a semantic layer over an artifact is for. And he raises design fixation against his own proposal, then answers it structurally rather than dismissing it.

medium · This is a proposal, not a study, and it should be carried as one: there is no experiment, no participant, no evaluation and no measurement of any kind anywhere in eleven pages. What raises it above an ordinary position paper is the quality of the argument. The need for the schema is derived rather than asserted, from the absence of a direct function-to-structure transformation; the knowledge kinds are each given a job; the routine, innovative and creative distinction is defined operationally against a state space rather than by intuition; and the author raises the strongest objection to his own design, fixation, and answers it with a specific structural mechanism. Against that, the worked example is a single window-design prototype, the schema's claims about matching how designers think rest on one citation to a design-studies book, and the anti-fixation answer is an argument with nothing behind it. Carry the framework, the syntax-semantics framing and the fixation exchange; treat every claim about what the schema does to a designer as untested.

sections.title: 4 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is the earliest clean statement in the corpus of what a semantic layer over an artifact is for, and it is worth quoting whenever the review needs to say why annotating a design or a document is not decoration. A CAD file holds the syntax: the elements and their relations, with nothing anywhere saying what any part is for. Anything beyond drawing pictures needs a translation to the semantics, and that translation lives in the designer's head unless something puts it into the artifact. Every annotation-overlay system in this corpus is answering the problem Gero states here, decades earlier and more precisely than most of them state it themselves. Two details are worth keeping. The semantics is function — the purpose, the why — not a richer description of the thing, so a semantic layer that only adds detail is not doing this job. And the whole apparatus exists because there is no direct route from what you want to what you build: behaviour is inserted as the bridge because nothing shorter works. A support that promises to map goals onto artifacts without that middle term is, on this account, either doing catalogue lookup or not designing.

rows.value: There is, however, no direct transformation capable of achieving this result... More generally, no direct transformation between function and structure exists, which leaves a requirement for an indirect transformation between function and structure... The use of this representation effectively provides a translator between structure, which can be seen as the syntax of a design, and function, which can be treated as the semantics of a design... traditional computer-aided design systems produce a design description in their databases that maps onto the syntax of a design. For these databases to be useful for other than purposes of graphic representation, a translation to the semantics of the design is needed.

(PDF p. 3) Why there is no direct transformation — The gap the whole schema exists to fill: designing transforms a set of functions into a design description, but there is no direct transformation capable of achieving this; the design description represents structure, drafting systems only turn structure into description, and the occasional direct function-to-structure mapping is catalogue lookup, which the author says is not designing. What remains is a requirement for an indirect transformation.
quotes: The purpose of designing is to transform function F (where F is a set) into a design description D in such a way that the artifact being described is capable of producing these functions. For example, when designing win- dows, some of the functions include the pro- vision of daylight, control of ventilation, and access to a view. The design description would take the form of drawings and notes. Thus, a naive model of design is F +D, where + is some transformation. There is, however, no direct transformation capable of achieving this result. A design description represents the artifact’s elements and their relationships; it is labeled structure S. In the window design example, the artifact’s elements are the glazing and the frame and their topology. Computer-aided drafting systems have become the means by which structure is transformed into a design description; that is, S+ D. Another model of design is F AS. Here, a transformation does occasionally exist in the form of a direct mapping between function and structure, often termed catalog Iookup. This transformation occurs at the ele- ment level of an artifact and is not considered designing. More generally, no direct transfor- mation between function and structure exists, which leaves a requirement for an indirect transformation between function and structure

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Structure is syntax, function is semantics — The syntax and semantics framing: the schema separates knowledge from the processes that operate on it and effectively provides a translator between structure, which can be seen as the syntax of a design, and function, which can be treated as its semantics; the author notes that traditional computer-aided design systems produce database descriptions that map onto the syntax, and that for those databases to serve any purpose beyond graphic representation a translation to the semantics of the design is needed.
quotes: Design requires a representation framework that has sufficient expressive power to cap- ture the nature of the concepts that support design processes. The use of a knowledge rep- resentation schema such as design prototypes provides such a framework. It separates the knowledge from the computational processes that operate on it. The use of this representa- tion effectively provides a translator between structure, which can be seen as the syntax of a design, and function, which can be treated as the semantics of a design. Such an articula- tion is useful not only in the production of designs but also in their analysis and evalua- tion. For example, traditional computer-aided design systems produce a design description in their databases that maps onto the syntax of a design. For these databases to be useful for other than purposes of graphic representa- tion, a translation to the semantics of the design is needed

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) Behaviour as the bridge, and reformulation — The bridge: function is transformed into expected behaviour, expected behaviour drives the selection and combination of structure through knowledge of what behaviours structures produce, and synthesised structures then produce their own behaviours, which can be a useful superset of what was expected; that surplus can widen the expected behaviours and through them the function being designed for, and an unsatisfactory comparison that structure cannot fix forces reformulation.
quotes: Another model of design is F+B, Be +S@,). Here, the function is transformed to expected behavior. This expected behavior is used in the selection and combination of structure based on a knowledge of the behaviors produced by this structure. This process is called synthesis. When structures are synthesized, they pro- duce their own behaviors, which can be a useful superset of the expected behaviors. This process can change the range of expected behaviors and through them the function being designed for, leading to a reformulation. Reformulation can also occur when the evalu- ation of the comparison between the behav- ior of the structure and the expected behavior is unsatisfactory and cannot be made satisfac- tory by manipulating the structure. This reformulation leads to a change in expected behavior

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) What design is for — The framing: designers are change agents whose goal is to improve the human condition through physical change; design exists because the world does not suit us, and where science begins from a description of the world and works towards causes and purposes, design runs the other way, positing functions and producing descriptions of artifacts able to deliver them.
quotes: Designers are change agents in society. Their goal is to improve the human condition in all its aspects through physical change. Although design for many continues to Articles remain a mysterious activity, it has been Designers are recognized as an change agents important activity for more than 4000 in society. years In approxi- mately 2000 B c , Hammurabi, king of Babylon, enacted a law that both recog- nized design and made it dangerous (figure 1). Design research has a number of goals, including a better understanding of design, the development of tools to aid human designers, and the potential automation of some design tasks. Design appears to be carried out differently from the way we are taught to understand the world, which is largely derived from the Greek view of the world. Science has been developed as a means of attempting to explain and understand the world around us. It begins with a description of the world (which in itself is not a trivial act to produce) and some behaviors and attempts to produce causal dependencies between them. Science then can be used to attempt to produce a purpose for the world. Design exists because the world around us does not suit us, and the goal of designers is to change the world through the creation of artifacts

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) The kinds of knowledge a prototype separates — The contents of the schema: function, structure, expected behaviour and actual behaviour held separately, plus relational knowledge making the dependencies between their variables explicit as a dependency network, qualitative knowledge giving the effects of modifying structure variables on behaviour and function along with normal value ranges, computational knowledge supplying the quantitative counterpart, and context knowledge identifying exogenous variables whose values must come from outside.
quotes: A design prototype separates function (F), structure (S), expected behavior (B,) and actual behavior (B,). It also stores relational knowledge between them (KJ as well as qual- itative knowledge (K,), computational knowl- edge (K,), and context knowledge (I$,). Relational knowledge provides and makes explicit the dependencies between the vari- ables in the function, structure, and behavior categories and can take the form of a depen- dency network. Relational knowledge identi- fies the relevant variables in going from function to behavior and behavior to func- tion and from behavior to structure and structure to behavior. Relational knowledge allows for the specialization of the informa- tion in a prototype to a specific design situa- tion (see Designing Using Design Prototypes). Qualitative knowledge (a subset of qualitative reasoning) is an adjunct to relational knowl- edge and provides information on the effects of modifying values of structure variables on behavior and function. Included here are the normal ranges of values of variables found in the generalization. Qualitative knowledge can be used to guide any decision-making process. Computational knowledge is the quantitative counterpart of qualitative knowledge and specifies symbolic or mathematical relation- ships among the variables. Computational knowledge is used to determine values of variables

quotes: Design requires a representation framework that has sufficient expressive power to cap- ture the nature of the concepts that support design processes. The use of a knowledge rep- resentation schema such as design prototypes provides such a framework. It separates the knowledge from the computational processes that operate on it. The use of this representa- tion effectively provides a translator between structure, which can be seen as the syntax of a design, and function, which can be treated as the semantics of a design. Such an articula- tion is useful not only in the production of designs but also in their analysis and evalua- tion. For example, traditional computer-aided design systems produce a design description in their databases that maps onto the syntax of a design. For these databases to be useful for other than purposes of graphic representa- tion, a translation to the semantics of the design is needed

rows.value: medium · The argument is clear and has been influential, but it is an untested framework proposal illustrated by one example.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the most useful paragraph in the paper, because the author raises the strongest objection to his own proposal and answers it with a mechanism rather than a reassurance. The objection is precisely the risk this review keeps finding: give someone a worked description tied to a set of goals and they will struggle to produce anything else. His answer is architectural. The schema never stores a link from function to structure; it stores each separately and connects them only through behaviour, so the association built from experience remains reachable while the direct nexus is broken. Whether that actually prevents fixation is untested here and, as far as this review has found, untested anywhere — which is a gap worth naming, because it is a cheap experiment and it has been available for thirty-five years. What makes it worth carrying regardless is the kind of proposal it is. Almost every answer to over-reliance in this corpus concerns quantity or timing: give less, take it away later, give it only on request. This one concerns the internal shape of the support — what it stores and what it declines to store — and says the same information can be made available in a form that binds or a form that does not. That is a design axis the corpus barely has.

rows.value: It is tempting to view the design prototype schema as producing a rigid transformation between function and structure that is incapable of providing the basis for anything more than parameterized design. Certainly, it can be argued that this schema readily supports the notion of design fixation, where the provision of a design description for a specified set of functions limits the designer's ability to produce structures other than those found in the design description. However, the delineation of function from structure and their connection through behavior breaks the function-structure nexus and still maintains the association derived from experience.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The routine, innovative and creative ladder is the only axis in this corpus that treats working outside the support as a named category rather than as the support failing. Each rung is defined by what the designer does to the state space the prototypes supply: stay inside it, stretch the ranges within it, or add variables that move it. Read against this review's question, that is a scale of independence from the support, defined structurally rather than by how much help was given. Two consequences follow. First, the narrowing is admitted as the mechanism, not apologised for as a side effect: the author says outright that partitioning reduces the space of potential designs and that routine work produces a space substantially smaller than the possible one. That is more honest than most of the corpus, and it matches what users of annotation tools elsewhere here describe as being funnelled. Second, and more awkward, it undermines the usual measurement. If the support supplies the state space, then work done well inside it is routine by construction, and no amount of competence displayed there says anything about whether the person could leave — which is exactly what nearly every study in this corpus measures and then reports as learning.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Made in passing, this is the strongest statement in the corpus of why withdrawing a support is not the inverse of supplying one. What experience installs is a connection between what a thing is for and what it is made of, and once learned it is difficult to unlearn. If that holds, then the effect of a support that supplies such connections does not stop when the support does: the person carries the associations, apt or not, into every later problem. Two consequences matter for this review. The failure modes are asymmetric — failing to install a connection is recoverable, installing the wrong one is not, or not easily — so the cost of a support that teaches a bad association is not bounded by the length of the intervention. And it explains why the fixation worry has teeth in this paper specifically: Gero's schema is in the business of installing exactly these connections, at scale and from generalised cases, which is why he has to answer for it. He offers no evidence for the irreversibility claim; he builds the architecture around it anyway.

quotes: A prevalent and pervasive view of designing is that it can be modeled using variables and decisions made about what values should be taken by these variables. The activity of designing is carried out with the expectation that the designed artifact will operate in the natural world and the social world. These worlds impose constraints on the variables and their values; so, design could be described as a goal-oriented, constrained, decision- making activity. However, design distinguish- es itself from other similarly described activities not only by its domain but also by additional necessary features. Designing involves exploration, exploring what variables might be appropriate. The process of explo- ration involves both goal variables and deci- sion variables. In addition, designing involves learning: Part of the exploration activity is learning about emerging features as a design proceeds. Finally, design activity occurs within two contexts: the context within which the designer operates and the context produced by the developing design itself. The designer’s perception of what the context is affects the implication of the context on the design. The context shifts as the designer’s perceptions change. Design activity can be now characterized as a goal-oriented, con- strained, decision-making, exploration, and learning activity that operates within a con- text that depends on the designer

In addition, designing involves learning: Part of the exploration activity is learning about emerging features as a design proceeds. Finally, design activity occurs within two contexts: the context within which the designer operates and the context produced by the developing design itself. The designer’s perception of what the context is affects the implication of the context on the design. The context shifts as the designer’s perceptions change. Design activity can be now characterized as a goal-oriented, con- strained, decision-making, exploration, and learning activity that operates within a con- text that depends on the designer
