cards.title: Why a diagram is (sometimes) worth ten thousand words
cards.meta: 1987 · Cognitive science · doi 10.1016/s0364-0213(87)80026-5 · Route B · Route C

rows.value: other
concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle

The paper that explains why an external representation can help without telling you anything new. Its central distinction is between two representations being informationally equivalent, meaning each could be reconstructed from the other, and computationally equivalent, meaning anything easy to infer from one is also easy to infer from the other. Diagrams and sentences can be the first without being the second. Three mechanisms are named: a diagram groups information that gets used together, so there is no search for the pieces an inference needs; it indexes by position, so elements do not have to be matched by symbolic label; and it supports perceptual inferences people make almost for free. That is a general account of how a support changes work without changing what is known, and it applies well beyond diagrams. The important half is the qualification in the title. A diagram helps only if it was built to group the right things, only if the perceptual inferences it happens to support are the useful ones, and only for a person who already holds the operations that read it. The authors explain the standard complaint that students refuse to draw diagrams by saying that students lacking those operations will find diagrams largely useless. There is no experiment here: the argument runs through worked problems in physics, geometry and economics.

medium · This is an analytical paper, and it should be weighed as one. There is no experiment, no participants and no measurement anywhere in it. The argument is carried by computational models of two informationally equivalent problem representations and by worked examples in physics, geometry and economics, with the claim being that the diagrammatic version supports the same inferences at lower cost. That is a demonstration of possibility rather than a finding about people, and the authors are careful about the difference: they flag their remarks on mental imagery as speculation and say psychological research would be needed to test it. Two further limits. The examples are chosen by the authors, so nothing bounds how often the advantage holds in practice; and the definitions of sentential and diagrammatic are stipulated for the analysis, which makes them precise but not obviously the categories people use. Carry the distinction, the three mechanisms and the preconditions as an explanatory framework of unusual clarity, and do not carry anything here as an effect size or a rate.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The distinction that makes a large class of supports intelligible. Two things can contain exactly the same information and differ enormously in what a person can get out of them, because the cost of drawing an inference is a separate quantity from what is present. That means a support need not add information to change what someone can do, and conversely that describing a support by what it tells you will miss most of what it does. For this review it supplies the vocabulary for a recurring puzzle: why rearranging what someone already has, a checklist, a visualisation, a diff view, a set of prompts, can change performance markedly. The answer here is that the rearrangement changes search cost, recognition cost and what has to be computed to be made explicit. It also sets up the sharper claim, since if the advantage is computational rather than informational then it depends entirely on the operations the person brings, which is where the paper ends up.

rows.value: Two representations are informationally equivalent if all of the information in the one is also inferable from the other, and vice versa. Each could be constructed from the information in the other. Two representations are computationally equivalent if they are informationally equivalent and, in addition, any inference that can be drawn easily and quickly from the information given explicitly in the one can also be drawn easily and quickly from the information given explicitly in the other, and vice versa.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: Three mechanisms, stated about diagrams and not really about diagrams. Grouping what gets used together so that nothing has to be hunted for; indexing by position so that elements need not be matched by name; and pushing work onto perception, which is nearly free. Any external artifact either has these properties or lacks them, which makes this a way of saying what a particular support does rather than that it helped. The paper also shows the properties being engineered rather than being lucky: the convention that a free-body diagram contains all the forces on one system exists precisely to make localisation hold, and novices break it by putting a force in the wrong body's diagram; expert labelling is minimal, with the two pictures drawn on top of each other so no correspondence has to be tracked; and arrow lengths are drawn to scale so the situation can be checked at a glance. Each of those is a design decision with a reason attached, which is rarer in this corpus than it should be.

Diagrams typically use location to group information about a single element, avoiding the need to match symbolic labels. Diagrams automatically support a large number of perceptual inferences, which are extremely easy for humans.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The most important claim in the paper for a review of supports, and the one usually left out when it is cited. If the advantage of an external representation is computational rather than informational, then it is entirely contingent on the operations the person already holds: the diagram is a place to run knowledge you have, not a substitute for knowledge you lack. So a support given to someone without the relevant competence is not weaker, it is useless, which is a far stronger statement than diminishing returns. Two consequences follow that matter well beyond diagrams. Non-use gets a rational explanation rather than a motivational one: the students refusing to draw diagrams are correct, because for them the diagram does not help, and the same reading is available whenever a support goes unused by the people it was built for. And the burden shifts, since the solver also needs to know how to construct a good representation, which is a second competence nobody supplies. The claim is argued, not tested; the alphabet and chess-notation cases are illustrations, and no experiment in this paper varies a person's productions and measures what a diagram then buys them.

rows.value: The advantages of diagrams, in our view, are computational... But this means that diagrams are useful only to those who know the appropriate computational processes for taking advantage of them. Furthermore, a problem solver often also needs the knowledge of how to construct a good diagram that lets him take advantage of the virtues we have discussed. ... Because a representation is useful only if one has the productions that can use it, we can readily understand the common complaint of physics professors that students refuse to draw diagrams or don't appreciate their value. If the students lack productions for making physics inferences from diagrams, they may not only fail to appreciate the value of diagrams, but will find them largely useless.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The word in the title that gets dropped when this paper is cited. The medium guarantees nothing: a diagram is capable of grouping what an inference needs and may fail to, and it inevitably supports some easy perceptual inferences which may be beside the point. Both failures are properties of the particular artifact rather than of the category it belongs to, so the same distinction that explains a good diagram's advantage explains a bad one's absence, and the authors say that this is probably why some diagrams help and others do not. For this review the transferable form is a warning about how supports get evaluated. Comparing a class of support against its absence answers a question nobody should be asking, because the variation within the class is where the effect lives. Two supports of the same kind, one grouping what is used together and one not, should behave completely differently, and a study that pools them will find a small average effect and learn nothing. This is also the paper's own hedge on its worked examples, since every one of them was chosen to have the properties.

Similarly, although every diagram supports some easy perceptual inferences, nothing ensures that these inferences must be useful in the problem-solving process. Failing to use these features is probably part of the reason why some diagrams seem not to help solvers, while others do provide significant help.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: A guess about the relation between the external artifact and the internal one, labelled as a guess. If mental images have the same localisation properties and are read by the same operators, then the external diagram and the internal one are the same machinery in two places, working in concert. That would be a strong answer to the question this review keeps returning to, of what happens to a capability when the external support is present, because on that account nothing is displaced: the person is running their own operations in a roomier memory. The authors flag it as untested and say much difficult research would be needed, which is a fair position and worth recording precisely because the claim is so often assumed. Note also what the speculation does not say. It offers no account of a person who has come to rely on the external version, and no reason to think the two memories stay in concert if the external one is always available. The scoped psychological commitments the paper does make are minimal and, forty years on, still uncontroversial: attention can focus on part of a diagram, cues there can be detected, and those cues retrieve operators from memory.

But much difficult psychological research, the exact character of which we can only dimly perceive, will be required to test this hypothesis. Until then it must remain a speculation.
